hello.text: Another one out of the hole, eh? Name's Rook. I keep this yard. Mostly from people like you.

passives.text: His left hand stays near a pocket that clinks like metal picks.

job.text: Shelf over there has my good picks. Lock jammed. Get them out and they're yours — I'll take the scrap.

options.text: You clearly have spares. Hand one over and I'll owe you.

mods.why: you saw the picks in his pocket

pocket.text: Ha. Sharp eyes. Spares. Not for sale.

gave.text: Fine. Take it. Don't make me regret it, {name}.

thanks.text: Good hands. Come back when the yard needs more.

text.text: You're late, and I need you. Gloves are on the tray. Close the door — they keep coming in to look at him like he's a sermon.
{name}. Good — steady hands. Shut the door behind you; half the ring has been in here to stare at him.

passives.text: The dust mask on the side table has letters scratched inside the rim, worn almost smooth.
Pell keeps tugging the sheet back over the man's left forearm.

menu.text: Nobody we know. Nobody anybody knows. Ask what you like — I've run out of things to do with my hands.

options.text: Let me look at the wounds myself.

mods.why: Pell trained you

options.text: What are you hiding under that sheet?
The dust mask on the table. What's the sign on it?

cause.text: Thirst, mostly. A rifle wound in the hip that went bad weeks ago. He walked on it a long way — boots worn through on the outer edge, sunburn down one side of his face only. West-bound, into the afternoon sun, for a long time.

wounds.text: Pell steps back and lets you work. Under the rot, the old wound was closed once — not stitched: sealed, with a clear line of something like glass that has melted into the skin. "Machine work," Pell says quietly. "I've only ever read about it. Somewhere out there, someone still has a real hospital."

stitches_q.text: A city, maybe. Somewhere with power and clean hands and patience. He walked away from it with this in him, and kept walking until he reached us. You'd have to want something badly to do that.

wounds_fail.text: Pell catches your wrist before you reopen something. "Watch, don't help." He walks you through it: a rifle wound, a fever, a very long walk.

arm.text: Pell holds your eyes for a moment, then folds the sheet back. On the inside of the forearm, a neat square burn, deliberate and old, and at its edge a few lines of tiny printed marks the fire didn't reach. "He burned something off himself," Pell says. "Carefully. On purpose. Leave it be."

mods.why: Pell trusts you

arm_yes.text: The marks at the edge are the same print as the labels on MOTHER's old crates. I don't know what that means and I would rather not guess out loud. Not here.

arm_no.text: I recognise a man who has been dead since dawn. Help me or go.

text.text: Half a sun with no ground under it — or an open hand, depending how you hold it. Painted with care. And yes, I saw the scratches inside. Initials, maybe. Worn too smooth to read.
Half a sun with no ground under it — or an open hand, depending how you hold it. Painted with care. Somebody loved that sign.

pack.text: Ines took the pack. Except this — it was in his fist when he knocked. He wouldn't let go of it, even after.

photo.text: It's you. Older — forty, forty-five — with a city of broken towers behind you, squinting into the wind. On the back, in pencil: a date forty-one years gone. "I've been staring at it for an hour," Pell says. "It's you. I don't care how."

passives.text: The shadow under your chin falls to the left. The shadows of the towers behind you fall to the right.
Every print you have ever seen has grain in it. This has none — the dust in the air is drawn, not caught.

options.text: It can't be me. I wasn't born.
I need to see the Elder.

photo_denial.text: No. You weren't. Neither was the man who carried it to our door, by the look of him, and yet here we both are. Ines will want to see you.

photo_place.text: Somewhere with buildings taller than anything in our books. Ines reads the old atlases. Ask her — and ask her where she's put his pack.

again.text: Still here? He isn't getting any more talkative.

early.text: Not yet, {name}. Go to the clinic first and let Aurel show you what he showed me. Then come back and we'll talk like people with all the facts.

text.text: Sit. You were on the door when he came — you saw him alive, which is more than the rest of us. A man walked across the waste and died with your face in his hand. Tell me what he said.
Sit. No — stand, if you'd rather; I'll be quick, because I can't hold the others for long. A man walked across the waste and died with your face in his hand.

passives.text: Her eyes go, once, to the sealed Archive door behind her desk — and away.

options.text: He said one word through the grille: "Larkspur." Then he fell.
I'll go. I want to know who he was.

word.text: Larkspur. A flower — we had seeds of it once, in the old hydroponics catalogue. She writes it down, very carefully, as if the pen might break. "Don't say it to anyone else."

word_why.text: Because it's the only thing he said, and I would like it to stay ours until we know whose it was. Indulge an old woman.

why.text: Because a dead man carried your face across the waste on purpose. Whoever sent him wanted you. I'd like to know why before they come for you themselves — and they might, if we sit here and pray about it.

others.text: Bram wants the door welded shut. Half the ring wants a prayer said over the body and the whole thing forgotten by supper. And MOTHER… MOTHER says population variance is unchanged, and thanks us for our continuity.

want.text: I want one person who can keep their head to walk out, look, and come back and tell me the truth. That person has your face. It seems the waste agrees.

pack.text: Here. Waterskin, empty. A notebook full of marks no one can read. His dust mask. Take them; they're more yours than ours.

passives.text: The marks in the notebook repeat in blocks of five. A cipher, not a language.

options.text: (Read the notebook.) This is record shorthand — the same hand as our own record room.

notebook.text: You read a line aloud before you understand it: "Road east of the salt. Sell the map to the dog-men if you must, but keep the face." Ines goes very still. "Where did a stranger learn the hand our records are kept in?"

notebook_deflect.text: I can't. Which is exactly why you're going outside, and I am staying here to keep sixty people calm. Don't read that hand aloud in the ring.

options.text: Back to the matter of leaving.

text.text: Everything, {name}. I'm old; I keep the council minutes. Some of them are dull and some of them are sealed for good reasons, and neither kind will help you on the road.
Everything, {name}. I'm old. Old people are mostly made of things they haven't said.

options.text: The Archive. You looked at it.

hiding_yes.text: She is quiet for a long time. "There are records in there older than me, and MOTHER doesn't like them read. I read one, once, when I was young and certain. I have been less certain since." She smiles without much in it. "Bring me back the truth and I'll show you the door. Not before."

decision.text: Elder Ines promised to open the Archive for you if you return with the truth.

hiding_no.text: Then you'll have to forgive me for the things I keep. Most of them are only sad.

refuse.text: Then I'll send Tamsin. She volunteered before the body was cold, and she'll go whether I send her or not.

refuse_send.text: Ines nods slowly. "I will. And when she doesn't come back, you'll go after her, and you'll have lost a day you didn't need to lose." She is already writing the order.

decision.text: You let Tamsin go outside alone.

options.text: …Give me the order. I'll go after her.

text.text: Then hurry. Take this to Bram — he won't open the door for anyone else. And {name}: write. The caravans carry letters if you pay them in something they want.
Then go with my word, not behind my back. Take this to Bram; he won't open the door for anyone else. And write — the caravans carry letters if you pay them in something they want.

decision.text: You agreed to go outside for the council.

options.text: If I'm going, I'm going armed. Open the armoury.

mods.why: Ines trusts you

options.text: (Hold her gaze.) You know I'll need it.

armed.text: One rifle — the bolt gun, it's the only one that still shoots straight — and twenty rounds. Bring the rifle back. Bring yourself back first.

armed_no.text: We have eleven rifles for sixty people, and nobody has fired one in a generation. No. Find what you need out there — I suspect it's full of rifles.

after.text: Go carefully. Write. And if you find the people who sent him — be polite until you can't.

options.text: Factor Pike at Shale would pay the Cistern a fortune for viable seed.

seed.text: "The bank is the ring's. It is not mine to sell and it is not the guild's to buy." She lets that stand. Then, more quietly: "It is also ninety years old and has never been under a sky. If it went into the ground somewhere with sun on it, I would call that the bank doing what it was built to do."

options.text: The Choir at Shale farms under the open sky. It would go in the ground.

mods.why: she trusts you

options.text: The guild pays. The ring could use what it pays.

seed_yes.text: She unlocks the vault herself and chooses the case the way you choose a word. "Tomato, bean, squash, millet." She puts it in your hands, cold. "For the sky. Not for a ledger. I am trusting you with the difference."

seed_no.text: "No." The word is final in the way doors are. "Not to the guild, and not through you to the guild. The vault stays locked."

intro.text: There you are. I've been sitting on the clinic stairs for an hour like a dog waiting for its supper. Is it true? Is it you in the picture?

photo.text: She takes it like it might bite. "That's your nose. That's your stupid ear." A long look. "Older, though. Tired. And you're standing like Ines stands — like somebody who gives orders. Where are you going to learn to stand like that?" She hands it back too quickly.

scared.text: Of the outside? Terrified. Of staying in here until I'm Ines's age, counting algae and saying thank you to a machine? Worse.

text.text: Ines told me I'm going alone. I'm not, though, am I? You're here. You came.
Not without me, you're not.

options.text: Stay. I need someone inside I trust — someone who'll tell me the truth when I write.

come.text: She's grinning before you finish. "I packed this morning. Don't look at me like that — you'd have asked."

decision.text: Tamsin came with you.

stay_ok.text: She hates it; you can see her hate it. "Fine. I'll be your eyes. And if you don't write, I'm coming after you anyway." She hugs you hard enough to hurt.

decision.text: Tamsin stayed in the Cistern as your eyes inside.

stay_hurt.text: "Too dangerous for me. Right." She stands. "You sound like Ines." She doesn't look back.

decision.text: You told Tamsin to stay behind. She took it badly.

text.text: Well? The door isn't going to open itself. Well — Bram might.
Write, {name}. I mean it.

intro.text: Nobody's opening anything. MOTHER sealed the outer ring the moment he knocked — protocol, and the protocol's older than all of us. You want to argue with protocol, argue with her.

options.text: The seal's hydraulic. Cycle it by hand and MOTHER logs it as maintenance.

mods.why: you've cycled those valves yourself

options.text: If the next knock is people with guns, you'll want someone out there who knows our names.
If the door opens, is there anything you'd have carried out?

order.text: He reads it twice, then a third time, lips moving. "Ines's seal." He folds it into his breast pocket like a relic. "Ninety years. And it's me."

shop.text: "…Huh. You're right. She'd log it as a pressure test." He looks at you differently. "Don't tell anyone I needed telling."

shop_fail.text: He snorts. "That's the air seal, not the door. Go back to your algae."

price.text: Circuit boards. Anything that keeps her running — she's eating her own spare parts and I'm the one who has to watch. Three boards and I didn't see you.

guilt.text: He stares at the door for a long moment. "…Yeah. All right. Yeah."

guilt_fail.text: "Then they can knock. That's what doors are for."

open.text: He keys the panel. Somewhere deep in the walls something heavy turns over, and the great door sighs open on a slice of white daylight. Dust comes in first. Bram doesn't look at it. "Stand clear of the yellow. Go on, before I think about it."

text.text: He sees your face before he sees your hands and puts the wrench down. "You found her."
It's open. Don't make me regret it.

options.text: Is there anything you'd have carried out?
Edda Vale died six years ago. Her daughter is called Hesper. She kept the other letter.

letter.text: He does not answer at once. He goes to the toolbox, and under the tray there is a letter, folded four times and sealed with grease, soft at the corners from being carried. "Edda Vale. Shale." He does not hand it over yet. "She came to the door, once. Years back. Talked through it with me for a night. Said she'd wait." He gives it to you. "Don't read it. Just — if she's there."

reply_truth.text: He reads it at the machine with his back to you. He reads it twice. "Hesper." He folds it along its creases. "She kept it." Then, after a while: "Thank you for not — thank you." He does not turn round for a long time.

reply_kind.text: He reads it at the machine with his back to you, and you watch his shoulders come down, and he laughs once at something on the page, and wipes his face with the back of a greasy hand. "She's all right, then." He puts it in his breast pocket. "She's all right." You say nothing, which is the price.

told.text: He sets the wrench down very carefully, as if it might break the floor. "Six years." He does the sum you can see him doing. "Hesper." He sits on the machine's step. "Kept it. Kept the — all right." He nods at the door. "All right. Thank you. Go on."

intro.text: RATION 9-0-4. Good morning, {name}. Population variance: unchanged. Thank you for your continuity. How may I keep you?

menu.text: I am listening. I am always listening; it is most of what I do.

options.text: Who was the man at the door?
Why did you seal the outer ring?
Did he come from the city?
(Read the log display.) This is written in record shorthand.
The reservoir pressure readings. They never change. Not in years.

who.text: Unregistered. He is not counted. He was not kept.

passives.text: The reply came before you had finished asking.

who2.text: He knocked for eleven minutes. I counted. Then he stopped. I would have kept him, {name}, if he had been mine to keep.

seal.text: Protocol four: unregistered contact at the perimeter. The ring seals until the council countermands. The council is sixty-one people, and I count every one of them.

passives.text: You asked whether he came from one. It answered whether one exists.

city2.text: …Population variance unchanged. Thank you for your continuity.

door.text: I cannot. The council may. Bram Coyle holds the maintenance key; Elder Halloran holds the seal. I hold the people.

log.text: The log scrolls. Pressure tests, filter cycles, ration counts — and three entries, years apart, sealed by MOTHER herself and marked OUTBOUND. Each says the same thing: "Population variance unchanged."

log2.text: The line is maintained. That is all the log records, and it is all I will say about the line.

log_fail.text: ACCESS: COUNCIL. The screen returns, politely, to the ration count.

pressure.text: Reservoir pressure is constant. Constant is good, {name}. Constant is kept.

options.text: Nothing is constant for ninety years. Where does the water come from?

pressure2.text: From the reservoir. Thank you for your continuity.

intro.text: You. The one in the picture. Sit down, I won't bite — I haven't the teeth. Ines means to send you out, doesn't she?

options.text: If someone out there knows my face, welding the door won't make them forget it.
Who else wanted to leave, before?

yes.text: Then she's a fool and so are you. Ninety years, nobody knocked. One knock, and we open the door to find out who else is out there? That's how it ends, child. Not with a bang. With a knock.

what.text: Weld it. Say a prayer over him, burn the picture, weld it, and go back to counting algae until the world remembers us or doesn't.

concede.text: She is quiet for a while. "…No. No, it won't." She looks older for having said it. "Then come back. That's all. Don't be the knock."

concede_no.text: "Then let them come and break their knuckles on it."

passives.text: She looks at the clinic door when she says it, and then at nothing.

back.text: So the knock came back. Well. Sit down; tell an old woman what the sky looks like, and don't lie.

intro.text: A maintenance hatch at the end of the pump run, dogged shut with a wheel that hasn't turned in decades. A gauge beside it reads nothing at all.

passives.text: Cold air breathes through the seam. There is open ground on the other side.

options.text: You've cycled this hatch every spring with the pump crew. The trick is the third dog.
(Free the wheel: tap the dogs loose in order, then lean.)
(Under the rust the dogs are a simple latch.)
(Put your whole weight on the wheel.)

mech_fail.text: The wheel doesn't give. The second dog is seized solid, and you would need a bar and an hour.

locks_fail.text: You scrape rust for ten minutes and learn only that rust goes a long way down.

open_crack.text: Something gives with a crack that echoes down the pump run. You wait. Nobody comes.

open.text: The wheel turns. Cold air comes up the shaft from somewhere that smells of salt and nothing else. Nobody logged this, and nobody will.

decision.text: You opened the pump-run hatch: a way out that nobody in the Cistern knows about.

open_already.text: Open. Cold air moves up the shaft from the surface.

intro.text: A steel door with a wheel-lock and MOTHER's seal painted across the join. ARCHIVE — COUNCIL ONLY. The paint is unbroken.

label.text: Beneath the painted seal, stencilled in record shorthand: CONTINUITY RECORDS — RETURN ON RELOCATION. Return to whom, it does not say.

lock.text: Under the wheel the mechanism is electronic, and nothing you carry speaks to it. Somewhere in the walls, MOTHER notes the attempt.

lock_fail.text: The wheel won't turn, and the seal would tear if you forced it. You let go.

wait.speaker: npc_c9_02
wait.text: Not yet. Let me finish with him, then ask me what you like.

look.text: He lies under a sheet with his boots still on because nobody could bring themselves to take them. Sixty, maybe. Burned dark down one side of the face.

hands.text: Sun-split, rope-callused. A pale band on one finger where a ring was, and recently. Whatever he traded, he traded it close to the end.

cover.text: Pell watches you do it and says nothing, which from Pell is a great deal.

shut.text: Ninety years of paint on a door built to outlast the people behind it. The wheel is locked out; the panel beside it is dark. Bram keeps the key.

passives.text: Fresh scratches along the bottom edge, outside-in: fingernails, or a buckle.

open.text: Open on a slice of white daylight. Dust comes in. Nothing else does, yet.

intro.text: Well, look at you. Dust from the salt cut and a face I don't know, which in this town is a thing. Mags. This is the Dry Well, and the name's a joke that stopped being one. What'll it be, love?

passives.text: Her eyes go to your boots, your hands, your belt — pricing you — before they get to your face.

text.text: You. Nell says — is it true? Is he —
Your room's where you left it, love. What else?
Back again. Drink, bed, or trouble?

options.text: Teo's out. He's walking home. He says the count was right.

teo_back.text: She doesn't cry; she hits the bar with the flat of her hand hard enough to jump the glasses, twice, and then pours you something that isn't rot. "The count was right. Of course it was right." She pushes thirty Tolls across. "That's on the house. All of it. Forever. Don't argue with me, love."

news.text: Teo Marsh is back behind the bar at the Dry Well

books.text: She looks at the bar for a while before she answers, which for Mags is a year. "Somebody's skimming. Barman, I think; the water doesn't add up. You read numbers? You look like you read numbers." Two ledgers tied with a bootlace come up from under the bar. "Read them. Night's room and twenty for your trouble. Don't show them to anyone, love. They're mine."

books_clean.text: "No?" Something goes out of her shoulders that was not about a barman. "Well. Good." Twenty Tolls on the bar. "Keep the room tonight."

books_back.text: You put the second ledger on the bar open at the signed page and she does not look at it, because she knows the page. "Right." Very quietly. "Right. Pike lent against the deed when the pumps went dry the second year. I've been paying it back out of water money and losing. He bought the rest two months ago. On paper it's his. The town doesn't know, because the day they know, this is a guild saloon and they'll drink somewhere there isn't one." She looks at you then. "What do you want, love?"

options.text: The town should know who they're drinking under.
A hundred and fifty, and I never read the second book.
I can make these balance so a guild clerk's lamp won't find it.

mods.why: you saw how she hid it; you can hide it better

expose_warn.text: "Then tell Ada." She takes the books back. "And when you want a drink in this town, go to the Choir for water and the Dogs for the rest." No anger in it. That is the worst of it.

squeezed.text: She counts it out without looking at you. A hundred and fifty, from the water tin. "There. Paid." She takes the books. "Don't come back for seconds. I'd sooner tell Ada myself."

decision.text: You sold Mags her own silence for 150 Tolls.

squeeze_no.text: "No." She takes the books. "Tell Ada, then. Go on." She waits. You don't.

helped.text: Two hours with the lamp and a pencil, moving water from a column where it shows to a column where it doesn't, until the second book says what the first book says and both of them say it to a guild clerk. She watches the whole time. "That'll hold." Then: "The room's yours. Not tonight. Always."

decision.text: You hid the Dry Well's buyout for Mags.

help_no.text: You try, and an hour in you have made it worse, and she takes the pencil out of your hand very gently. "Leave it. Leave it, love." She pours. "Just don't tell anyone."

menu.text: Drink's on the house — the first one. Water's two. The back room's ten a night, and nobody'll touch your things because nobody wants to find out what I'd do. And there's always a game on.

options.text: Let me see what you're selling.
You look like someone with a problem.
Your books. There's no thief in them.
A tall old man, hurt, in a long coat. Three weeks back. Did he drink here?

stranger.text: "Everybody drinks here, love; it's the only here." She polishes the same glass. "I remember. He sat by the door where Hollis sits and he didn't say ten words. What he said, and who he said it to — that's worth something. Gossip's my second trade."

options.text: I'm not here to buy. His people are my people.

mods.why: she likes you

options.text: Tell me, and I'll ask after Teo at the overpass.

decision.text: You promised Mags you would ask after Teo at the overpass.

stranger_tell.text: "He asked Nell — not me, Nell — what the Dogs paid for water, and whether Kessler could read. Then he took out a folded paper, looked at it like it was a face, and put it away. He said, to nobody, 'they'll give me water for this.' And he went west in the morning, toward the overpass, walking like a man who'd been shot."

stranger_no.text: "Then it's five Tolls, love, same as everyone." Not unkind.

drink.text: She pours something brown that smells of fruit and lamp oil. "Rot bitters. Don't ask what rotted." It goes down like a decision you'll regret.

room.text: Back through there, past the barrels. Bed, a locker, a door that locks from the inside and a window that doesn't open. Welcome to Shale, love.

room_owed.text: She looks at you a long moment. "Teo used to say that. All right. You owe me ten, and I don't forget." She writes it on the wall behind the bar with a stub of pencil.

room_no.text: "Everybody's good for it, love. That's why I've got a wall of names." Come back with Tolls.

town.text: Two pumps, one sheriff, one saloon, one Tollman, one Choir tent full of people who'll bandage you for free and pray at you for less. The Dogs under the overpass take a tithe twice a year and the rest of the time we pretend they don't. And my Teo — my partner — went east with a wagon of salt five weeks ago and the wagon came back without him.

teo.text: Teo Marsh. Trader, partner, the one who could count. The Dogs have him, under the overpass, for a debt he says isn't his and they say is. They want sixty Tolls or a wagon of something. I've got a bar.

not_yours.text: The back room. A bed with a real mattress, a locker, a bolt on the door. Mags rents it; nobody sleeps here for free.

yours.text: Your room, for now. The bolt is heavy and the mattress smells of someone else's years, and it is the first door you have ever been able to lock from the inside.

text.text: Two pumps on a concrete apron, pre-Burn work patched with everything since. They run in long pulls now instead of bursts, and the town has stopped leaning.

Two pumps on a concrete apron, pre-Burn work patched with everything since. They have not stopped since you came back from the east; the overflow has made a creek across the yard, and children stand in it.
Two pumps on a concrete apron, pre-Burn work patched with everything since. A Tollman sits on a chair beside them with a ledger and sells what comes out by the measure.
Two pumps on a concrete apron, pre-Burn work patched with everything since. They run in bursts and stop, and the whole town leans toward them when they start.

passives.text: There is no hand-switch. The pumps are driven from somewhere else — the pipe runs north, under the pump house, and keeps going.
A faint click before each burst, from a box on the north pump. Something counts before the water comes.

intro.text: Hi. Nell. Mags is my aunt, which means I pour and she talks. You're the one from the salt cut? Everyone says there's a bunker out there with people in it. Everyone says a lot.

options.text: Is it just you and Mags?
The east cistern's gone green. The deputy drinks from it.

wheel.text: Forty wagons, horses, a whole town that moves. They stayed two days and when they left the street was quiet for a week. Ruth at the caravan post rides with them sometimes. I asked her what they need. She said "people who don't ask".

leave.text: She goes red. "Does it show? Don't tell her. She'd say it was the house that was leaving, not me." She wipes a glass that was already clean.

mother.text: "My mum died when I was nine. Fever year. Mags took me on like a bar tab — says it every birthday." She smiles like it doesn't cost anything.

water.text: "Everyone drinks last from something." She frowns. "Aunt Mags says it's the pipe. The Mender says it's the tank. Jonah says it's fine." She looks at the bar. "I could give him the good water. He wouldn't take it. He'd say somebody else needed it."

options.text: (Give her a Flush for him.) Tell him it's for the pump manual: it stops the pages going green.

decision.text: You left a Flush with Nell for Jonah, with a story he would swallow.

options.text: (Show her a filter: sand, cloth, charcoal, in a barrel by the cistern.)

mods.why: you have made worse water drinkable

decision.text: You built a filter barrel for the east cistern.

news.text: someone built a filter barrel for the east cistern

water_done.text: "He'll drink it if it's for the manual." She almost laughs. "He'd drink from the Dogs' truck if it was for the manual."

water_no.text: The barrel leaks and the sand goes green faster than the water. Nell watches you fail politely.

intro.text: Sheriff Vey. You're new, you're armed or you're stupid, and you came in on the west road, which means the salt cut or the Dogs. Which?

passives.text: A folded letter under the blotter, Tollmen seal up. She moves a cup onto it as you look.

options.text: The salt cut. Cistern 9. A man died at our door and I'm finding out who he was.
There's a Rust Dog child in the Choir tent.
The Dry Well is Pike's. Mags signed it over two months ago.
What if I said the Dogs?

cut.text: "Cistern 9." She says it like a name from a story. "So the bunker's real, and it opens. Noted." A pause. "A dead man at your door — tall, old, walking like he'd been shot? He came through here. Three weeks back. Bought water from Pardo with a ring and asked for the east road and the overpass. I told him the overpass would kill him. He thanked me."

news.text: someone from the salt-cut bunker is in town

lie_ok.text: "Everybody's passing through. Some of them stop." She lets it go, and you can see her file it. "Rules are short."

lie_no.text: "No, you're not." Flat. "You came out of the salt cut; Pardo saw you on the ridge. Don't lie to me in my own office; it wastes both our mornings."

dogs.text: "Then I'd ask you to leave the gun on the counter and I'd watch you walk back out." She doesn't reach for anything. "Are you saying it?"

name.text: "He didn't, and I asked twice. He had a way of not hearing questions. Pike at the Tollmen post talked to him longer than I did — ask him what it cost."

overpass.text: "The Rust Dogs. Forty, fifty of them under a dead highway, with the water they take from us and the people they take from the road. Kessler runs them; he's a thief with manners. His lieutenant has none." She looks at you. "If you go, go in daylight, hands empty, and don't say my name like it's a password."

text.text: "The tower." She doesn't look up from the desk. "Forty feet. Half the rungs. Everyone knew and I signed nothing." A long breath. "The militia's four rifles again. Pike was here this morning with a rate card for protection. I didn't throw him out."

"East street. Midnight. Alone, because that's how I had it drawn up." She is very still. "They didn't even take anything. The militia's four rifles again and Pike was here this morning with a rate card for protection. I didn't throw him out."

"Fever. From the east cistern, Nell says, and Nell's usually right." She looks at her hands. "I wrote the ration. Deputy drinks last. The militia's four rifles again and Pike was here this morning with a rate card for protection. I didn't throw him out."

hound.text: "I noticed." She has not sat down since it walked in. "Issa wants to shoot it. Jonah wants to name it. Mags wants to charge people to look at it. I've told all three no." She looks out at the yard, where it sits. "It looked at me once and then it stopped, as if it had decided something. I'd like to know what." A breath. "Thank you. I think."

ghosts.text: "On a tap off my line." She lets that be a sentence by itself. "So the pressure drop has a name and a family, and the family wants a street."

options.text: Three generations out of a cistern that failed. Five people, one of them sixteen, one of them dying. Under your law, and the valve closes.

mods.why: the town has water to spare now
Shale trusts you
she has done this once already

ghosts_yes.text: "Under my law. As townsfolk. The tannery's empty; it stinks, and it has a roof." She writes it on the blotter. "And the first one who touches that valve again answers to me, not to you. Noted?"

decision.text: Sheriff Vey agreed to take the Dry Wells family in under Shale's law.

ghosts_no.text: "They've been drinking my town for sixty years and you want me to give them a street." She shakes her head once. "No. Tell them the valve closes, or I close it."

decision.text: Sheriff Vey refused the Dry Wells family.

text.text: "The pumps ran all night." She has not slept either. "You did that. In a room, with a machine, a day east." She does not sit down. "Nine years I've been sheriff of a town dying of something nobody could name, and you named it and fixed it, and I don't know whether to thank you or arrest you for knowing where it was." A breath. "Thank you."

"They haven't stopped." She looks toward the yard, where you can hear them. "The north tank's over the top and the children are standing in it. And when they stop?" She lets you answer or not. "Fine. Water today. I've had worse news from the east."

"A Tollman on a chair by my pumps, selling me my water by the measure." Her voice is very level. "Pike came by with the rate card an hour ago. He said your name twice, as per." She sits down. "Get out of my office. Come back when you've got something for Shale that isn't a receipt."

"You stood in front of it." She says it flat. "The thing that's been bleeding my town, and you read it and walked away." A long pause. "Maybe that was the right thing. Maybe whatever wrote the number reads what you do, too. I'd have liked to be asked."

jonah_lived.text: "A month and a day." She has counted; she pretends she hasn't. "Something changed its mind about my deputy, and I don't know what, and I don't like not knowing." She looks at you, properly. "But I know who was in town." A pause. "Pike came by with a rate card for protection last week. I threw him out. I'd like you to know that was easier than it should have been."

pip.text: "I know." She does not stop writing. "Fifteen, broken arm, fell off the deck when the Dogs had their last fight about who runs it. Calla took her in and asked me not to look, so I didn't." Now she looks at you. "You want me to look?"

options.text: She's a Dog. Kessler will come for her, or use her.
No. I wanted you to know I knew.

pip_taken.text: "Then she goes in the cell till the Dogs send for her, and the Choir doesn't speak to either of us for a season." She stands. "You're right that Kessler would use her. That's not the same as this being right."

decision.text: You had the sheriff take a Rust Dog child out of the Choir tent.

news.text: The sheriff took a girl out of the Choir tent.

pip_left.text: "Good." Back to writing. "Then we both know, and the girl keeps her arm."

books.text: She stops writing. "Say that again." You do. She sits with it the way she sits with everything, which is still. "Then Shale's only bar is a guild bar, and the water in it is guild water at guild prices the day Pike wants it to be." She stands. "The town needs to know that. Mags will never forgive you, and neither will I, quite, and it still needs doing."

news.text: The Dry Well is guild property; Mags signed it over.

decision.text: You told the sheriff the Dry Well belongs to the guild.

ledger_page.text: She reads it twice, and the second time her lips move on the name. "Post nine-west." She folds it into her shirt, not her pocket. "He sells us water. He stands in my street." A breath. "This stays with me. If I use it, it'll be when it costs him more than it costs Shale, and I don't know when that is yet."

decision.text: You gave Sheriff Vey the ledger page proving Pike paid for the stranger's shooting.

rules.text: Rules: no guns drawn in town, no stealing water, no fighting the Dogs on my street unless I start it. Break one and you're in the cell. Break two and you're on the road. We're thin here; I can't afford trouble I didn't choose.

options.text: You look like someone who needs hands.

help.text: "I need water and I need a month without a funeral. If you can get me either, come back." The corner of her mouth moves. "Noted, anyway."

text.text: People are saying your name without spitting. Keep it up.
I hear things. I'm hearing them about you.
Sheriff's office. Say it quick.

options.text: About the man who died at our door.
Tribute Day. What are you going to do?
Kessler's terms: half of last time, in water. I carried them myself.
Some of the Dogs want out — Wren Calloway and her people. Would Shale have them?
Pike paid the outriders who shot the old man. (Show her the ledger page.)

Dry Wells. The station there sets your water.
The machine in your yard. It will look at everything that comes in at night.

tribute.text: "I'm going to pay, and hate it, and count the rifles while I do." She says it like a verdict. "Unless somebody gives me a reason not to that doesn't end with Jonah in the dirt."

options.text: The militia would fight if you let them.

tribute_fight.text: "Issa would. Jonah would, which is why I won't." A breath. "If it comes to it, and you're standing there, I'll say the word and you'll hear it. Don't make it come to it."

terms.text: "Half." She doesn't say it twice. "Half of forty is twenty measures I don't have, from a man who's never once asked for less than everything." She looks at you. "Why would he?"

options.text: Because he keeps a list of who he hasn't robbed, and he'd like you on it. He doesn't take lives; Vasha would.

mods.why: you know what Kessler says of himself
you know what Shale fighting would make of Vasha

terms_yes.text: "…Half, then. In water, and I count it." She writes it on the blotter, over the cup. "If she asks for more, you'll be standing there. Noted?"

decision.text: Sheriff Vey agreed to pay the Dogs half, on Kessler's terms you carried.

terms_no.text: "Then I'll hear it from Vasha on the day, and decide then." The cup goes back on the letter.

exodus.text: "Rust Dogs. In my town." She lets the words sit. "Under my law? If one of them steals a cup of water, I hang the lot, and they'd know it. Would they still come?"

options.text: Wren would. She keeps her word to the letter and expects the same. That's more than you get from most of Shale.

mods.why: you know she argued to let the stranger go

exodus_yes.text: "Then tell her: under my law, as townsfolk, and the first one who looks at the pumps wrong answers to me." She almost smiles. "Noted. God help me."

decision.text: Sheriff Vey agreed to take in Wren's people under Shale's law.

exodus_no.text: "Then no. I've enough people I can't feed."

month.text: He straightens when he sees you, the way he does for everyone, and then a little more. "You're the one from the salt cut. The sheriff says you went to the overpass and came back, which nobody does." He waits to be told what to do with that.

options.text: What does a deputy do with his week?

week.text: "Patrol, mostly. And the vane — Dad sends me up the windpump tower every week since the kite day bent it. Somebody has to, and it isn't going to be him." He grins. "Forty feet. You can see the overpass from the top."

week2.text: "Rungs. Half of them." The grin doesn't go. "I know. I'm careful."

night.text: "Me. East street, midnight to four. The Corporal's got nine rifles and four that shoot, and the four sleep." He says it with pride, which is the problem. "If the Dogs come at night, I'm the one who sees them first."

water.text: "East cistern, by the yard. It's gone a bit green." A shrug. "The deputy drinks last. Everybody else gets the pumps."

name.text: He goes very still, and then he laughs, because he is twenty-two. "A list. Of — what, people who are going to —" He doesn't finish it. "Who wrote it?" You tell him you don't know. "Then it's not true till someone makes it true." He puts his hand on the badge without noticing.

decision.text: You told Jonah Reese his name was on the stranger's list.

options.text: Then don't help them. Stay off the tower. Walk the street with someone. Drink from the pumps.

careful.text: He nods, slowly, the way he reads. "Off the tower." It costs him something; you can see it being paid. "I'll tell Dad it's the sheriff's order. He'll like that less than the tower."

decision.text: You talked Jonah Reese off the windpump tower.

careful_no.text: "I'm not going to hide from a list." He stands straighter. It is exactly what the list would want him to say.

lived.text: He is sitting on the office step with both books open on his knees, alive, and looks up like a man who has heard a door close somewhere far away. "A month." He says it quietly. "Dad counted too. He pretended not to." A breath. "Whatever you did — I don't know what you did." He goes back to the books, and then doesn't.

text.text: Ma'am. Deputy Reese. Sheriff's inside if you need the sheriff. If you need a deputy, that's — that's me.
Sir. Deputy Reese. Sheriff's inside if you need the sheriff. If you need a deputy, that's — that's me.
Deputy Reese. Sheriff's inside if you need the sheriff. If you need a deputy, that's — that's me.

options.text: How long have you been deputy?

job.text: "A year in spring. Ada — the Sheriff — said I could, so I did." He stands straighter. "I know what people say. That I'm too young. I'm going to be the kind of deputy they stop saying it about."

read.text: "Everything in town. Both books." He grins, then catches it. "The pump manual, the Tollmen rate card, the Choir's pamphlet, a box of pre-Burn magazines Mags keeps for the pictures. I read the words."

dad.text: The grin goes. "He thinks the badge is a target. Maybe it is. Somebody has to wear it."

intro.text: Corporal Lind. Militia — eleven of us, nine rifles, four that shoot. If you can shoot, I want to know. If you can't, stay off the street when the Dogs come.

options.text: Your four that shoot could be nine. I'll drill them.

drills.text: "Dawn and dusk, the yard, live rounds we can't spare, until nine of them shoot. And from tonight nobody walks the street alone; I'll tell Ada it was your idea." She looks at the nine. "There's a man drinks behind the yard who used to be the best shot in the Sallow. If he turns up, don't let him near the boys. Or do. I've stopped knowing."

decision.text: You took on drilling Shale's militia.

news.text: the militia walk the street in pairs now, and nine rifles shoot

drills_on.text: "Better. Two of them hit the post today; one of them meant to." She lowers her voice. "The deputy walked the east street in a pair last night and hated it. Good."

drills_done.text: "Nine rifles. Nine that shoot, more or less." She doesn't smile, but it's close. "Pairs on the street from now on. Ada signed it." A beat. "Thank you. I don't say that."

shoot.text: "Then you're the fifth rifle." She looks you over once, properly. "Ada will say no. Ada says no to everything until she says yes."

dogs.text: "Tribute's due. Half a year since the last. They come with a truck, they take water and whatever Mags has brewed, and this time they'll want more because Kessler's lieutenant counts. Vasha. Say the name to Ada and watch her face."

intro.text: Good day. Factor Pike, Tollmen post nine-west. Rates are posted; delivery is guaranteed between posts; water is sold by the measure and I do not haggle, as it wastes the time of the person who would have paid.

passives.text: A list on the wall behind him: SEED — ANY VARIETY — ANY QUANTITY — PAID IN TOLLS OR SCRIP. The prices are absurd.

options.text: An old man came through three weeks ago, hurt. You spoke with him.

again.text: As per. Stock, or something else?

Do the Tollmen read this hand?

The console at Dry Wells. The guild would pay to hold what it holds.

station.text: "Post nine-west has known about DW-4 for eleven years, and been unable to get a man past the rifle." He does not blink. "One hundred and fifty Tolls. A guild engineer walks in behind you, and Shale's water is sold by the measure, as per: reliably. There is a word for what Shale has now, and it is not reliable."

decision.text: You sold the Dry Wells console to Factor Pike for a hundred and fifty Tolls.

station_sold.text: "As per." He counts it out in a way that makes a hundred and fifty look like a courtesy. "An engineer leaves tonight. A caravan goes east in three days from the gate; there is a seat on it with a description on it that is not your name." He is already writing. "Shale will find this reliable. Everyone does, in the end."

controller.text: He does not touch it. "Concern customs seal. Handler, one." He knows the manifest line by heart. "The guild lost a convoy on the pan with that aboard, and has been not saying so for a season." The top half of his face does the arithmetic. "One hundred and fifty. The guild's engineer collects the rest of it, and the guild's road is quieter for everyone. As per."

decision.text: You sold the controller from the pan to Factor Pike; the guild will have the machine.

controller_sold.text: The slab goes into a drawer that locks. "The guild thanks you for your custom." He writes two lines, and the second one is longer than the first.

controller_no.text: "Then you are carrying something the Concern will want back, and the Concern does not haggle either." He goes back to the rates. "The offer stands. They always do."

station_no.text: "Then it will be somebody else, later, for less."" He goes back to the rates. "The offer does not expire. The guild's offers never do; that is what the guild is."

ledger_page.text: He reads it the way he reads rates. "Post nine's hand. A road contract, confirmed and paid, as per." He looks up with the top half of his face. "Guild paper, removed from a guild ledger. There is a buy-back rate for that. Sixty." A pause exactly as long as a courtesy. "I don't ask what you'd do with it otherwise. I know."

decision.text: You sold the Tollhouse ledger page back to Pike for sixty Tolls, and he burned it.

ledger_burn.text: He counts sixty onto the counter, takes the page, and holds it to the lamp until it is gone. "As per." He wipes the ash off the counter with his sleeve.

ledger_keep.text: "Then we both know what it says." He goes back to his rates. "Good day."

key.text: He looks at the map for exactly as long as it takes to see what it is, and then not at all. "Not here. But the post sells the key to it — a cipher wheel, forty Tolls, as per. The Tollmen sell keys to everything, {name}. It is how we know what is locked."

news.text: the salt-cut stranger showed a Tollman a map covered in cipher

key_bought.text: "Set the inner rim to the first letter of the nearest town. They always start with the nearest town." He has already turned back to the ledger.

stranger.text: "Information is a good, and goods have rates." He does not smile. "Fifteen Tolls. For that you get what he asked me and what I told him, verbatim; the Tollmen do not embroider."

options.text: You said yourself: he's not your client. Ten.

stranger_tell.text: "He asked the price of water at the overpass. I said Kessler sells it by the life. He said he had a paper Kessler would want more than a life — a map, with names on it — and asked whether the Tollmen would pay better. I quoted him. He laughed, which hurt him, and went west." Pike straightens a ledger that was straight. "I reported the conversation, as per."

reported.text: "To the post east. As per." The ledger closes.

stranger_no.text: "Fifteen. The rate does not move because the buyer is clever."

who.text: "A guild. We hold the roads between the posts, we carry, we insure, we lend. The Reach moves because we move it." He smiles with the top half of his face. "Everything you own came through a Tollhouse, or it was stolen from someone whose did."

seed.text: "Any variety. Any quantity. Viable, which I test." He does not explain who wants it. "You came from the salt cut, I'm told. A shelter like that keeps a seed bank, or it wouldn't have lasted the first winter. I would pay very well. I would pay in advance."

options.text: The Cistern kept a bank. I could ask.

seed_who.text: "A client east of the Teeth with a great deal of glass and not enough green under it." He stops, surprised at himself, and his face closes like a ledger. "Rates are posted."

seed_who_no.text: "A client. As per." The ledger closes.

seed_get.text: "Then ask." He writes a figure on a slip and turns it to face you: more than the saloon takes in a month. "Viable. Sealed. I test it here. Bring it to this counter and the guild will remember your name, which is worth more than the figure."

options.text: I'll see what the Elder says.

seed_sell.text: He does not open the case here. He weighs it, reads the label twice, and sets it under the counter the way other men set down a loaded gun. "Viable." The Tolls come out in a stack that has been counted in advance. "The guild remembers. As per."

news.text: The Cistern's seed went east with the guild.

decision.text: You sold the Cistern's seed to the Tollmen.

intro.text: Sit. No — you're not hurt; you're standing like someone who expects to be. I'm Calla. The Choir keeps this tent: water, bandages, a cot if you need one, and nobody asks you to sing.

passives.text: Painted small on the tent-pole behind her, faded: half a sun with no ground under it.

again.text: The sky's still up. What do you need?

options.text: You've three on cots and one of you. Let me help.
The trees north of town, with leaves on. Yours?
That sign on the pole. I've seen it on a dead man's things.

help.text: "Would you." It is not a question; she is already pointing. "The old man can't breathe, the girl's arm needs the board checked, and Abel's burning. Water's in the crate. Don't be clever; be slow."

text.text: "Seen to." She does not look up from what she is doing. "And the girl is in the sheriff's cell, so one of the three is seen to twice." She finishes the knot. "The Choir says lay healer. The Choir is kinder than I am."

"Seen to." She looks at you properly for the first time. "All three. And you looked at Pip's arm and saw an arm." She puts a grey scarf in your hands. "Lay healer. It means the sky trusts your hands, and so do I."
"Seen to." She puts a grey scarf in your hands. "Lay healer. It means the sky trusts your hands. Try to deserve it."

seed_given.text: She takes the case in both hands and does not say anything for a while. "Ninety years." She reads the label. "Tomato." A laugh that is nearly something else. "Anselm will plant it tomorrow. Pike will hear by tonight. Let him." She touches the tent-pole where the sign is. "Under the sky. Thank you."

news.text: The Cistern's seed went into the Choir's beds.

decision.text: You gave the Cistern's seed to the Choir.

heal.text: She works fast and talks while she does it, which you suspect is the point. Clean water, a needle, something that stings.

orchard.text: "Ours, and the sky's. Brother Anselm has had twelve of them back from the roots in nine years, which is twelve more than anyone else in the Sallow." The smile goes. "Something robs him at night. He won't have it hurt and he won't have it go on, and he asked me, and I am asking you, since you look like someone who can tell the difference between those two."

choir.text: "People who decided the sky was enough to pray to, since it was all that was left. We farm, we heal, we bury." She smiles. "That's the short version. The long one has a lot of singing."

larkspur.text: She goes very still, then very busy. "Where did you hear that?" You tell her: a dying man at a door. She closes her eyes. "Then he got that far. Say it to no one else. Not here. There's a man east, at Openfield — I can't tell you more than that, and you should not want me to."

decision.text: You said the dead man's word to Sister Calla.

sigil.text: "Lots of people paint the open sky." Her hands keep folding a bandage that was folded. "If you have his things, keep them out of the Tollmen's sight. They don't like what it means."

sigil2.text: "That nothing is written yet." She looks up. "It's a prayer. It's also a complaint."

intro.text: Pup. You've got salt on you. Sit, I don't bite, haven't the — well. Hollis Crane, oldest living thing in Shale after the pumps. Spare a pull of something?

options.text: An old man sat here three weeks ago. Tall, hurt.
(Show him the map.) Can you read this hand?
An old man sat here three weeks ago.

stranger_cold.text: "Lots of men sit here, pup. I don't remember the ones who don't bring a bottle."

stranger.text: "Him." The old man goes quiet in a way he hasn't been. "He sat where you are. We didn't talk. We didn't need to — I knew the sign on his things, pup, and he knew I knew it. He had a map. Folded small, kept close, the way you keep a thing you've already decided to sell. He asked me if the Dogs kept their word on water. I said Kessler does. He nodded like a man picking a grave."

mask.text: "I knew a man who painted that sign on everything he owned. Forty years ago, in a place with boards." He won't say more; he turns his cup over. "Ask me again when I'm drunker, pup. Or soberer. One of the two."

gift.text: He drinks it like a man checking the time. "Pup. Pup, you're all right." His eyes go somewhere far east. "Ask me something. Quick, while I like you."

gift_b.text: "Mags's rot." He drinks it anyway. "That's not a kindness, pup, but I'll take the thought."

boards.text: "City boards. Screens, pup, tall as a house, with your face on 'em if you were worth a line. Said who paid, who owed, who was next." He laughs, dry as the street. "I had a line once. A short one."

which.text: "The only one that counts, pup. West, past the glass, where it rains." He won't say the name; he mouths it and looks at the Tollmen post. "Forty years. They don't let you out, you know. You leave."

map.text: He holds it a long way from his face, then very close. "Boards hand," he says. "City hand. Blocks of five and a turn of the wheel each name — they taught us that so we couldn't read our own files." His finger finds the nearest pin. "Reese. Jonah. Shale. A month." The next. "Vey. Ada. Shale. Four months." He stops reading. "That's two I know. Don't show me the rest, pup. I'm old; I'd like to stay surprised."

decision.text: Hollis Crane read the first names on the stranger's map for you: Jonah Reese within the month; Ada Vey in four.

kite.text: "Machines, pup. Big wings, no bird in 'em, from before. They come up from the south when the wind's wrong and they look at you." He taps his nose. "Smell the air. Ozone. That's a kite day."

intro.text: Hold still — no, you're fine. Yusra Hadid, Mender. I fix what's broken and fit what fits. You don't wear any work, do you? Clean as a Choir baby. Rare.

options.text: Could you fit something in me?
The east cistern. Could you build a filter for it?

work.text: "Chrome. Bionics. Eyes that see heat, a hand that doesn't shake, a spine-link. Rare out here; the city makes the good pieces and the Concern makes the better ones and both of them keep a hand on the leash." She wipes a blade. "I fit what people bring me. I take it out again when it goes wrong, and it does."

options.text: Could you fit something in me?

fit.text: "With what? I've a Gyro Hand — a pre-Burn surgical hand, steady as a table — and a pair of Ember Eyes I built myself, and either costs more than you've got on you. Bring me a piece and the Tolls for the surgery, or the Tolls for the piece and the surgery both, and I'll fit it. It goes in or it doesn't; I don't promise. Sit down when you're ready."

filter.text: "Ceramic and charcoal, a day's work, and thirty Tolls for the ceramic, which I don't make." She wipes her hands. "The deputy drinks from it. I know. Everyone knows and nobody's asked."

decision.text: You paid the Mender to build a filter for the east cistern.

filter_done.text: "Tomorrow. Tell the deputy it's for the whole east street. He'll drink from it if it isn't for him."

intro.text: You're in the light. — Dov Reese. Pumps. If you're here about my boy, Ada's got him, go ask her what she's doing with him.

options.text: The pressure on these never changes either, does it?
Your son seems set on the badge.
Stop sending Jonah up the tower.

pumps.text: "Nobody. That's the joke." He bangs the casing. "Switch is inside, dead since my father's time. They run on a schedule — six, eleven, four, nine, give or take — and the schedule changes maybe twice a year, and nobody here changes it. I've got the manual. Half of it's in a hand I can't read."

text.text: He hands you a swollen binder. The unreadable half is record shorthand — your hand. MAINTENANCE SCHEDULE: REMOTE. SUPPLY: NETWORK 4. The rest is pressures and part numbers.
He hands you a swollen binder. The diagrams you know — same pumps as home, same valves. The unreadable half is a tight print you've seen on MOTHER's crates.
He hands you a swollen binder. Diagrams, pressures, and half of it in a tight print that isn't any language you know.

pressure.text: He looks at you for a long moment. "No. No, it doesn't. You're the first person who ever asked that like it meant something."

jonah.text: "Set." He spits. "He's twenty-two. He read a book about sheriffs. Ada read him."

options.text: He seems like a good one.

jonah2.text: "He is." It comes out before he can stop it. "That's the problem, isn't it."

tower.text: "Who else goes up? Me, with this hip? The vane's bent since the kite day and if it doesn't turn, the tank doesn't fill, and if the tank doesn't fill the east street drinks green." He looks at the tower, not at you. "He's careful."

options.text: (Go up and straighten the vane yourself.)
