decision.text: You paid Old Pardo to climb the windpump tower so Jonah would not.

options.text: He's your son. You know what half the rungs are.

decision.text: You made Dov Reese climb his own tower instead of sending his son.

fixed.text: Forty feet of rungs, half of them, and a vane that straightens with a crowbar and a word. From the top you can see the overpass. When you come down Dov has not moved. "Right," he says, which is a word people use here when they mean thank you.

decision.text: You climbed the windpump tower and straightened the vane yourself.

fix_no.text: Twenty feet up a rung lets go under you and you come down the hard way. The vane is still bent. Dov says nothing, which is kinder than it sounds.

paid.text: Pardo takes the Tolls and looks at the tower like an old enemy. "Forty feet," he says. "I did it at sixty." He does it again.

son.text: He is quiet for a long time. "Half of them," he agrees. "Right." He goes to get the crowbar himself, and the hip, and the ladder.

son_no.text: "Don't tell me what I know." He bangs the casing.

intro.text: Water? Two a measure, one if you carry your own cup, nothing if you're dying and I believe you. Pardo. I sit here. That's the job.

options.text: A tall old man bought water from you. With a ring.

clock.text: "You listened. Nobody listens." He holds up a finger each. "Six, eleven, four, nine — the hours the water comes. For thirty years. Then one spring it was five, ten, three, eight, for two months, and then it went back. Somebody turned a dial. Not here." He looks north, past the pump house, past the ridge. "Not anywhere here."

who.text: "If I knew that, pup, I'd sell it. I'm not Pike." He sips his own water. "Something counts, and the water comes."

stranger.text: "The ring's here." He opens his hand: a plain band, worn thin on the inside. "Three weeks back. He drank like a man who'd forgotten how. Asked the way to the overpass. I said the Dogs. He said he knew." He closes his hand. "Ten Tolls and it's yours. It should go back to somebody."

ring.text: Inside the band, worn almost away, two letters and a mark like half a sun.

intro.text: Caravan post. Ruth Avel; I ride with the Wheel when they pass and sit here when they don't. Goods, ammunition, and letters — a wagon leaves when a wagon leaves. Pay in Tolls or in something a wagon wants.

options.text: Any work riding beside a wagon?

letters.text: "Write it where you sleep — Mags's room, a camp, anywhere with a table. I carry it. If the person's where you say they are, you get an answer in a few days. If they aren't, you get the letter back, eventually, with dust on it."

wheel.text: "Nomads. Two hundred wagons across the Reach, in rings of forty. Neutral, armed, owed by everyone. We go where the Tollmen don't tax and we tax ourselves." She shrugs. "If you ever need to be somewhere else, and I mean *else*, the Wheel is how."

text.text: "You've got it. The salt wagon, Tollhouse 9, the guild road. Keep it in your eye."

"Sefa's salt wagon goes to Tollhouse 9 with the Tollmen's caravan, and the guild guards the guild's wagons and nobody else's. Sixty Tolls at the gate for walking beside it with a gun. It's the Wheel's job to give, but I can put your name on it; she'll have heard of you by the time you get there."

escort_yes.text: "Done. Walk the Tollhouse road from here; the wagon leaves when you do. If the road asks for something, it's asking the Wheel."

text.text: "Close. On the pan south-west of town, where the old road was. Four days, then they turn east toward Dry Wells." She marks it on your map with a thumbnail. "Walk out before noon and you'll eat with them."
"Out on the Dry Wells pans this week, east. Four days, then north under the orchard." She marks it on your map. "Say Ruth sent you and Sefa will feed you before she asks what you want."
"North, under the Burnt Orchard. Four days, then the overpass side, which nobody likes." She marks it on your map. "Go by the orchard lane; the Choir will point you on."
"The overpass side this week, where the Dogs can count them. Four days, then back by Shale." She marks it on your map. "Go in daylight and go slow. Sefa likes slow."

look.text: A board on a post: SHALE — WATER BY THE CUP — NO DOGS. The road runs west into hardpan, toward the salt cut and, further, the line of a dead highway against the sky.

passives.text: Old prints in the crust at the road's edge, kept by three dry weeks: one man, boots worn on the outer edge, a long drag on the right leg. He went west — not toward the salt cut, but north-west, toward the highway. And he was alone.
Scuffs where somebody sat down hard against the post, and a dark stain in the dust that the wind hasn't taken yet.

intro.text: Hold it. Hands out, palms up — that's the rule. Wren's rule. She's got you from the deck right now and she doesn't miss, so smile.

options.text: I'm here to talk to Kessler.

in.text: Everyone is. Walk slow. The hall's the coach under the deck. Don't touch the dogs, don't touch the tank, don't touch Vasha.

in_teo.text: Mags's man. He's in the cage; he's fine; he does Perpetua's counting. Kessler decides about him, or Perpetua does if you pay her first. Walk slow.

in_ada.text: …She did? Then you're brave or you're stupid, and Kessler likes both. Walk slow, and don't say her name inside like it's a password.

in_stare.text: He holds it for three seconds, which is two more than most. "…Fine. Fine! Walk slow. Wren's still got you."

intro.text: Brindle. Gate. Nine years a Dog; I was seven. Wren says I talk too much, so I'm not talking.

options.text: Where were you before the Dogs?

wren.text: "Everything. Tracks, wind, where to stand so the sun's behind you." He glances at the deck. "She's leaving. Everybody knows. Nobody says. Don't tell her I did."

before.text: "A wagon. The Tollmen took the wagon for a toll and my mum for the rest." Flat, practised. "Kessler took me for nothing. So."

intro.text: Sit. No — stand; it's not a long talk. Brindle says you walked in with your hands out, so you've got manners or no gun. Which?

passives.text: A folded paper under the lamp on his table, held flat by a shotgun shell.
The coach smells of dog, and of soap. Somebody here washes.

options.text: Both. I'm from the salt cut — Cistern 9. A man died at our door.
Manners. I'd like to keep them.

cut.text: "The bunker." He doesn't blink. "The old man said that too, at the end, when Wren brought him in across a dog. 'Tell the bunker.' Tell them what, I asked. He didn't have the water left to answer, so I gave him some, and he gave me a paper, and he walked west to die on your step." A pause. "Fair?"

options.text: Fair. Tell me about the paper.

menu.text: Ask. I'll answer what's free. The rest has a price, like water.

options.text: The map he carried. I want it.
Tribute Day. What do you take from Shale?

map.text: Water for a paper. He said the paper was worth more than my camp, and I believed him, because a dying man doesn't lie about prices. I can't read it. Nobody here can. Vasha wants to sell it to the Tollmen. The Tollmen have already asked, which is why I haven't.

options.text: Play you for it. Dust. My stake against the paper.
The Tollmen know you have it. Pike reported him — "as per".
Give it to me, and I'll carry your terms to Shale before Tribute Day.

mods.why: you know what he wants from Shale

price.text: Eighty Tolls. Or the rifle on your back, if it's the bolt gun — Jack says the bolt gun shoots straight, and nothing here does.

decision.text: You bought the stranger's map from Kessler for eighty Tolls.
You traded the Cistern's bolt rifle to Kessler for the stranger's map.

wager.text: "Fair." He clears the table with his forearm. "Twenty Tolls or the rifle, against the paper. First to thirty. I don't cheat; I don't need to."

prize.label: the stranger's map against twenty Tolls

decision.text: You won the stranger's map from Kessler at Dust.

prize.label: the stranger's map against the bolt rifle

decision.text: You won the stranger's map from Kessler at Dust.

fear.text: He is quiet for a while. "…Then it's a stone in my boot, not a paper." He takes it from under the lamp and pushes it across. "Take it out of my camp. When they come asking, you were never here, and I never had it. Fair?"

decision.text: Kessler gave you the map to be rid of it, once he knew the Tollmen were asking.

fear_no.text: "Let them come. They've come before." He puts a hand flat on the lamp. "Price is eighty."

terms.text: "You'd do that." He thinks about it the way he does everything, slowly and once. "Half what we took last time. Water, not drink. Vey hears it from you, not from Vasha's truck. If she pays, nobody dies, and you keep the paper." He slides it across. "If she doesn't, I'll know who talked."

decision.text: Kessler gave you the map in exchange for carrying his tribute terms to Shale: half of last time, in water.

terms_no.text: "She wouldn't take terms from me. She won't take them from a stranger with my paper in their pocket." He almost smiles. "Price is eighty."

handover.text: The paper is soft as cloth from handling. Marks in blocks of five, a drawn line of road, and twelve places on it pricked with a pin. "Don't read it here," Kessler says. "Whatever it is."

teo.text: The trader. His partner's brother owed forty; he says it's not his debt. Debts are family here; it's how we've lasted. Sixty with the keeping. Pay it, or make me a better offer, or talk to Perpetua — he counts for her, and she's fond.

decision.text: You paid Teo Marsh's debt to the Rust Dogs.

news.text: someone bought Teo Marsh out of the Dogs' cage

options.text: A better offer: free him, and I carry your terms to Shale for Tribute Day.

decision.text: Kessler freed Teo Marsh in exchange for your carrying his tribute terms to Shale.

news.text: the Dogs let Teo Marsh go

options.text: Let me talk to him first.

teo_free.text: "Fair." He raises his voice without seeming to. "Lute! The trader walks." Then, to you: "Tell Mags the count was right. She'll know what I mean."

tribute.text: Twice a year. Water, mostly; what Mags brews; a cow, when they had cows. They pay it and nobody dies. Vasha wants more and Vey wants to give nothing and I'm the man in the middle who keeps a list of who I haven't robbed.

options.text: What if Shale fought this time?

tribute_fight.text: "Then I'd lose Dogs, and they'd lose a town, and Vasha would be chief by morning. And you'd have done that." He looks at you. "Fair?"

who.text: "Forty people the road dropped, under a road the sky dropped. We take the tithe; we don't take lives. That's mine. It's the only thing that is, and it's why Vasha counts."

after.text: You've got your paper. Don't read it here, and don't tell Vasha what it says if you ever find out.

text.text: One lamp. The shotgun across his knees, where it always is. "Late," Kessler says. "Vasha sent you. She sends everyone, in the end."
He looks at you, and then past you, to where Vasha stands by the fire. "Not yet, I think," he says, to nobody.

decision.text: You went for Kessler in his hall, with Vasha behind you.

options.text: She did. I'm telling you instead.

decision.text: You warned Kessler of Vasha's coup instead of carrying it out.

warned.text: He doesn't reach for the gun. "Fair," he says, after a long time. "Then you'll want the paper, and I'll want her out of my camp, and we'll both get one of those." He gives you the map.

decision.text: Kessler gave you the map after you warned him of the coup.

intro.text: {name}. I've heard it twice already today; it's a good name for a grave. Vasha. I run the part of this camp that bleeds; Kessler keeps the list.

passives.text: A pistol-grip submachine gun on a strap, and her thumb never leaves the safety.

options.text: What do you want from me?

again.text: Say it again. Your name. I like how it sounds when you're careful.

menu.text: Everything, eventually. Today I'll settle for a conversation.

options.text: The paper Kessler took off the old man.
What do you want with Shale?
Tollhouse 9. I want through it, and I don't want to pay.

map.text: The paper. Kessler will sit on it until the Tollmen lift it off his corpse, or he dies of old age first, which is the same thing slower. You want it. I want a camp that isn't a charity. He's in that coach every night with one lamp and a shotgun he's never fired at a person. You see where I'm going.

options.text: You want me to kill Kessler.
I see where you're going. I'm not going there.

coup.text: "I want the hall. Tonight, after the fires. You go in; I come in behind you. What happens, happens. The paper's yours. The camp's mine. And Shale learns what tribute means when someone counts."

decision.text: You agreed to help Vasha take the camp from Kessler.

coup_yes.text: "After the fires. Don't be clever; clever is Kessler's."

coup_no.text: "Then you're Kessler's. That's a shorter list than you think."

text.text: The fires are down. She tilts her head toward the coach. "Go on."
After the fires. Not before.

after_coup.text: She steps over him without looking down and takes the paper from under the lamp. She holds it a moment, then holds it out. "A deal's a deal. I don't need to read it; I know what it says about me." Outside, the camp is very quiet.

decision.text: Kessler died in his hall. Vasha leads the Rust Dogs and gave you the map.

news.text: Kessler of the Rust Dogs was killed in his own hall; Vasha Kade leads now

betrayed.text: She looks at you the way she looks at the pens. "You told him." Nothing else. The thumb is on the safety.

shale.text: "A well with people around it. I'm going to take the well. The people can stay if they're useful."

kessler.text: "He keeps a list of who he hasn't robbed. I keep count of who's hungry. Guess which list is longer."

raid.text: "The guild pays Kessler to leave the highway alone. The guild has never paid me." She looks east, where the wall is. "Four Dogs and me, at the verge, when you walk up to the gate. You start it. We finish it. The warehouse is ours, the road is yours, and the guild learns the Sallow has teeth." A beat. "Kessler won't know until it's done."

decision.text: You agreed to hit Tollhouse 9 with Vasha and four Dogs.

raid_yes.text: "We leave tonight. Walk the highway like you own it; we'll be in the salt. Don't pay them. If you pay them I'll know what you are."

intro.text: Don't stand on the skyline. — You're the salt-cut one. I found him, you know. Your old man from the salt cut. Out past the west track, sitting against a post with his boots off, talking to the boots.

said.text: "That he'd been shot by people who were paid to shoot him, and that he'd rather give the paper to a thief than to a bank. He meant Kessler. He meant it as a compliment."

brought.text: "Across a dog. He weighed nothing." She looks west. "I wanted to let him go east, where he was pointed. Kessler wanted the paper. Kessler got the paper, the old man got water, and he walked west to die on your step. Everybody got what they wanted. That's the camp."

options.text: The paper. I want it. Help me.
Come to Shale. You and whoever follows you. Sheriff Vey will take you in, under her law.
Did he have anything else on him? Besides the map.

mods.why: she has decided you are all right

steal.text: "…You want me to lift it out of Kessler's coach." A long look at the west track. "I'll do it. Tonight. The price is you: when you leave, I leave with you, and you don't ask about the girl until I tell you."

decision.text: Wren agreed to steal the map for you, for a place at your side when you leave.

steal_yes.text: "After the fires. Find me here. Don't be near the hall."

girl.text: "That's asking." She goes back to watching the road, and the conversation is over for now.

steal_now.text: "Wait here. Watch the road for me — it's the one thing nobody else does." She is gone an hour, and comes back with the paper and no expression at all. "Kessler sleeps like a man with a list. Let's go, before he reads it."

decision.text: Wren stole the stranger's map from Kessler's hall. She leaves with you.

news.text: something was taken from Kessler's coach in the night

exodus.text: "…She said that." Wren is very still. "If it's true, I bring the girl, and Brindle, and Sprat, and the paper, and Kessler keeps his list and his camp. Tonight. If it isn't true, I'll know, and so will Vey."

decision.text: Wren took the map and her people to Shale on your word that the sheriff would have them.

news.text: some of the Rust Dogs walked into Shale and asked for the sheriff

leaving.text: "Brindle talks." Not angry. "Everyone's leaving; most people just do it by dying. I'd rather walk." She doesn't say where.

page.text: She takes a folded page from inside her hood: a leaf torn from a notebook, the same tight marks. "He was tearing it up to burn it when I found him. This one he dropped. I can't read it. Can you?"

page_no.text: "A waterskin and a bad hip." She isn't going to say more today.

text.text: She has stopped on the pavement across from the boarded garage and is not looking at it. "Dogs had that." It is all she says for a while. "I was six. Perpetua carried me down the stair the night the Rustmouths took the bridge, and Kessler carried the cache key, and Fenn stayed because of his knees." She looks at it now. "He's still in there. I can smell the stove."
"Two riders, no dust." She means: nothing to report. "Where next?"

haunt.text: "The cache is under the bench by the south wall; Fenn sits on it, which is the point of Fenn. The key was Kessler's and went with Kessler." She breathes out. "Fenn will open it for me. He won't open it for you. Let me do the talking, for once."

home.text: "Home." He says it like a sum that finally came out. "Mags shouted for an hour and then fed me for two. I owe you a count, and I keep my counts." He is already behind the bar, where the books are.

options.text: The Tollmen's wall on the highway. Could you write a pass the gate would take?

pass.text: "I kept Kessler's books and Kessler keeps the guild's waybills, because he can't read them and likes the paper." He takes a sheet from under the bar, and writes for a minute in a hand that isn't his. "Bearer and goods. Hold it like you've had it for years."

intro.text: You're not a Dog. You're — are you from Shale? Did Mags send you? Tell her I'm fine. Tell her it's forty, not sixty, and I can prove it, I've got the whole thing in my head —

options.text: Mags sent me. She's running the bar alone.
How did you end up in here?

mags.text: He puts his face in his hands for a moment. "She'll kill me. She'll kill me and then she'll feed me. Tell her the count was right. The brother's debt was forty and it was never mine."

options.text: How did you end up in here?

how.text: "Mags's brother ran salt east and owed the Dogs for passage. He died owing. The Dogs say debts are family. I say I'm not family, I'm a partner, and nobody out here can tell the difference." He laughs, badly. "I taught Perpetua to keep books. She likes me. It doesn't help."

out.text: "Kessler wants sixty. Perpetua would take forty, if you ask her like she's a person. And the lock on this gate is Jack's work, and Jack's work is bad — but there are eyes on it all day."

free.text: "They let me out. They actually —" He stops, breathes. "I'm going home. Walk with me as far as the road? I don't trust my legs."

options.text: Go. I'll see you in Shale.

text.text: The cage gate: a chain and a padlock that Sallow Jack made from two other padlocks. The fires are down; the nearest Dog is asleep against the pier.
The cage gate: a chain and a padlock that Sallow Jack made from two other padlocks. Lute is watching you from the pens, and Brindle from the gate.

decision.text: You picked the cage open in the night and let Teo Marsh walk.

news.text: the trader walked out of the Dogs' cage in the night

decision.text: You went at the cage lock in daylight, in front of the Dogs.

picked.text: The second padlock gives the way Jack's work gives. Teo is already standing.

pick_fail.text: Jack's work is bad, but it is bad in two places at once. You get the chain off and not the lock, and put it back before anyone turns over.

open.text: The cage stands open. The cot still holds the shape of a man who counted to stay sane.

text.text: Kessler's table, one lamp turned low. The folded paper under a shotgun shell. Kessler on the cot an arm's length away, breathing like a man with a list.
Kessler's table. The folded paper under a shotgun shell, and Kessler at the table.

decision.text: You lifted the stranger's map from under Kessler's lamp while he slept.

news.text: something was taken from Kessler's coach in the night

lifted.text: The shell rolls a quarter turn and stops. Kessler does not. You are out of the coach before you breathe.

caught.text: The shell rolls off the table. "Fair," Kessler says from the cot, without moving, and the shotgun is in his hands.

decision.text: Kessler caught you at his table in the night.

bare.text: Kessler's table. The shotgun shell, and nothing under it.

intro.text: Dog-mother. Forty years in this camp; the dogs are mine, the races are mine, the memory's mine. The dogs say you're not afraid, which means you don't know enough yet.

options.text: The old man from the salt cut.
The Tollmen's wall. Can you write a pass the gate would take?

pass.text: "I kept the guild's books at Ninebridge for six years before I kept the Dogs'. I know the paper and I know the hand." She holds out her own, palm up. "Thirty Tolls. Or nothing, if you're the one who got my bookkeeper out of that cage."

pass_done.text: She writes it on the back of a guild waybill she has had for six years, folds it twice, and gives it to you warm. "Hold it like it's yours. The sergeant looks at hands, not paper."

stranger.text: "Wren brought him in across Biter. He paid Kessler in paper and me in a story, and the story was worth more." She waits to be asked.

story.text: "That the city counts us. All of us, out here, under a road. That it has a list, and the paper is the list, and the names on it have dates." She shrugs. "I'm sixty. My date's whatever it is. But I'd like to know Kessler's."

teo.text: "Forty with me; sixty with Kessler, who adds the keeping. He taught me to keep books, that one, and then he kept them too well." She looks at the cage. "Pay me forty and I'll say I lost the count. I've lost worse."

decision.text: You paid Perpetua forty Tolls to lose the count on Teo Marsh's debt.

news.text: the Dog-mother let Teo Marsh go

paid.text: "Lute. The trader's count is done." She doesn't look up from the dogs.

races.text: "Race day's when I say. The Dogs settle things on it — who leads the next run, who eats first. Come back when I say, and bring something to lose."

intro.text: Sallow Jack. Everything shoots; nothing shoots straight. Brass is money, powder is money, a bolt rifle is a month's money. What are you carrying?

tollmen.text: "Pike. Don't tell Kessler." He grins. "Kessler knows. Everyone sells to the Tollmen in the end; the trick is to be the last one."

bolt.text: "That one." He looks at it the way other men look at water. "Kessler would give you the paper for it, I think. I'd give you forty Tolls and my undying regret."

look.text: A road tanker's tank on blocks, SHALE WATER CO-OP still stencilled on the side under a painted dog. It is three-quarters full. A Dog with a revolver sits on the sandbags.

passives.text: The outlet valve is a bad weld on a good fitting. It would take a wrench and a minute, and it would drain into sand.

look.text: Kessler's chest: a locker with a padlock, and on the lid in chalk a list of names with lines through most of them. The paper isn't in here. It's under the lamp.

text.text:
Sheriff. Twice a year, and you still make me ask.

We walked. Somebody cut the truck's fuel line in the night, so we walked, with a cart, and I am not in a mood.
Sheriff. Twice a year, and you still make me ask.
Forty measures of water, everything the bar has brewed, and the salt-cut face there tells me what the bunker's worth. Kessler may have said less. Kessler isn't here.
Forty measures of water, everything the bar has brewed, and the salt-cut face there tells me what the bunker's worth.

passives.text: Four Dogs. Two revolvers, a sawn-off, a pipe. Issa has the bolt rifle on the office roof and Vasha has not looked up once, which means she knows.

options.text: Kessler's terms were half of last time, in water. The sheriff has agreed to them. Take it and go.
Kessler's terms were half, in water. I carried them. Sheriff — half.

mods.why: the sheriff trusts you

options.text: Shale pays nothing this year. Walk home, Vasha, and tell Kessler his list just got longer.

mods.why: the militia counts you as a rifle
they came on foot

options.text: Your truck's cut. You carry what you can carry, and you carry it now.
(Pay it yourself.) Forty Tolls, and the water stays in Shale.

terms_ok.text: "Kessler's terms." She laughs, once, without anything in it. "Half, then, if the sheriff says and Kessler says and the salt cut says. Count it, Sheriff. I'll be counting too." The Dogs load twenty measures onto the cart. She looks at you the whole time.

decision.text: Shale paid the Dogs half, on Kessler's terms you carried; Vasha Kade left with less than she came for.

news.text: the Dogs took half the tithe this year, on the chief's own terms

terms_fail.speaker: npc_sh_01
terms_fail.text: "I said nothing about half." Flat, in front of the town. "Say the number, Vasha."

zero.text: A long silence. The Dogs look at her; the town looks at the Dogs. "…Then it's on you," Vasha says, very quietly, and takes only the drink. "Say your name again, salt cut. I want it right."

decision.text: You talked Vasha Kade down to nothing on Tribute Day. The Dogs went home with drink and no water.

news.text: Shale paid the Dogs nothing this year and the Dogs walked

zero_fail.text: "No." She doesn't raise her voice. "Forty measures. Now the salt cut has made it fifty."

truck.text: She looks at the cart, and at the four Dogs, and at the forty measures she cannot carry. "Ten measures. And the drink." The town hears it. "Whoever cut my truck: I'll find you. I find everyone."

decision.text: With their truck cut, the Dogs could carry only ten measures out of Shale on Tribute Day.

news.text: the Dogs came on foot and left with a quarter of the tithe

pay_you.text: Vasha weighs the Tolls in her hand and then, deliberately, does not count them. "The salt cut pays Shale's water." She pockets it. "That's a thing I'll remember." The Dogs take the drink and leave the water where it is.

decision.text: You paid the Dogs' tithe yourself, in Tolls, and Shale kept its water.

news.text: the one from the salt cut paid the Dogs' tithe out of their own pocket

text.text: "Noted." She looks at Issa on the roof, and at Jonah, and at you. "We pay." Jonah's face does something. "Forty measures. Load it, and get out of my town."
"We pay." She doesn't look at Jonah. "Forty measures. Load it, and get out of my town."

decision.text: Shale paid the Dogs' tithe in full on Tribute Day, on the sheriff's word.

news.text: Shale paid the Dogs' tithe in full

text.text: "…Noted." The word she promised. "Issa."
"You don't speak for Shale —" and then Issa, from the roof: "They do now." Ada closes her eyes for exactly one second. "Issa."

decision.text: Shale fought the Rust Dogs at the wells on Tribute Day, on your word.

text.text: A pre-Burn flatbed kept alive by Sallow Jack and spite: the Dogs' truck, the one that carries the tithe. The fires are down and the nearest Dog is asleep against a pier.
A pre-Burn flatbed kept alive by Sallow Jack and spite: the Dogs' truck, the one that carries the tithe. Lute is twenty paces off, watching the pens — and you.

joins.text: "Right." He puts the bottle on the far side of the fence. He picks up the rifle. "I count things. Out loud. You'll get used to it or you won't." He looks east, where the road is, and his face does something you weren't meant to see.

decision.text: Ilya Strand came with you, east, toward Vasha Kade.

joins_shot.text: The bottle goes. He watches the glass fall for a second longer than anyone else. "Right." He picks up the rifle. "I count things. Out loud." He doesn't look east. He doesn't have to.

decision.text: You outshot Ilya Strand's bottle and he came east with you.

news.text: Ilya Strand walked out of Shale with the salt-cut stranger, sober

refuses_shot.text: You miss. He doesn't say anything, which is worse. Then he shoots the bottle, from the fence, sitting down. "Right."

text.text: "Three days." He means sober. He is counting those too. "Right."
"Wind's from the east." He has the rifle slung and his hands are steady, mostly. "Right."

options.text: You talk about the wind a lot.

p_vasha.text: "When." He likes the word. "She knows my name. I want her to know why before. After is after." He counts something. "You'll have an opinion. Keep it until then."

p_wind.text: "Wind's the thing you can't see that moves the thing you can." He shrugs. "Three nights east on a hunt because the wind was right. Right." He doesn't say anything else for a while.

halt.text: A rifle shot takes the top off the sandbag beside you, and then a voice from behind the fire barrel, flat as the ground: "Far enough. That was the one I had to spare." A woman in a hood with a bolt rifle, older than her voice. Somewhere behind her a kid is whistling, and stops.

passives.text: She worked the bolt and did not chamber. The next one is a bluff or a prayer, and she counted it out loud for a reason.
Smoke from three shacks, a planter with something green in it, and a line worn in the dust where water has been carried every day for years. People live here, and not many.

options.text: I came from Signal Hill. The relay there feeds a line to this station. DW-4.

decision.text: You told the rifle at Dry Wells where the line comes from, and she let you by.

options.text: (Look at the station, not at her.) Twin reciprocating, pre-Burn, a header tank on a tower. Same as the ones I grew up under.

options.text: I don't know what valve. I came for the station. Whatever is in it sets Shale's water, and Shale is dying of it.

shale_no.text: "Shale doesn't send people who don't know what the valve is." The bolt goes back, and this time it comes forward. "Go home. Tell them the pressure drop is the drought."

hill.text: "DW-4." The rifle comes down slowly, like something being put back where it lives. "Nobody's called it that since Grandmother's father. He had it painted on the door." She looks at you a long moment. "Then you know more than Shale does. Come and tell her what you know."

pumphand.text: "Grew up under." She says it twice, trying it. "Under." The rifle goes across her chest. "Then you'll know what the clock sounds like. Eleven. Come and tell Grandmother what it sounds like where you're from, because she's never heard anyone else say it."

ilya.text: "Sable." Ilya, beside you, not raising his voice. "It's Strand. I brought the cartridges in the spring. I brought this one." A silence in which the kid starts whistling again. "Strand," she says. "You still owe me three." The rifle goes down.

through.text: She steps out from the barrel without lowering the rifle all the way, which is how she walks everywhere. "The shacks are ours. The station's Grandmother's. The tower's nobody's and don't climb it; Wick's up there and he bites." A nod at the long concrete building. "She'll want to see you before you touch anything that hums."

intro.text: "Sable. I shoot things for the family and I count what I shoot with." The rifle lies across her knees on the sandbags. "Seven rounds. Six, now. I don't spend one on Shale unless Shale brings a wagon."

options.text: The pumps run on a schedule. Who sets it?
The pumps run on a schedule. Who sets it?

why.text: "Because the water under this floor is theirs, and the valve on the line is ours, and Shale has a sheriff who'd call that a word that ends with a rope." She shrugs. "We take a trickle. A trickle in Shale is a bucket. A bucket here is five people alive."

station.text: "The pumps, and a room at the end with a door that was locked when Grandmother was a girl, and a light that's green on the other side of it. Her father had the key. She has it now. She doesn't go in." A beat. "It makes a noise before eleven. Every day. You'll hear it."

schedule.text: "Not us. Not Shale; Shale thinks it's the weather, or God, or the Tollmen. Grandmother says the city. I say it doesn't matter who, it matters that it's on time." She looks east. "Something that's been on time for ninety years is a thing I don't want to meet."

text.text: "The graveyard, then the glass, then a bridge with a town on it. I've walked it twice." She looks at the station, where the pumps are running outside the clock. "You did a thing in there that somebody east will come to look at. I'll walk you as far as the glass, so you're not the first thing they see. Past that you're on your own, and so is everyone."
"East is east. Don't get shot." She goes back to counting.

decision.text: Sable Marr will walk you east as far as the glass.

escort.text: "When you go, come past the sandbags and say so. I'll have the rounds I've got."

hostile.text: She is behind the sandbags with the rifle.

intro.text: An old woman in a chair that was built for sitting, hands folded on a stick, eyes that measured you from the window before you reached the door. "Sable let you by, so you said something true. Sit. I'm Oriel Marr. My father was the pump man here, and his father before the Burn, and that chair you're not sitting in was his." She waits. Under the floor, something clicks, and the pumps begin.

passives.text: The cough she is holding in is wet. Lungs, not dust. She has been holding it in for a long time.
The key on the cord round her neck is brass, worn to gold where a thumb has rubbed it for sixty years and never once turned it in a lock.

options.text: Who are you people? Nobody in Shale knows you.
Eleven o'clock. Sable said you'd say listen.
The station. Sable says it's yours, and that there's a room at the end nobody goes in.
Shale could take you in. Five people, under the sheriff's law.
Sheriff Vey says yes. Under her law, as townsfolk, and the valve closes.
(Forty Tolls.) For the road. The windpump graveyard, then the glass. There's nothing here once the schedule changes.
Stay, then. I won't tell Shale about the valve.

text.text: She does not look at you. The chair is still the only thing in the room built for sitting.
"It's quiet under the floor, or it isn't. Either way, you did it." She looks at the chair, then at you. "Sit, this time."
"The chair's still empty."

options.text: The room at the end of the station.

who.text: "Ghosts. That's what the Tollmen call us, when they call us anything." She smiles with half her face. "We came out of a hole in the ground, same as you by the look of you. Not yours. Another one, east, with a number on it. Its pumps stopped when I was nine and the door didn't open, and my father opened it with a bar. Forty of us walked. Five of us are here."

why_here.text: "Because it was the only building on the road my father knew the inside of. He'd been sent here once, before, to read a gauge. He read it again and said: this one still answers to somebody, and somebody is feeding Shale through it, and Shale will never come looking at the thing that feeds it." A click under the floor. "He was right for sixty years."

clock.text: "Six, eleven, four, nine. Every day since before I was born, and twice a year the numbers move and nobody here moves them." She taps the floor with the stick. "That's Shale drinking. When the numbers moved last spring, Shale got less. Shale thinks it's the drought. It isn't the drought."

station.text: "My father's room. He said whatever was in there wasn't ours to touch, and then he died of the same thing I'm dying of, and I've kept it the way he left it." Her hand goes to the cord. "You want the key. Everybody who gets past Sable wants the key, in the end."

options.text: (Tell her what the clock sounds like where you come from.)
Give it to me and I'll see your family stays. Whatever is in there, I use it for them first.

mods.why: you treated her cough before you asked
you listened to the whole story
she has decided to like you

key_pumphand.text: "Then it's the same clock." She lifts the cord over her head as if it weighs what it weighed when she was nine. "He'd have given it to one of his own. Go and read his gauge." The key is warm. "And if the thing in there asks you for a word, the word is on the first page of his book. He never let me read past it."

decision.text: Oriel Marr gave you her father's key because you knew his clock.

key_given.text: She looks at you for the length of a pump run, and then lifts the cord over her head. "For them first." The key is warm from sixty years of being held. "If the thing in there asks you for a word, the word is on the first page of his book. He never let me read past it."

decision.text: Oriel Marr gave you her father's key on your word that the family comes first.

key_no.text: "Everybody says first." Her hand closes on the key. "My father said it, about Shale. Come back when you've done something for us that wasn't a sentence."

key_taken.text: She does not resist, which is worse than if she had. The cord comes over her head; her hair catches in it. "There," she says. "Now you're the same as the thing in there."

decision.text: You took the station key off Oriel Marr's neck.

stay.text: "Under a rope, you mean. The valve's a hanging in Shale." She considers it anyway, which is more than you expected. "Juno would go. Wick would go and come back. Cato would stay for the valve and Sable would stay for Cato. Ask your sheriff. If she says yes and means it, I'll decide for all of them, which is what I'm for."

go_shale.text: "As townsfolk." She says it like a word in another language. "Then close the valve yourself, so Cato can hate you and not me, and we'll walk. I have walked out of one place with less." She stands, which takes a while. "Tell your sheriff: five, and one of them coughs."

decision.text: The Dry Wells family walked to Shale under Sheriff Vey's law.

news.text: five people out of a dead cistern have come in off the Dry Wells track and the sheriff has given them the old tannery

no_shale.text: "No." She nods as if she had bet on it. "Then we stay, and the valve stays, and when Shale comes it comes. It was always going to." A click under the floor.

decision.text: Shale refused the Dry Wells family; they stay on their trickle.

move_on.text: She looks at the Tolls a long time before she takes them. "The graveyard, then the glass. My father walked it the other way." She puts the money in the stick, which is hollow. "Sable will say no and come anyway. Give us a week."

decision.text: You paid the Dry Wells family to move on east.

leave_be.text: "Then you're the first from that direction who didn't." She closes her eyes. "Eleven o'clock. Listen."

decision.text: You left the Dry Wells family on their trickle and told Shale nothing.

after_fight.text: She is in the chair. She has not moved. "You shot at my family from behind a sandbag they filled. Take the key. Take the chair. There's nothing in that room worth what you paid for it."

intro.text: "Beans. In a planter. In Dry Wells." She does not look up from them. "Grandmother says that's a joke. I say it's beans. They don't care what they're a joke about."

options.text: Your grandmother's cough. (Give her a knit kit for it.)

decision.text: You left medicine for Oriel Marr's lungs with her granddaughter.

options.text: Your grandmother's cough. (Show her how to steam the lungs: a bucket, a cloth, the stove.)

decision.text: You showed Juno Marr how to ease her grandmother's lungs.

options.text: Would you go to Shale, if they'd have you?

cough.text: She looks up for the first time. "She'll say she doesn't need it. Give it to me and I'll put it in the tea." A pause. "Thank you. Nobody from that way says thank you either, so."

cough_no.text: She listens, and nods, and you can see her deciding it is nonsense.

shale.text: "Tomorrow." No hesitation at all. "I've never been anywhere with a second street. Don't tell Cato I said it. Don't tell them about the valve."

hostile.text: She has a knife and no idea what to do with it.

intro.text: "The valve's mine." He says it before you have asked anything. "Grandmother says when, I say how far. A quarter turn at eleven, back at noon. Shale never missed it. Shale never will."

options.text: Shale is missing it. The schedule has been cut; they're drinking at sixty-two parts in a hundred.

cut.text: "Then it was the city cut it, not us." He does not move. "Our quarter turn was there before the cut and after it. You want somebody to blame for Shale, there's a room at the end of the station with a green light in it. Go and blame that."

close.text: "You close it and I open it. You break it and we die here, slow, in front of Grandmother." He picks up the pipe, not to use it, just to have it. "Which do you want to be?"

closed.text: He is standing by the valve with the pipe in both hands and does not look at you. "Noon," he says. "It's past noon."

intro.text: A kid on the tower ladder, barefoot, with a sling in his belt. "I can hear it. The click. Sable says it's the pipe cooling. It isn't. It's before, not after."

passives.text: He is right. A click, then the pumps. Something counts first.

east.text: "The graveyard. Pumps like ours with no water in them, standing up in a line. Past that it shines, all day, and you can't look at it." He points. "I went as far as the first one. There was a bird."

shale.text: "I've seen its water go past under the floor." He thinks about it. "Is it big? Does it have a tower?"

hostile.text: He is up the tower and has stones.

locked.text: A steel door at the east end of the pump hall, painted with a number worn to a shape: 4. The lock is a good one, pre-Burn, oiled by someone who never opened it. Behind it something hums at a pitch you feel in your teeth.

mods.why: you have stood on the other side of locks like this
a pipe for a lever

opens.text: The lock turns like it was oiled yesterday. The hum gets louder, and greener.

forced.text: The frame goes before the lock does, with a noise the whole of Dry Wells hears. Across the yard, somebody puts a rifle down on a sandbag very carefully.

pick_no.text: The pins are pre-Burn and cut to a tolerance nobody has made since. Twenty minutes, and the pick comes out bent.

force_no.text: The door does not care. Your shoulder does.

open.text: The door stands open on the green light.

wake.text: A console the width of the wall, dust on everything but the screen, which is clean because it has never been off. DW-4 — SUPPLY SCHEDULE — NETWORK 4. Below, a table: downstream nodes, allocations, times. SHALE — 0.62 — 06:00 11:00 16:00 21:00. C9 RESERVE — HELD. UPSTREAM AUTH: LINK UP. LAST CHANGE: 194 DAYS. ORIGIN OF CHANGE: UPSTREAM.

passives.text: 0.62 is not a measure of water. It is a fraction of something else: a target. The schedule is written to hold Shale at a number.
The change log is in record shorthand. Your hand. Every entry is signed the way the Cistern's outbound logs are signed.

decision.text: You set Shale's allocation at Dry Wells to the full measure. Something upstream will notice.

restore_no.text: The console rejects the number twice, and the second time it logs you: a line in shorthand, the hour, the attempt. The screen goes back to the table. Patient.

keep_sure.text: SHALE — 0.62. The pumps on their clock. Shale thinner every year, in a way nobody there can name. Somewhere upstream, a line in a book stays as it was.

options.text: (Leave it. It isn't yours to change, and whatever changed it can change it back.)

decision.text: You left the Dry Wells schedule as you found it: Shale at 0.62.

kept.text: The screen does not change, because nothing has. At eleven, under the floor, the pumps start on time.

text.text: SHALE — 1.00. ORIGIN OF CHANGE: DW-4 LOCAL. The pumps are running outside the clock, and the log's last line is yours.
FAULT — GOVERNOR. The table is frozen at a number the pumps no longer read. Under the floor they run flat out, and the screen has stopped pretending to know.
GUILD OVERRIDE — POST NINE-WEST. The table has a new column, and the column is headed PAID.
SHALE — 0.62. Nothing has changed, which was the choice.

c9_after.text: C9 RESERVE — HELD — INFLOW: NETWORK 4 — SETPOINT: CONSTANT. The reservoir you grew up under is not a reservoir. It is a tank on a line, and the line comes through here.

look.text: A pressure panel, gauges in a row, one needle alive. Under them a governor box with a lead seal, and pressed into the lead a half-moon like the one on everything the Tollmen carry. Older, though. Much older.

passives.text: The governor is what listens to the console. Break it and the pumps run on their own pressure, flat out, until the aquifer or the bearings give up.

broken_now.text: The seal goes, then the box. The pumps lurch, miss, and come up together at a pitch the hall was never built for; the floor hums; the tower pipe sings. Through the door the console says FAULT and then says nothing. Shale will have water tonight. All of it, until something gives.

decision.text: You broke the governor at Dry Wells. The pumps run flat out, for Shale, until something gives.

break_no.text: The box is built like the door. You skin a knuckle on the seal and the needle does not so much as tremble.

broken.text: The governor box is in pieces on the floor. The pumps do not stop.

look.text: A hand-wheel on the line where it leaves the hall, going north under the floor toward Shale. Off it, a branch, newer, hand-made, running west toward the shacks. The paint on the wheel is gone on exactly one quarter.

passives.text: A bypass. The family's tap. Whatever Shale gets, this takes a little first.

decision.text: You closed the family's bypass at Dry Wells.

closed_now.text: A quarter turn, then another, against sixty years of habit. The branch line ticks as it drains. Across the yard a kid stops whistling.

close_no.text: The wheel is seized at the quarter. Someone has made sure it only goes one way.

closed.text: The wheel is shut. The branch line is dry and quiet.

text.text: Two pumps the size of houses, pre-Burn and patched since by somebody who knew them. You could strip the near one blind; you did, at home, every spring. The box on it that clicks before every run is the only thing on it you never saw there.

Two pumps the size of houses, pre-Burn and patched since by somebody who knew them: brass where there was brass, scrap where there wasn't. Between runs they tick as they cool. A box on the near one clicks before every run.

passives.text: The click is the click on the north pump in Shale's yard. The same box. Counting.

look.text: A table with one book on it, swollen with sixty years of being read: a pump man's diary. Gauges, dates, a drawing of a door. The first page is a line of block capitals, underlined twice.

read.text: The first page: MAINT AUTH — MARR — DW4 — "ELEVEN". Then forty years of readings in a hand that gets smaller. The last entry, from before you were born: "Shale cut to .62. Not drought. Told no one. Who would I tell."

text.text: "Take it," says Oriel from the chair, without opening her eyes. "I know what's in it. I've had sixty years."
Nobody says anything. The book is lighter than it looks.
She watches you put it under your coat and says nothing, which is worse than if she had.

gone.text: The table, and the mark where the book was.

intro.text: "Factor Pike's compliments." A guild engineer with a ledger open on the console and a flask of good water beside it. "Allocation is by the measure now, and the measure is posted. Shale will find it reliable. Everyone does, in the end."

halt.text: Two bikes across the track, engines ticking as they cool, and a man with a ledger open on the tank. "Guild road." He does not look up yet. "Papers, or the rate."

passives.text: The ledger has a column headed FEES and no column headed RECEIPTS. Whatever you pay here stays here.

options.text: There's no receipts column in that book. I'll pay the post, not you.
(The pass is forged, or there is no pass.) I came through the gate like anyone.

mods.why: you have told this story before

passed.text: He checks the stamp against a card from his pocket, writes a line, and closes the book. "Bearer and goods. As per." The bikes do not move; you go round them.

courier.text: The seal gets a longer look than you do. "Courier." He writes your description in the book, not your name, the way the clerk did. "The road is yours. Don't open it."

paid.text: The coins go into a pocket, not the tank bag. A line in the book. "Guild thanks you for your custom."

skim.text: The pen stops. The other rider finds something interesting on the horizon. "Post nine-west will have your description," he says, and then, closing the book: "Go on."

skim_no.text: "The rate is the rate." He writes something longer than a line. "Five. Or the road is closed to you between here and the post, which is a long way round."

bluffed.text: He looks at you the way the gate did. "Everyone comes through the gate like anyone." But he writes nothing, and the bikes do not move, and you go round.

bluff_no.text: "No stamp." He says it to the other rider, not to you. "No stamp is a fee." Ten Tolls, or the road closes.

raid.text: The ledger closes before you have reached the bikes. "You." The rider's hand is on the carbine. "The gate at nine. You were with the Dogs." There is nothing to show him.

ran.text: The bikes don't do rock. You lose them in the first gully and your breath in the second.

ran_no.text: The first shot is over your head. The second is not meant to be.

fire.text: A man by a fire that went out a day ago, one leg out straight in front of him and the trouser cut away above a knee that is the wrong colour. He has the machete across his lap and does not lift it. "Don't," he says. "Whatever it is. Just don't."

passives.text: Not a bite: a cut, deep, a week old, gone septic. A knitkit and a clean dressing would save the leg today. Tomorrow is a different question.
His pack has been gone through, by him, several times. Water: none. He has been here two days.

options.text: (Treat the leg. A knitkit, a bandage.)

decision.text: You treated a dying drifter's leg on the road.

news.text: the salt-cut stranger stopped for a drifter on the road and doctored a leg nobody else would have

decision.text: You robbed a dying drifter on the road.

news.text: someone stripped a crippled drifter on the salt track and left him

kite.text: "A kite." He watches you not believe it. "Big wings, no bird in them. It came down on the pan at dusk and sat, and I went to look, because I'm a fool, and something on it opened and I ran, and I fell on my own blade. I know. I know how it sounds." A shrug. "It's still out there. South, on the white."

treated.text: He makes a noise through his teeth while the knitkit does its work, and then another, different noise. "Amory," he says. "Pell Amory. I don't forget a face. I'll be in Shale if the leg holds and at the overpass if it doesn't, and either way I owe you a thing I can't name yet." He gives you the machete. "I'll get another."

water.text: He drinks half and stops himself, which is the hardest thing you have seen anyone do this week. "Amory. Pell." He looks at the leg. "If you've got anything for this, I'm listening. If you haven't, go on, and don't look back, I hate that."

options.text: (Treat the leg. A knitkit, a bandage.)

decision.text: You treated a dying drifter's leg on the road.

robbed.text: He does not fight you for it. "Fine," he says, to the fire that is out. "Fine."

again.text: He has nothing left to say to you.

halt.text: Two of them come up out of the ditch where they were lying in the shade, scrap plates and a sawn-off and a zip gun, and the one with the gun says what they all say. "Water. Then we'll see."

passives.text: They are a long way from the overpass on foot, and the one with the zip gun is counting her rounds with her thumb. Scouts, not a raid.

options.text: Kessler knows my face. Say my name at the overpass and see what it buys you.

options.text: (Say nothing. Let them look at you.)

watered.text: He drinks, passes it, and the woman drinks the rest without taking her eyes off you. "Shale's," he says, of the water, tasting it. "Pipe. Go on, then."

named.text: The name does something to the man's face. "Kessler's." He looks at the woman. She shrugs. "Then you're Kessler's problem," he says, and sits back down in the ditch.

named_no.text: "Everybody knows Kessler." The sawn-off comes up a little. "Water."

feared.text: You do not say anything. After a while the woman says a name that is yours, and something that was done at the overpass, and the man lowers the sawn-off and looks at the ditch as if it had been his idea to sit there.

known.text: They know you before you are close enough to be a threat, and the greeting is a lifted hand and a lowered gun. "Kessler's friend." The man grins with what teeth he has. "Water, if you've got it. We're a long way from the pipe."

wren.text: "Calloway." The man says it before Wren has said anything. "Thought you were dead, or Shale, which is the same." Wren says nothing for long enough that he looks away first. "Go on," he says, to you.

trough.text: Two horses at a stone trough with water in it, which is impossible, and a grey man in a long coat filling it from a skin without hurry. He has seen you for a mile. "Horses first," he says. "Then you."

passives.text: The trough is fed: a buried line, a tap, a stone to hide it. The Wheel has water on roads nobody else knows have it.

options.text: The Wheel. Forty wagons. I've heard of you.

who.text: "Forty-one, since spring." He pats the near horse. "A town that moves. We trade with everyone and owe no one, and we go where the water is, which is never where the map says." He looks at you properly for the first time. "You walk like someone with a long way to go and no horse. The Wheel has horses."

where.text: "East of the dead pumps, this month, in the lee of the hill. Next month, who knows; the mother does." He names her: Sefa. "Come with something to trade and a horse's worth of manners and they'll feed you. Come with the guild's paper and they'll feed you to the dogs."

night.text: A man on the track at night, walking east with one hand held out in front of him flat, palm down, as if the air were a wall he was following. No pack. No water. He does not stop when he sees you; he does not see you.

passives.text: Dehydrated three days at least. Pupils wrong. He should be dead and is walking instead, which happens, for a while.
On the back of his hand, where it catches your lamp: a mark burned off, the way the stranger's was.

east.text: "East." He says it to the air in front of his hand. "It said east. It said my name and then it said east and then it said a number, and the number is where I stop." He walks on. He is not hurrying. He will not get there.

stopped.text: He is lighter than he should be and does not struggle; he just keeps leaning east, the way a plant leans. Up close his lips are cracked white and his eyes are somewhere else. "I had a name," he says. "It's in the book now."

decision.text: You stopped a man walking east to die and gave him water.

watered.text: He drinks like a child, and for a moment the eyes come back from wherever they were and look at you, and are afraid. "Don't let it read yours," he says, quite clearly. Then the hand goes out flat again, and he leans. You can walk him to Shale, if you are going that way, and he will go east again the first night.

slipped.text: He goes past you like water round a stone and does not look back, and in a minute the dark has him.

axle.text: A guild wagon down on one corner, the mule looking at the horizon, a carter on his back under the bed and a guard with a shotgun who watches you instead of the road. "Axle," says the carter, from under the wagon. "If you've got hands, I've got water. If you've got a gun, he's got a bigger one."

options.text: (Get under and look at the axle.)

mods.why: you have had worse things apart

fixed.text: A split block and a bent pin; an hour with a bar, a wedge and a lot of the carter's opinions, and the wagon stands up. He pays like a man who has been told to: ten Tolls and two waters, counted twice. "Guild thanks you for your custom." The guard lowers the gun a finger.

decision.text: You put a guild wagon back on its wheels on the road.

fix_no.text: The block is split through and the pin is not coming out for anyone without a forge. You get grease to the elbow and the carter's respect, which is worth nothing. "Post will send a wagon," he says. "Eventually."

again.text: "Still here." The mule has not moved either.

wheel.text: The wagon stops the way a wagon stops when it has decided to: a crack, a lurch, and the left rear wheel leaning out from the axle like a drunk from a doorway. Ansel is already under it. "Pin's sheared. I've a spare pin and no spare hands. Lift, or wait for somebody who can."

mods.why: you have had your hands in worse

options.text: (Take the weight while he sets it.)

fixed.text: The pin goes in on the second try and the wheel comes true. Ansel wipes his hands on the salt sacks. "Kin would have charged me for that." He looks at you. "I'll tell her you didn't."

lifted.text: You take the corner of the bed on your shoulder and the world goes red at the edges for the length of a held breath, and then the pin is in and Ansel is saying "down, down, down." He does not thank you. He hands you the water first, which is the same thing.

fail.text: The pin goes in crooked and comes out again, and the second time it bends. Ansel says nothing, which is worse. In the end it is a Tollmen guard off the guild's wagon who sets it, and writes something in a book.

waited.text: Four hours of salt and sky. A guild guard comes back down the line at last, sets the pin in a minute with a tool made for it, and tells Ansel the Wheel owes the guild a favour. Ansel says the Wheel owes nobody. The guard writes it down anyway.

halt.text: Two of them, on foot, from behind the cut where the road bends: scrap plates, one carbine between them, and the easy manner of people who have done this before. "Salt." Hale nods at the wagon as if introducing it. "Salt pays. Forty, and the road's yours."

options.text: Kessler counts you. Does Kessler know you're out here collecting?
The Wheel feeds Dogs when the tribute's late. You want to be the one who ended that?

kin.text: Hale's manner goes somewhere else. "He doesn't." Nettle has already stepped off the road. "Didn't see a wagon. Didn't see you." They are gone into the cut before Ansel has finished reaching for the gun under the seat.

talked.text: It lands. Nettle looks at Hale; Hale looks at the salt; the salt does not look back. "Go on, then." He steps aside with a flourish that costs him something. "Tell the old woman the Dogs let her through."

talk_no.text: "Forty," Hale says, as if you had not spoken, and Nettle's hand finds the carbine's strap.

paid.text: The Tolls go into a plate pocket. "Pleasure." They are off the road and gone. Ansel, from the seat: "That's the Wheel's forty. Tell her, not me."

intro.text: A woman with a burn down one side of her face and a coil of green wire over her shoulder, halfway up the last tower with a pair of cutters. She looks down at you the way the towers do. "Copper's mine. Say what you're here for from down there; I'm not coming down for a face."

passives.text: She is stripping the wind-generator coils, not the pump wire. Somebody is paying for coil copper, which means somebody is winding motors.

options.text: The ruts going east. The Wheel?
A drifter on the road said a kite came down on the pan.
The ruts going east. The Wheel?
A drifter said a kite came down on the pan.

pumps.text: "Nothing killed them. Somebody turned them off." She taps the tower with the cutters. "Vanes are locked, not seized. Brakes set from the valve house, all six, same day. Water went down the pipe to somewhere that mattered more, and the troughs went dry, and the farm that was here walked to Shale and became Shale." A shrug. "Sixty years. The game still comes at dusk. Habit."

wheel.text: "Forty-one wagons and a woman called Sefa who could sell sand to the pan. They camp east, in the lee of the hill, a week at a time, and they buy my copper and sell me back the horseshoes it came from." She almost smiles. "Go with something to trade. Go without the guild's paper. And don't touch the horses."

copper.text: "The Wheel, for the shoes. And a man at Tollhouse 9 who doesn't write it down, for Tolls, and he sends it east, and east of that I don't ask." She winds the coil tighter. "Someone's building motors. Someone always is."

kite.text: She stops cutting. "South. On the white. I saw it come down." She comes down the tower after all, slowly. "It sat two days and then it went up again, and where it sat there's a truck now that wasn't there before, and I don't go near it, and nor does the game." She points, south and west, across the pan.

hostile.text: She is behind the tower with the zip gun.

look.text: A windpump: a lattice tower, a vane the size of a door locked side-on to the wind, a rod down the middle that has not moved in sixty years. At the foot, a pump head with its brake set and a brass plate: NETWORK 4 — FIELD 2 — No. 3.

passives.text: The brake is a remote one. There is no handle. It was set from somewhere else.

view.text: From the top the pan is a sheet of hammered tin, and the hill east has a smudge of smoke in its lee, and south-west, far out on the white, something square that throws a shadow the wrong colour.

fall.text: A rung lets go and you learn the height of the second one from the ground.

look.text: A valve bank in a concrete box: six levers, all set the same way, each wired to a solenoid, and the solenoids wired to a cable that goes out through the wall and under the pan. A stencil above them: FIELD 2 — BRAKE — REMOTE.

passives.text: The cable runs east along the pipe line, toward the pump station at Dry Wells and whatever is upstream of that. This field was switched off by the same hand that sets Shale's schedule.

mods.why: you have freed worse

released.text: Six levers, six solenoids forced, and outside, one after another, the vanes come round into the wind with a noise like a town waking up. The rods move. Nothing comes up the pipes; the water went somewhere else sixty years ago. But the troughs fill, slowly, from what is left in the ground, and by evening there will be game at them.

decision.text: You freed the windpumps on the pan; the troughs fill again.

news.text: the dead windpumps on the pan are turning again

release_no.text: The solenoids are stronger than you are. One lever moves a hand's width and goes back.

look.text: In the middle of the ring: a machine the size of a big dog, sitting the way a dog sits, grey plates over a frame that is all angles, four legs folded under it, a head that is one lens and no mouth. Salt has drifted against its flank. It is not moving. It is not rusting either.

passives.text: The lens is not dark. Deep in it, something the colour of a pilot light is on, and has been on for a long time. It is not dead. It is waiting.

Pre-Burn, and not city work: a maker's mark on the shoulder plate, a crown over a gear. Military or something that bought from the military. The folded legs are a rest state: it sat down on an instruction, and it will stand on one.

again.text: The machine sits in its ring. The lens is on you now, and was not before.

touch.text: Warm. Not sun-warm: warm from inside, like a sleeping animal. Under your palm something in the plates shifts the width of a hair and settles, and the lens, which was looking at the truck, is looking at you.

controller.text: The slab warms in your hand the moment it is in the lens's line, and a single point of light comes up under its surface and holds. The machine's head lifts an inch. It is listening to the thing you are holding, and through it, to you.

options.text: (Tell it to stand, and follow, and keep Shale.)

mods.why: the manifest names what it is
you know whose it was

options.text: (Tell it to stay. Keep the controller.)

decision.text: You left the machine on the pan sleeping and kept its controller.

woken.text: It stands. Four legs unfold with a sound like a gate, salt pouring off the plates, and it is taller than you expected and quieter, and the lens turns once around the whole horizon and comes back to the slab in your hand. It takes a step toward you and stops, exactly where a dog stops. It will walk at your heel to Shale and sit in the sheriff's yard and nothing will come into that town at night that it does not look at first.

decision.text: You woke the machine on the pan and sent it to keep Shale.

news.text: a grey machine the size of a dog walked into Shale at the salt-cut stranger's heel and sat down in the sheriff's yard

wake_no.text: The slab goes dark in your hand. The head lowers the inch it had lifted. Whatever you said, it was not the word, and it has gone back to waiting for someone who knows it.

kept.text: The head settles. The light in the slab goes down to a point and stays. Somewhere east, you think, somebody has a slab like this one and is not using it, and does not know that you are.

text.text: The ring in the crust, empty. The salt is already drifting into the shape it sat in.
It sits in its ring, and will, until the guild's engineer comes with the slab you sold and says the word. You feel the lens on your back all the way to the edge of the pan.
It sits. The lens follows you. The slab in your pack is warm.

look.text: A guild truck on its side, the half-moon on the door, the cab crushed where it rolled and the trailer split. The skid behind it runs half a mile straight: it was going fast, in a straight line, away from something, and then it was not going at all. No bodies. Drag marks, two, toward the ring.

passives.text: The engine is whole; the cab is not. The truck did not fail. Something stopped it the way a hand stops a toy.
The drag marks go toward the ring and do not come back. In the crust beside them, prints: four-toed, each the size of your spread hand, pressed deep.

intro.text: A man on his knees at the foot of a tree with leaves on it, packing wet cloth round the roots with the care of someone dressing a wound. He does not get up. "Brother Anselm. You'll be from Shale, or through it. Mind the rows; the living ones are the ones with the cloth."

passives.text: Twelve living trees out of a hundred-odd dead: root-stock that survived the Burn under the ash, coaxed up over years. Nobody else in the Sallow is growing anything on a tree.

options.text: How do you keep a tree alive out here?
Sister Calla says something is robbing you.
You said they take the green ones. Who does?
There's a gap in the north wall with a Dog's plate dropped in it.

text.text: He is at the rows again, and the cloth is dry, and he looks up when you come as if he has been waiting to.
"Mind the rows."

options.text: How do you keep a tree alive out here?
There's a gap in the north wall with a Dog's plate dropped in it.

trees.text: "You don't. The tree keeps itself alive; you keep the ground from killing it." He pats the cloth. "Shade the roots, water them at dusk so the sun doesn't take it, and bury what dies at the foot of what lives. The Burn didn't kill the roots. It killed everything above them and then it killed the people who'd have waited." A breath. "The Choir waits. That's most of what we are."

thieves.text: "Twice a week, since the fruit set. They come over the north wall and take the green ones, which nobody takes, because they're sour enough to take the skin off your tongue." He stands, finally, slowly. "Petra heard them. Two, small. Dun says the prints are a Dog's, and Dun would know." He looks at the rows. "I don't want them hurt. I want them to stop. Those are two different things and I only know how to ask for one."

stakeout.text: "A Dog's plate." He turns it over in his hand as if it might be a seed. "Then it's what Dun said. Small, and from the overpass, and hungry enough for green fruit." He gives it back. "Wait for them, if you will. By the beds, after the lamps are out. I'll tell the novices to sleep through it." A pause. "Don't hurt them."

decision.text: You agreed to wait for the orchard thieves by the seedbeds at night.

text.text: "They're in Petra's tent. The small one cried for an hour and then ate four." He shakes his head. "Two Dogs, under the open sky. The overpass will want them back, or it won't, and either way they eat. Thank you. I don't know yet what I've thanked you for."

"You took them back." He says it without blame, which is worse. "Then they'll come again when they're hungry, and someone with a gun will be waiting instead of you. Or they won't come, and I'll wonder what the Dogs do with children who get caught." He goes back to the cloth.

"The sheriff's cell." He looks at the north wall a long time. "She'll feed them. She'll send to the overpass. The overpass will say they're not theirs." He kneels again. "I asked you not to hurt them. I should have said what I meant."

"You let them go." A nod, slow. "With fruit, Petra says. Then they'll come back, and I'll leave the green ones on the wall, and we'll call it a tithe and not a theft." He almost smiles. "The sky is open. So is the wall."

fruit.text: "Two." He counts them into your hand from his pocket, small and hard. "Sour. Eat them anyway; you'll not have had one. Tell Shale the Choir grew them, and tell them it took nine years."

seed_given.text: He opens it there in the rows, which Calla would not have, and holds a single seed up to the light between finger and thumb like a jeweller. "Bean." His voice goes. "Ninety years in the dark and it's a bean." He closes the case. "Tomorrow. The south beds. Pike will hear; let him hear it from the plants."

news.text: The Cistern's seed went into the Choir's beds.

decision.text: You gave the Cistern's seed to the Choir.

intro.text: A girl with her braid full of dust, thinning seedlings in a bed with a knife no longer than her thumb. "You're not Choir. You walk like a wall." She says it as a fact, not a complaint.

options.text: Brother Anselm says you heard the thieves.

heard.text: "Two nights. Whispering, by the beds, and the wall scraping." She points with the knife. "North. One of them said Mote, run. So one of them is Mote." She goes back to the seedlings. "They took the green ones. You'd have to be starving. I was, once; I'd have taken the green ones."

choir.text: "Because they feed you first and ask what you believe after, and after goes on for a long time." A shrug. "Sister Calla took me off the road at Shale with a fever. I stayed. I'd have stayed for the fruit."

intro.text: A big young man hauling at the well rope, with the look of someone who was built for something else and is working at this one. "Dun. I draw the water. The well's forty feet and the bucket's thirty-nine, so I draw it twice."

options.text: Anselm says you know a Dog's footprint.

prints.text: "Scrap-plate sole, two straps, the left one mended with wire. Kids' size." He lets the bucket down. "Kessler doesn't send kids over walls. Kids go over walls when there's nothing on the right side of them." He looks north. "Catch them and don't take them back. That's all I'll say."

dog.text: "Till I was twelve, and then Perpetua said I had a face for walls and gave me to the Choir with a sack of salt, as a trade." He draws the bucket up. "I don't go back. I don't say why."

look.text: A post with a board on it, and on the board, burned in with a wire: an open circle, and under it, THE SKY IS OPEN. Below that, smaller, in another hand: and the wall is low. Someone has left two green fruit on the ledge.

A well with a windlass and a rope that has been spliced four times. The water, when the bucket comes up, is clear and tastes of stone, not pipe: this is not the network's water. It is the orchard's own.

filled.text: Clean water, for once, for nothing.

look.text: A gap in the north wall where the stones have been taken down a course and put back wrong. In the rubble on the orchard side, scuffs, and a scrap of something that glints.

passives.text: Two sets of prints, small, scrap-plate soles. They come at night and go the same way, north-west, toward the overpass road.
The glint is a Rust Dog's plate, the little kind they wear on a cord, snapped off its wire.

plate.text: A thumb-sized scrap of plate with a dog's head scratched on it, the way the overpass marks its own. A child's cord through it.

beds.text: Two shapes at the beds in the dark, filling a sack with green fruit, so intent that you are three steps away before one of them looks up. A boy with a shiv and a girl with the sack, neither of them sixteen, both of them all eyes. "Mote," the boy says. "Run."

options.text: Don't. Nobody here is going to hurt you. Put the sack down and sit.

mods.why: you can say Dun's name
the Dogs have heard of you

wren.text: "Kip." Wren does not raise her voice. "Mote. Your mother's Fen, under the third pier, and she thinks you're at the salt." The boy's shiv goes down. The girl starts to cry, silently, the way children do who have learned not to be heard.

grabbed.text: You have him by the collar before the shiv is up, and he goes limp the way a kid goes limp who has been grabbed before. The girl does not run. She will not leave him.

sat.text: They sit. The story comes out of the girl in pieces, with the sack in her lap: the overpass has been short since the tithe, the little ones eat last, the orchard has fruit on trees and nobody shoots at you here. "They're sour," she says, as if that were the crime. "We only take the sour ones."

options.text: Stay. The Choir feeds you first and asks after. Ask for Dun; he was one of you.

decision.text: The two Rust Dog children who robbed the orchard stayed with the Choir.

news.text: two Rust Dog children are sleeping in the Choir's tents at the orchard
two of the overpass's children went to the Choir and did not come back

options.text: I'll walk you back to the overpass. Tonight. Whoever is short there can answer to me.

decision.text: You walked the orchard thieves back to the overpass.

options.text: The sheriff's cell, and she can send to the overpass for you.

decision.text: You handed the orchard thieves to Sheriff Vey.

options.text: Take the sack. Take the green ones, always, and nothing else, and go over the wall where the stones are loose.

decision.text: You let the orchard thieves go with the green fruit.

choir.text: The boy looks at the tents as if they were a trap with the teeth showing. The girl looks at the trees. "They've got fruit on them," she says, and that decides it.

returned.text: Four hours in the dark, the girl asleep on your back for the last one, and a lamp at the overpass gate that knows you. Whoever is short there will be shorter. But they are home, and the Dogs will remember who walked them.

cell.text: Ada does not ask you what they did. She looks at their feet and sends Jonah for blankets, and the boy says one word, which is a Dog's word for a cage.

go.text: They are over the wall before you have finished the sentence. The sack goes over first. In the morning Anselm will find two green fruit left on the shrine, which is a kind of receipt.

ran.text: They are gone over the north wall with the sack, and the stones come down behind them. You will not catch them tonight, and tomorrow they will know the beds are watched.

text.text: "Oh, it's you." A nod, almost a smile. "Dust's up. Mind the wells, they're slippy when they run."
"Hm." They look past you. "Don't know anything. Ask the sheriff."
"You're not from here." Not a question. "We get a few. Most go on east. Water's two a measure if you're asking."

a0.text: "Office is the one with the flag that was a sheet once. Knock; she doesn't like surprises."

a1.text: "Mags has a room behind the saloon, if you've got ten and don't mind the noise. The Choir'll put you on a cot for nothing and pray at you for less."

a2.text: "Comes when it comes. Twice a year somebody turns a dial somewhere and it comes less." A shrug. "Nobody here knows where the dial is."

text.text: "Give us a hand with this?" They laugh. "No. Go on. You've done enough for one town."
"Two more loads." They don't stop. "Talk fast."

a0.text: "Scrap, salt, water, whatever's heavy. The guild pays by the load and weighs it light."

a1.text: "Work's work. Beats the overpass. Beats the road." They heft it. "Doesn't beat much else."

text.text: "Looking or buying?" The stall is three planks and a cloth, and everything on it has been owned before.

a0.text: "Odds. Wire, a lamp that works, a boot that doesn't. Pike has the real stock; I have what Pike won't touch."

a1.text: "Anyone with Tolls. Drifters, Dogs on a quiet day, the Choir when they've sold fruit. Guild scrip at a discount, and don't tell Pike I said so."

text.text: "Don't." They say it before you have asked anything. Then, softer: "Spare a water?"

a0.text: "Somewhere with a name. It's gone; I'm not. That's the whole story, friend."

a1.text: "East, like everyone. Or west, if east doesn't want me." They look at the road. "The road doesn't care."

text.text: "The sky is open, friend." A grey scarf, clean hands, a look that is kinder than the place. "Are you hurt? We don't charge for asking."

a0.text: "That the sky keeps no books. That what's buried under it is free. That's most of it; the rest is farming."

a1.text: "The tents by the west wall, with the sign on the pole. Sister Calla is there; she'll see to you before she sees to herself."

text.text: "Kessler's friend." A nod with no warmth in it, which from a Dog is warmth. "Don't steal anything. That's our job."
"What are you looking at." Scrap plates, a knife, a face that has been hit more than once. "Keep walking."

options.text: What is it like, under the overpass?

a0.text: "Dry. Loud. Nobody dies alone, which is more than Shale can say." They spit. "Kessler counts us. That's the deal."

text.text: "Move along." The carbine stays where it is, which is the courtesy. "Nothing to see. If there was, you'd have paid for it."

a0.text: "Quiet is the job. Loud is a report I have to write." A glance at the road. "Dogs came by last month. I wrote it."

text.text: "Horses first." They finish with the horse before they look at you. "Trade or go; the Wheel doesn't stop for talk."

a0.text: "Where the water is. The mother decides; the rest of us find out at dawn." A shrug. "It's a good way to live if you don't need to know."

text.text: "Got a light?" They don't want a light. They want to know what you are, and they decide fast.

a0.text: "Whoever's standing on it. Right now that's me, and I'm not selling, so."

text.text: "Wash it. Then come back." They say it without looking up, to anyone, about anything.

a0.text: "Always. Dust in the lungs, salt in the cuts, the water doing what the water does. Sit if you're bleeding; otherwise I'm working."

intro.text: She does not get up. She looks at your boots, then your hands, then your face, in that order, and nods at the fire as if it were a chair. "Sit. You're a guest till you're not. Sefa Oduya; this is my wheel. Eat first; then tell me what you want from it."
