options.text: Is there work on the road?

text.text: "Road-kin." She moves her stick so there is room by the fire. "Sit. What have you brought us from the places that don't move?"
"Guest." The nod again. "Sit. The water's been paid for."

options.text: Is there work on the road?

wheel.text: "Nine families, seven wagons, four horses, no address." She counts it on her fingers like a thing she has said a thousand times, because she has. "We carry what towns want between towns that don't talk. Salt east, water west, letters both ways, people sometimes. We stop four days and move. Anyone who stops longer than four days is a town, and towns get taxed, and towns get Dogs. We don't."

tollmen.text: "The Tollmen tax a road. We are not on a road; we are beside one. Pike pretends not to see the difference and we pretend not to see Pike." A thin smile. "That is the whole treaty. It has held thirty years."

join.text: "You don't. You ride with us until somebody says kin and nobody says no." She shrugs. "Share a road. Pay a debt. Don't steal. It isn't a secret; it's just slow."

text.text: "East, toward the Dry Wells pans, on the fourth morning. Then north under the orchard, then the overpass side, then back here by Shale. A ring. It's in the name."
"North, under the orchard, on the fourth morning. Then the overpass side, then Shale, then back to these pans. A ring. It's in the name."
"West, the overpass side, on the fourth morning. We don't go under it; we camp where the Dogs can see us and count us. Then Shale, then the Dry Wells pans, then back here. A ring."
"Shale, on the fourth morning. Then the Dry Wells pans, then under the orchard, then back here where the Dogs can count us. A ring. It's in the name."

job.text: "There's always work on the road, and most of it is walking next to a wagon with a gun and not shooting it." She looks you over again. "We've a wagon of salt going to Tollhouse 9 with the Tollmen's caravan. The guild's guards guard the guild's wagons. Ours needs its own. Sixty Tolls at the gate, and the Wheel remembers who rode."

job_yes.text: "Then it leaves when you do. Walk the Tollhouse road from Shale and keep the wagon in your eye. If the road asks you for something, remember it's asking the Wheel."

son.text: "He does." She lets the fire have a moment. "He's right that a well that doesn't dry is worth more than a road that doesn't end. He's wrong that you can own one without owing somebody. I had a town once. It is under the salt now." She looks at you. "Don't tell him I said he was right."

intro.text: "You're the one from Shale." He has been watching the camp the way a man watches a room he wants to leave. "Dario. Hers." A nod at the fire. "Is it true the well there runs all year?"

options.text: It runs. The town fights over it.
Your mother's salt wagon. Tell me about the road.

well.text: "Everybody fights over everything. At least a well is worth it." He turns a cartridge over in his fingers. "We fight over which pan to stop on."

town.text: "I want a door. One that shuts." He says it quietly, because the ring has ears. "She thinks a door is a cage. She's not wrong about the old towns. But the old towns are gone and the salt took them, and Shale is still there." He looks at you. "You've lived in a place with a door. Is it a cage?"

options.text: A door is a door. What you do behind it is yours.
Your mother kept nine families alive without one.

door.text: "That's what I think." He almost smiles. "Don't tell her you said so."

road_answer.text: "She did." He puts the cartridge away. "And she's tired, and nobody says so, and the Wheel will turn until it doesn't." He looks at the horses. "Four, now."

road.text: "Dogs on the road sometimes, when the tribute's late. A ford that isn't a ford after rain. And the Tollmen's own guards, who'll help you with a wheel and charge the Wheel for the help." He shrugs. "Keep the wagon in your eye. That's the whole job."

intro.text: "Not behind her." Mirren Kade doesn't look away from the horse. "Front, slow, hand out. There. Now she knows you." A nod. "Horse-master. I'm not selling."

options.text: Could I ride one, if I needed to be somewhere fast?

horses.text: "Two pull, two rest, one dies every winter and I don't replace it, because there's nothing to replace it with. The Tollmen have mules. Mules eat less and think less. I'd rather have horses and think."

ride.text: "When you're kin, maybe. A horse is a road that carries you. We don't lend roads." She finally looks at you. "Ride with the wagon first. Then ask again."

intro.text: "Everything on the blanket walked here." Tulla Oduya spreads her hands over it: water, jerky, cartridges in paper, a lamp, strips of Holdfast. "So did the price. Looking or buying?"

letters.text: "To anywhere the Wheel stops and most places the Tollmen do. Write it at a caravan post; it rides with the next wagon. Replies come back the same way, when they come."

read.text: Two ledgers. The first is the Dry Well as everyone sees it: water in by the barrel, water out by the cup, rooms, Dust stakes, the barman's wages, the barman's shortfalls circled twice. The second is thinner and newer, and the figures in it are the first ledger's figures with the air let out of them.

passives.text: The second set isn't a thief's work; it's a lender's. Interest against the deed, compounding; a buyout line, signed, dated two months ago; the margins initialled in the Tollmen's half-moon hand. On paper the Dry Well is Factor Pike's. The town drinks here and does not know.
The numbers in the second book are the first book's numbers made smaller in the same places every month — not stolen, hidden. Hidden from whom?

options.text: (It is a buyout, and she is hiding it.)

again.text: The books, as before. You know what is in them.

cot.text: An old man on a cot, breathing like a bellows with a hole in it. Each breath is a decision. "Dust," he says, when he can. "Forty years of it. Don't — don't fuss."

options.text: (Sit him up, open the tent flap for air, make him breathe slow with you.)
(Give him water, a sip at a time.)

eased.text: It takes a quarter of an hour and all of your attention, and at the end of it he is breathing in the rhythm you gave him and not his own. "Where'd you learn that." You don't answer. "Don't tell me. Keep it."

eased_no.text: You sit him up and the coughing gets worse before it gets better, and then it does not get better. Calla comes and does something with her hands to his back, and he sleeps. "Next time," she says, "ask me first."

watered.text: He drinks the way a wall drinks rain. It will not fix his lungs. It fixes the next hour. "Two a measure," he says, meaning the water, meaning thank you.

done.text: He is asleep, or doing a good impression of it. His breath is slow.

cot.text: A girl of fifteen or so with her left arm strapped to a board, watching the tent flap and not you. "It's fine. It's fine. Calla did it. I don't need —" She stops when you sit down. "Who are you?"

passives.text: The sleeve of her good arm has ridden up. On the forearm, in blue, badly: a dog's head with a bolt through it. The overpass puts that on its children.

options.text: (Check the splint and re-tie it; the board has slipped.)
(Replace the board with a proper splint.)

set.text: The board had slipped a thumb's width; another day and the bone would have set wrong. You re-tie it the way Calla would, and the girl watches your hands the whole time instead of the flap. "You're good at that." Suspicious. "Who taught you?"

set_no.text: You get the knot wrong twice and she hisses the second time. Calla takes over without comment. "Next one," she says.

splinted.text: A real splint, padded, buckled. She looks at it as if it were a bracelet. "That's a lot of a thing to waste on me."

dog.text: She goes white, then red, then still. "Don't." Barely a whisper. "Calla knows. Calla doesn't care. The sheriff would. Kessler would." Her good hand has found the edge of the cot. "I fell off the deck. That's all. I fell off the deck and the Choir picked me up. Please."

decision.text: You kept a Rust Dog child's secret in the Choir tent.

options.text: The sheriff will hear it from somebody. Better it's from me, with you ready.

kept.text: "Okay." She breathes. "Okay." The flap stops being the only thing in the tent.

warned.text: "Then I'll be gone before you get there." She is already working at the strap with her teeth. Calla, from the other cot: "Pip. Lie down." Pip lies down. Nobody looks at you.

done.text: She is watching the flap again, but less.

gone.text: The cot is empty and stripped. Calla has not said a word to you since.

cot.text: A big man shaking under two blankets in the heat of the day, eyes wet and far. "Kit?" he says, to you. "Kit, the rope." Then, closer: "Sorry. Sorry. Thought you were —" The fever takes him back.

options.text: (Cool him: wet cloth, the blankets off, water by the spoon.)

mods.why: you have water to spare for it

options.text: (Sit with him an hour and keep him drinking.)

cooled.text: The blankets come off over his protests and the cloth goes on, and in half an hour the shaking is a shiver and the eyes are his own. "Who's Kit?" you ask. "Nobody," he says, and sleeps.

cooled_no.text: He fights the cloth and wins, and the fever climbs, and Calla comes with something bitter in a cup and says nothing at all, which is her way of saying it.

sat.text: An hour of spoon and cup and the far side of a fever. Toward the end of it he knows where he is. "You're the one from the salt cut." Everyone is. "Thanks."

intro.text: "Two cups a day." She says it before you have asked anything, the way the whole town says the price of water. "Hesper Vale. If you're selling, I'm not buying, and if you're buying, it's two a measure like everyone."

options.text: I've a letter for Edda Vale.

text.text: She looks at you the way you look at a tool you have decided not to use again. "Did he read it?"
"Did you take it back to him?" She does not ask what he said.

letter.text: The name stops her. She takes the letter and does not open it. "My mother." The salt wind moves the dust between you. "She's been under the pan six years. The lung." She opens it then, and reads it standing in the street, and when she has finished she folds it along its own creases and holds it against her stomach. "He thinks she's alive. He thinks she's been waiting."

options.text: Write him what she would have written.

truth.text: She sits down on the edge of the trough and writes on the back of his letter, slowly, stopping twice. "That she kept it. The thing he sent before. That she talked about the door." She gives you the sheet. "That she's gone, and I'm here. He can do what he likes with the rest."

kind.text: "I won't lie in her hand." But she tells you, in pieces, what her mother used to say, and how she said it, and you write it down in a hand that is nobody's, and when you read it back to her she turns away. "Give him that, then. God help you both."

decision.text: You wrote Bram a letter from a dead woman.

kind_no.text: "No." Flat. "She's dead. Either tell him or tell him nothing. I won't help you make her say things."

tell.text: "Then tell him." She keeps the letter. "Tell him she kept the other one. Tell him I'm called Hesper. He'll know why."

text.text: The toll-warden lifts a hand from the sandbags without getting up. "Twelve to cross. One of that's the porters' now, so you can feel good about it. Pay, ticket, or courier."

The toll-warden steps out from the sandbags with a shotgun on a sling and a face that has said the next sentence ten thousand times. "Ninebridge. Twelve to cross. Pay, ticket, or courier — there's no fourth thing."

passives.text: The porters sitting under the ramp with their straps off are the reason the warden looks tired. Nothing has moved up the ramp today but people.

options.text: (Show the sealed packet.) Courier. For the Exchange.
(Show the Tollhouse stamp.) I've paid the guild once.
What are they doing under the ramp?
I'm not paying twelve to walk on a road.

stamp_ok.text: He looks at the stamp, and at you, and decides it is not worth the sentence. "Wall's stamp. Not the bridge's. Eight, and don't tell the bridge."

stamp_no.text: "That's the wall's stamp. This is a bridge. Different thing, same guild, twelve."

strike.text: "Sitting. Straps off. They want a tenth of the crossing for carrying it up the ramp, which they will not get, because the guild has it in writing that they're back on the third day." He says it flatly, like a man reading off a card. "Goods wait. People can walk."

passives.text: In writing. He glanced at his pocket when he said it, where a folded paper makes a square under the cloth.

courier.text: "Courier." He touches the seal with one finger as if it might be hot. "Hall's mid-span. The Grand Factor signs for paper herself. Don't drop it in the river." He waves you through.

in.text: "Guild deck past the sandbags. Mind the ninth span — planks on the south side. Block's on the far bank if you're buying people, Exchange is mid-span if you're buying paper, the Span if you're buying the other thing."

threat.text: The shotgun does not move. A guard you had not seen steps out of the booth behind you. "Then you're a loss to the bridge, and we write losses in the river." He waits. "Twelve."

decision.text: You drew on the guild at the Ninebridge toll.

fight.text: The warden has nothing to say to you now that the guns are out.

intro.text: "Esk Varga. Toll-warden, Ninebridge west." He does not offer a hand; he has a count going. "If it's about the rate, the rate's on the sign. If it's about the porters, I've a job going."

options.text: You said they're back on the third day. Who says?

again.text: "Warden." The count goes on behind his eyes.

job.text: "Forty backs under the ramp. Talk them up the ramp with their straps on, on the guild's terms, and the guild pays eighty. I'd do it myself but they know my face, and I'm the face." He shrugs. "They're back on the third day regardless. You'd be saving them two days of hungry. Call it charity."

options.text: What makes you sure about the third day?

third.text: "The guild." A beat too long. "The guild is sure about a lot of things. It has paper on most of them." He looks at the camp, and for one second he is a man and not a post. "Third day. I've seen the paper."

bridge.text: "Nine spans when it was built. Eight when the river stopped — the ninth went into the bed the same year, with the market on it, and the guild bought the other eight from whoever was standing on them. Planks across the gap. Twelve to cross. That's the history."

claim.text: He has heard. "Straps on, terms unchanged, and the Grand Factor asked me who did it." He counts eighty from a belt pouch into your hand without looking at it. "Don't drink it here. They're watching."

paid_out.text: "Paid. We're square." He looks at the ramp, where the goods are moving.

text.text: A new line is painted on the rates board, and the warden has a new way of not looking at you. "A tenth to the porters. First time the bridge ever paid for its own legs. The Grand Factor says it's a cost."
"Straps on. Goods moving. The paper was right, which it usually is." He does not say thank you; the guild does not.
NINEBRIDGE — CROSSING 12 — GOODS BY THE MEASURE — TICKET-HOLDERS FREE — COURIERS FREE — and under it, fresh paint over old: PORTERS' TENTH, PAID AT THE RAMP.

NINEBRIDGE — CROSSING 12 — GOODS BY THE MEASURE — TICKET-HOLDERS FREE — COURIERS FREE — NO CREDIT — THE GUILD IS CREDIT. Someone has scratched FOR WHOM under the last line and someone else has painted over it, badly.

read.text: A plank painted in tar: STRAPS OFF. A TENTH OR NOTHING MOVES. — THE BACKS OF NINEBRIDGE. Under it, smaller and newer: DAY TWO.

intro.text: A broad man with a porter's shoulders and a porter's ruined knees sits by the fire with his strap coiled beside him like a sleeping dog. "If you're the guild's, say so and I'll save us both the breath. If you're not, sit. We've water. We've nothing else."

options.text: The warden says you're back on the third day.
(Pick up a strap.) Where do you want it?
(Pay the tenth yourself. 60 Tolls) Call it a loan against the guild.
You'll lose. The guild has it written. Go up the ramp and keep your knees.

mods.why: you have seen the paper and can describe it
they have heard what you did to the guild

options.text: The warden says the third day.
You'll lose. Go up the ramp.

mods.why: you have seen the paper

what.text: "A tenth of the crossing. Twelve Tolls a head comes over this bridge and not one of them goes to the backs that carry the goods up the ramp. One in ten. The guild says the bridge can't afford it." He looks up at eight spans of concrete. "The bridge was free when it was built."

third.text: "They said that before we sat down. Third day. Like weather." He turns the strap over. "I don't know how they know. I know that if a man tells you how a fight ends before it starts, he's either lying or he's fixed it. And the guild doesn't lie; it's too dear."

sheet.text: He reads slowly, lips moving over the guild's capitals. NINEBRIDGE — PORTERS' STOPPAGE — ENDS THIRD DAY, STRAPS ON, TERMS UNCHANGED. Dated the day before they sat down. He reads it twice. Then he stands, which takes a while, and holds it up so the fire can see it. "They wrote our ending before we started," he says, not loudly. "Then we're off their page." Forty people put their straps down harder.

decision.text: You gave the Ninebridge porters the guild's forecast of their defeat. They sat past the third day and won.

won_now.text: On the fourth morning the goods are still at the foot of the ramp and the Grand Factor sends the warden down to the fire with a rate painted on a board. A tenth. Voss does not gloat; he puts his strap on. "First time," he says, "the bridge paid for its legs."

carry.text: "We're not carrying. That's the point." He looks at your shoulders. "But the goods at the foot of the ramp are the guild's, and if a stranger carried them up — for free, mind, and slow — the guild would have to decide whether that was a strike broken or a strike with help. Make the warden decide something. I'd like to see his face."

mods.why: you have the back for it

carry_ok.text: You carry from the foot of the ramp to the sandbags from first light to dusk, slow, alone, in front of forty people who do not help and do not stop watching, and by the afternoon the warden has sent for the Grand Factor twice. At dusk a board comes down the ramp with a rate on it. A tenth. "He decided," Voss says, and puts his strap on.

decision.text: You carried the guild's goods up the Ninebridge ramp alone until the guild gave the porters their tenth.

carry_no.text: Your shoulders go at noon. Voss sits you down by the fire kindly and does not say anything, which is worse. "Tomorrow, maybe. Or not. Nobody's counting but the guild."

pay.text: He looks at the coin for a long time. "That's a day's tenth. One day." He does not take it yet. "If the guild sees a stranger pay what the bridge won't, either they match it or they're shamed in front of their own deck. The Grand Factor doesn't like to be seen. Try it."

decision.text: You paid the Ninebridge porters a day's tenth out of your own pocket and shamed the guild into matching it.

pay_done.text: By evening a board comes down the ramp with a rate painted on it, and a guild clerk with a face like a closed drawer to say the guild had always meant to. A tenth. Voss hands you back twelve of your sixty. "The first day's. Ours now."

break_ok.text: You talk the way the guild talks, in numbers, and you do not raise your voice, and you describe the paper. Something goes out of the fire. Voss looks at the ramp for a long time. "Third day," he says. "Straps on." Forty people stand up slower than they sat down, and none of them look at you, which is its own kind of looking.

decision.text: You talked the Ninebridge porters back up the ramp on the guild's terms.

break_no.text: "Keep your knees." He says it back to you, slowly. "That's what they said to my father when the ninth span fell with him on it. Sit down or go up the ramp, stranger, but don't tell a porter about his knees."

broken.text: He is carrying. He does not stop, and he does not look at you, and the forty behind him have learned your face the way porters learn a step that gives.

won.text: He is carrying, with his strap on, and when he passes you he lifts two fingers off the strap. A tenth. "Off the page," he says, and goes up the ramp.

read.text: THE SPAN — BITTERS · WATER · DUST · BERTHS — NAMED FOR THE ONE THAT'S MISSING. A hull door in a wall of welded scrap, and lamplight under it.
THE EXCHANGE — NINEBRIDGE — PAPER BOUGHT AND SOLD — TICKET-HOLDERS AND COURIERS — THE FLOOR CLOSES AT NINE. The guild's half-moon, cast in brass, bolted to a shipping container.

Four planks, bolted to the south parapet where the ninth span used to be, over forty feet of air and a riverbed of concrete pieces. A sign: SINGLE FILE. NO GOODS. The guild charges twelve to cross a bridge and will not spend two to mend it.

look.text: A table scarred with dice-cup rings, three stools, and a chalk tally nobody has rubbed out since the river stopped. Lazlo deals. Ask at the bar.

intro.text: The man behind the bar has forearms like bridge cable and a beard with bitters in it. "The Span. Bitters, water, Dust, a berth if you're clean and thirty if you're not." He nods at the corner table without looking at it. "Don't buy her a drink. She'll let you."

options.text: Let me see what you've got.

again.text: "Bitters, water, Dust." He is already pouring something.

options.text: Let me see what you've got.

berth.text: "Berth A. A bed, a locker, a door that locks from your side. Thirty, once, and it's yours for as long as I'm alive and you don't bring the guild to my door." He puts a brass tag on the bar. "Berth B is hers. Has been for years. Don't ask."

berth_done.text: "South side, first box. Sleep well. Nobody does, on the bridge; the river talks even when it's dry."

her.text: "Odile. She was the Exchange, before there was a Grand Factor to be it. Wrote the first paper they ever sold, they say. Drinks on a tab older than the bridge and the Grand Factor pays it, which tells you something, and I've never worked out what." He wipes the bar. "She'll talk to you. She talks to everyone. Listen anyway."

text.text: "The porters, mostly. And a stranger from the salt cut asking after things on the floor." He looks at you. "That'll be you."

"The porters sat down. Guild says third day. Lot four on the block's young, which draws a crowd. And the Grand Factor's had a packet coming from the west for a week and keeps asking the warden if it's come."

not_yours.text: Berth A: a shipping container with a bed in it and a bolt on the inside of the door. Lazlo rents it. Thirty, he said.

yours.text: Your berth. A bed with a real mattress, a locker, a door that locks from your side, and the river talking under the deck all night though it has been dry for ninety years.

hers.text: Berth B. The door is bolted from inside though nobody is in it: Odile's, Lazlo said, for years. A reading-glasses chain hangs on the handle.

gone.text: Berth B. Empty now but for a shabby coat on a nail she did not come back for, and the tab, which Lazlo says the Grand Factor will keep paying because nobody has told her to stop.

intro.text: A woman of fifty-some in a good coat gone shabby sits at the corner table with reading glasses on a chain and a glass of bitters she is not drinking. She looks at your boots, your pack, the way you stand, and has priced you before you sit. "You came in over the planks and you didn't look down. Either brave or from somewhere flat. Sit, my dear. I don't bite; I negotiate."

passives.text: Her left hand is chrome: an old, beautiful piece, every joint visible, that she uses to turn the glass the way other people use a breath.
Three rounds on the table, none paid for, and the barkeep has not pressed her once. Somebody pays her tab and it is not her.

options.text: (Show her the packet, sealed.) What is this?
Who paid for the riders who shot a man at Tollhouse 9?
Come with me. Unwind your trade on the road.

text.text: "My dear." She turns the glass. "The offer stands. Offers are the only things I keep."
"Back. Sit. The bitters are terrible; that's why they're free."

options.text: Who paid for the riders at Tollhouse 9?

who.text: "Odile Marchetti. I was the Exchange, before there was a hall to put it in — I wrote the first sheet the guild ever sold, on this bridge, on a crate, and the girl who held the ink is the Grand Factor now." She does not sound bitter; she sounds like someone quoting a contract. "I left. One leaves. There is a trade I made that I would like to unwind, and one cannot unwind a trade from inside the house that holds it."

trade.text: "I shorted a town." She says it plainly. "Bet that it would fail, by a date, and sold the bet. The town is called Shale, and the counterparty is — well. The counterparty is the reason I drink here and not there." She finishes the bitters at last. "You've a Sallow look. Is it still there? Shale?"

shale_yes.text: "Good." Something in her unclenches by one notch. "Then the trade is still open, and I am still wrong, and that is the best news I have had in a year. Take me with you, my dear, when you go east. I'll pay my way. I know what the paper means, and I know the hand on most of it, and I have one chrome hand that has never lost at Dust."

exchange.text: "Futures." She taps the table with the chrome finger. "Sealed sheets: a place, a date, a thing that happens. Bought from somebody who knows; sold to somebody who wants to be on the right side of it when it does. The seal is the product — open it and it's only news." She watches you work that out. "Yes. Somebody knows. No, I won't say who, at this table, for free."

who_knows.text: "The city." She says it the way the Sallow says *rain*. "Its machine keeps books on everyone it has ever seen the face of, and it writes down what they'll do, and some of what it writes leaks out through the guild, for a price, in sealed sheets. The outriders who shot your man were protecting the trade. Everyone on this deck is." She turns the glass. "That's free. Everything after this costs."

map.text: She puts the glasses on and does not touch the cloth. For a long time she reads the blocks beside the pins the way other people read faces. "Oh, my dear." Very quietly. "That's ours. That's the Exchange's hand — the notation, I mean; I taught it to the girl who taught it to the clerks. Twelve lots." She takes the glasses off. "I can read every one of these. Two a night; more and the eyes go, and the eyes are the only thing I have that isn't borrowed."

price.text: "A seat at your fire, east. And when we reach the place that holds my trade, one hour of your time and no questions until it's done." She holds out the chrome hand. "That is the whole contract. I've written longer ones for less."

packet.text: She weighs the packet in the chrome hand without touching the seal, turns it to the lamp, and sniffs the wax. "Water." She hands it back. "That's a schedule. A number and a date for a town's water — the seal's the floor's, the paper's the Precinct's, and the number is written in a hand that has never been thirsty. Somebody here buys a town's water by the measure, in advance." She looks at your Sallow boots. "Yours, I expect. Deliver it or don't. Opening it costs more than you have."

text.text: "The floor. The protection account, out of the Sarr ledger, by the floor's order — two riders, four days, *westbound traveller, confirmed*. I'd swear to it, and I've read the line." She looks at you steadily. "You wanted it from someone who was there. I wasn't. I was here, hearing it done."

"You'll want it from the ledgers, in the hand that wrote it, and you'll want to be sure. I can tell you where it is written: the floor's protection account, the Sarr ledger, after the closing line for the week the Tollhouse paid two riders four days' wage." She shrugs. "Or ask the Grand Factor. She'll sell it to you. She sells everything."
"That costs, my dear, and I don't know you yet." She turns the glass. "Ask me again when you do."

join.text: She stands, which she does well for someone who has been sitting for a year, puts the glasses in the coat, and leaves the glass. "Lazlo. The tab stays open; let her keep paying it." At the door she takes your arm with the hand that is not hers. "Two blocks a night, my dear. Any more and the eyes go."

decision.text: Odile Marchetti, who was the Exchange once, left the Span with you to unwind a trade.

news.text: the old trader with the tab left the Span with a stranger from the salt cut

waiting.text: "Well? Are we going, or shall I order?"

text.text: "Don't let me near the floor. I'll start pricing things." She says it lightly. She is not joking.
"Weather's turning, my dear. I mean the money. I always mean the money."

options.text: Who paid for the riders at Tollhouse 9?

party_trade.text: "Not here. At a fire, with the map out, and nobody's ledger within a day's walk." She looks east. "I'll read you two names a night. You'll wish I read slower."

text.text: She has the glasses on and the fire at her back, so the light falls on the cloth and not in her eyes. "The next two, then. Or let me rest them."
She has the glasses on and your map weighted flat with a tin. "Two a night. Sit; this is slow, and I want you to see how it's done so that when I'm gone you can do it badly yourself."

read_two.text: She reads the way a surveyor walks: the first block, the second, back to the road. "The second lot: KESSLER, the overpass, day forty-five — *by Kade's hand*. The third: VEY, ADA, Shale, four months — *resigns; a company town*." She takes the glasses off and presses the bridge of her nose. "That's two. Your sheriff and your raider. Both written on the same cloth as your deputy." She folds the map for you. "The eyes go. Tomorrow."

decision.text: Odile read the second and third names on the stranger's map by firelight.

read_more.text: "The next blocks are east of here — names from the farms and the city, and I'd rather read them with the places under our feet; the notation leans on the place." She closes the glasses. "Get us east, my dear. I'll read as we go."

camp_trade.text: "I shorted Shale: sold a sheet that said the town fails by a date, to a buyer who wanted it to. The buyer was the city's machine, through the guild — it buys its own forecasts back when they go against it, to see who's selling. I didn't know that then. I know it now, and the sheet is in the Exchange archive with my name on it, and I would like to tear it up with the hand I have left." She looks at the chrome one. "That is the whole of the trade."

intro.text: A guard in guild grey fills the hall door with a carbine held the easy way. "Floor's for ticket-holders and couriers. Day ticket's fifteen if you've business and no paper."

options.text: (Show the sealed packet.) Courier, for the Grand Factor.

mods.why: you know the Grand Factor is waiting on a packet from the west

night.text: The night guard at the hall door is asleep on his feet, the way guards learn to be, carbine hooked in an elbow. The door behind him is on a latch.

sneak_ok.text: The latch lifts on a breath and you are in the dark of the hall with the board humming to itself and the clerk asleep over her ledgers.

sneak_no.text: The latch clicks. The guard's eyes open without the rest of him moving. "Fifteen. Daylight." The carbine is pointed at the deck, which is a courtesy.

courier.text: He checks the seal against a card and steps aside so fast you feel the draught. "Office is at the east end. She's been asking."

odile_ok.text: The name does something to his face. "Her." He steps aside. "She still drinks here? Tell her the tab's — never mind. In."

talk_ok.text: You say it the way the guild says things, and he decides that whoever is expecting you outranks him. "In. Don't touch the board."

in.text: He steps aside. "Clerk's at the desk. Board's not for touching. Office at the east end is by appointment, and she makes them."

door.text: A container door with GRAND FACTOR stencilled on it and a brass half-moon for a knocker. From inside, the sound of a pen.

options.text: (Knock.) I've something to sell that she'll want to buy.

mods.why: you can drop a name she has not heard in years

talk_ok.text: A pause in the pen. "Everything is for sale. Come in and name it."

talk_no.text: "Not at that price." The pen goes on.

intro.text: The floor clerk has ink on three fingers and a face arranged for not being looked at. "Lots are on the board. Sealed sheets are by the lot number; the floor takes a tenth on resale. If you're selling a contract, I need the paper and a thumb. If you're buying, I need the sum first." She does not ask what you want. People on the floor say.

passives.text: A folded sheet in her sleeve, the guild's paper, with the seal cut clean — a copy, by the ink on her fingers, and not for the board.
The board shows lots and sums. Accounts — who paid whom — are not on it; they are in the two ledgers under her hand, which she turns face down when you look.

options.text: The protection account. Two riders, four days, Tollhouse 9.
I've a debt contract to sell.
(Put the sealed case on the desk.) From the board at Old Market. By hand, unopened.
The line. You said you'd get it.
I've a debt contract to sell.
(Put the sealed case on the desk.) From the board at Old Market.

case.text: She does not open it. She does not ask. A receipt comes across the desk already written, as if the case had been expected since morning: RECEIVED — EXCHANGE FLOOR — ONE CASE, SEALED. "Tell the hatch it still ticks," she says, not looking up. "They like to know."

case_new.text: The new clerk weighs it, listens to it, and puts it under the desk without a receipt. "Half-Price's," he says, to the board. "Tell the hatch the floor has it."

what.text: "Futures. A sealed sheet says what happens at a place on a date. You buy it, you're on the right side of the date. You don't open it; opened, it's news, and news is free." She says it like the rates. "Where they come from is not a floor question."

protection.text: Her pen stops for exactly as long as it takes to decide. "Accounts aren't lots. Accounts are the Grand Factor's." She turns the ledgers a quarter-inch further face down. "The floor closes at nine. I lock them in this desk." It is not clear whether that is a warning or a map.

leak.text: The colour goes out of her. "For — " She looks at the hall door, where the guard is, and back. "For people who'll be on the wrong side of a date and can't afford to know it. The porters. A farmer in Openfield, once." Her hands are flat on the ledgers. "Tell her and I'm on the block by nine."

options.text: Get me the protection line — two riders, four days — and I never saw a sleeve.
The Grand Factor will want to know.

deal_ok.text: "Come back before nine." Her voice is steady and her hands are not. "And when you go up to her, say the clerk sent you. She'll believe that. She thinks I'm hers."

deal_no.text: "I copy forecasts. I don't copy accounts. There's a difference and it's the difference between the block and the river." She will not look at you again today.

report_warn.text: She does not beg. She squares the ledgers. "Then do it before nine. I'd rather be sold in daylight."

kept.text: She breathes out. "Thank you is a floor word. I'll say it anyway." A beat. "If you need the office — say the clerk sent you."

line.text: She slides a torn corner of guild paper across the desk under a lot card. In her small clerk's hand: PROTECTION — TOLLHOUSE 9 — TWO RIDERS, FOUR DAYS — "WESTBOUND TRAVELLER, CONFIRMED" — PAID FROM THE SARR ACCOUNT, BY ORDER OF THE FLOOR. "That's the line. That's all of it. Don't read it here."

sell_contract.text: "Lot four. Sable Calloway, fifty-eight and interest." She reads the paper, not the person. "The floor pays ninety; it takes its tenth off the buyer's end, not yours. Thumb here." She does not ask where the debtor is. The floor never does.

sold.text: The thumb. The sum. The paper goes into a drawer with others like it. "Lot four," she says to nobody, and writes.

asleep.text: The clerk is asleep on her folded arms over the two ledgers, ink on her cheek. The floor is dark but for the board's green.

reported.text: The desk is empty. The ledgers are in the Grand Factor's office now, and a new clerk with no ink on him is learning the board. Lot nine on the block this morning was young and knew her numbers.

options.text: (Put the sealed case on the desk.) From the board at Old Market.

look.text: The board: a pre-Burn screen in a brass frame, green on black, lots scrolling — a place, a date, a sum, SEALED. NINEBRIDGE PORTERS 3RD DAY, 40. OPENFIELD HARVEST, 120. SHALE WATER 0.62, 200. A keyboard under a hinged lid, the lid padlocked, the padlock open.

options.text: (Lift the lid. Find the accounts behind the lots.)

mods.why: you know the accounts are kept apart from the lots
nobody is watching the screen but you

shale.text: SHALE WATER 0.62 — a sealed sheet for sale at two hundred, dated the month you were at Dry Wells. Somebody has bought one already; the lot count has gone from three to two.

pull_ok.text: Behind the lots, three keys deep, the floor keeps its books in the same green. PROTECTION. The week the Tollhouse paid two riders four days: TOLLHOUSE 9 — WESTBOUND TRAVELLER, CONFIRMED — PAID, SARR ACCT, BY ORDER OF THE FLOOR. You copy it onto the back of a lot card in the dark and close the lid.

pull_no.text: The screen blinks, thinks, and shows you a single word — LOCKED — and a sum: FIFTEEN, for the clerk to open it again. The guard at the door has turned his head.

locked.text: LOCKED, in green. The clerk will open it for fifteen and a look.

day.text: Two ledgers under the clerk's hands, face down. She does not move them and she does not look up.

mods.why: you know which of the two to turn

night.text: The clerk is asleep across the two ledgers with her cheek on the open page. The other is under her elbow.

options.text: (Ease the lower one out and read by the board's green.)

read.text: PROTECTION, in the clerk's small hand, week after week: outriders' wages, posts, "confirmed". The week after the stranger reached your door: TOLLHOUSE 9 — TWO RIDERS, FOUR DAYS — "WESTBOUND TRAVELLER, CONFIRMED" — PAID FROM THE SARR ACCOUNT, BY ORDER OF THE FLOOR. You copy the line onto a lot card and put the ledger back the way it lay.

caught_day.text: Her hand comes down flat on the page before yours reaches it. "Accounts aren't lots." The guard at the door has turned round. "Floor's closed to you today."

caught_night.text: She wakes the way clerks wake, all at once and quietly. "Don't." A whisper. "He'll hear. Go out the north door and I never saw you, and don't come back tonight."

done.text: Two ledgers. You have what was in them.

static.text: The pen stops. "For nothing." She says it the way other people say a death. "A sealed sheet is worth what it is worth because it is sealed. A girl who says the sheet aloud in a gang street is a hole in the floor." She writes a figure and turns it to you: two hundred. "The name of the street, and the tower. Riders will fetch her at dawn, with a sheet of her own, and she will be sealed where sealed things are kept, and fed, and listened to by people who pay."

options.text: The Saints' tower in Bridgeward. Under the mast. (200 Tolls)

decision.text: You sold the Exchange the Saints' girl who hears the city's wire.

static_sold.text: "Sealed." The figure goes into the ledger under a line that says nothing about a girl. "The floor thanks you. The floor always thanks you; it is the floor's only expense."

closed.text: The Grand Factor does not look up. "By appointment."

intro.text: A woman of nearly sixty with silver hair swept back and a pen she has not put down since you came in. Clocks on every shelf, none of them agreeing. "Imelda Sarr. Grand Factor." She looks at you once, the way the board looks at a lot. "Everything is for sale. Say what you want and I'll say what it costs, and we'll save each other the part where you pretend it's free."

passives.text: The clocks: each is set to a different day, not a different hour. She keeps time by dates.

options.text: (Put the packet on the desk.) From Tollhouse 9. Sealed.
What is it you sell here?
Who paid for the riders who shot a man at Tollhouse 9?
You sell Shale's water by the number.
Your clerk copies paper for the porters.
I broke your strike. I'd like more than eighty.
I know where your forecasts leak. A girl in Bridgeward hears them off the city's wire and says them for nothing.
I've a debt contract. Lot four.
(Put the packet on the desk.) Sealed.
What is it you sell here?
Who paid for the riders at Tollhouse 9?
You sell Shale's water by the number.
Your clerk copies paper for the porters.
I broke your strike. I'd like more than eighty.
A girl in Bridgeward says your forecasts for nothing.
I've a debt contract. Lot four.
About the broken seal. The service.

packet_ok.text: She checks the seal against the pad of her thumb, not a card, and for the first time the pen stops. "Unopened. Nine days." She counts forty onto the desk without looking at the coins. "Bearer's fee. And a ticket, if you haven't one — the guild likes a courier who doesn't read." She puts the packet in a drawer that locks. "That was water, if you wondered. You didn't wonder. Good."

decision.text: You carried the guild's packet from Tollhouse 9 to the Exchange unopened and were paid for it.

packet_opened.text: She looks at the seal for a long second and then at you with something like interest. "Opened. Then it's news, and news is worth nothing, and the bearer owes the floor the price of the lot." She writes a number: three hundred. "Or a service. The guild prefers services. Coin is so impersonal."

debt_paid.text: "Square." The number is crossed out with one line. "Most people choose the service. I'll remember that you didn't."

text.text: "There was a stoppage under my ramp. It's over, one way or the other, so that's gone. There'll be another thing. There always is." She writes DEFERRED beside the number. "I'll send."
"Forty porters under my ramp with their straps off. Put the straps on them. Esk will pay you the eighty he pays anyone; the debt is what I'll forgive." She goes back to the pen. "Go on."

service_done.text: "Straps on. The number's gone." She crosses it out. "You'd make a factor, if you had the patience. You don't."

what.text: "Certainty." She does not smile. "Sealed sheets: a place, a date, what happens. Most people want to be on the right side of a date. Some want to be the date. Both pay." The pen moves. "Where the certainty comes from is a floor matter and the floor is me."

paid.text: "The protection account." She does not pretend not to know. "Two riders, four days, a traveller walking west with something that was ours. It's a line in a book, and lines in books are for sale." She writes a number without looking: two hundred. "Or make me want to tell you, which is cheaper and takes longer."

decision.text: You bought the Exchange's protection line from the Grand Factor for two hundred Tolls.

options.text: You'll tell me for nothing, because then I'll remember who told me.

mods.why: Odile taught her, and you can say so
a factor's hand is owed the floor's books
you carried her paper unopened

options.text: I'm a factor's hand. The books are mine to read.

paid_free.text: She considers that for longer than she has considered anything since you came in, and then she laughs, once, short. "Yes. All right." She writes the line on a lot card in a hand like a knife and slides it across. "Two riders, four days, the Sarr account, by order of the floor. The floor is me. Remember who told you." The pen goes back to work. "That cost me nothing. Everything after it will cost you."

paid_told.text: "The traveller was carrying paper that was ours, and paper that was ours is the floor's business, and the floor protects its business. That is the whole of it. It cost us two riders' wages and it cost him more, and I would do it again at that price." She looks at you properly. "You came a long way to be told something you knew."

water.text: "The city rebalances. We buy the rebalancing." She says it like a rate. "A number for a town's water, a date; whoever holds the sheet knows what the town will drink before the town does. Pike sells the water; I sell the knowing. The town has it worst, but the town always does."

rook.text: The pen stops. "Does she." Not a question. "Amity Rook. Six years. Never late." She looks at the door to the floor. "Lot nine tomorrow, then. The floor can't have a leak; the whole product is the seal." A beat. "You'll have told me for a reason. Name it."

options.text: A hand's ticket. I'd like to be more than a bearer.

decision.text: You gave the Exchange's clerk to the Grand Factor for a factor's hand's ticket. She went on the block.
You sold the Exchange's clerk to the Grand Factor for a hundred Tolls. She went on the block.

rook_sold.text: "Done." She writes a name on a lot card. The clocks go on disagreeing. "Fen will have her by nine. Don't be on the east bank; people find it hard to watch."

rook_back.text: "The floor doesn't forget. It defers." She writes something small. "She'll be watched. You've bought her a month, perhaps. That's not nothing; months are what we sell."

hand.text: "You put the straps back on forty backs with words. That's a factor's work." She takes a brass ticket with a notch in it from a drawer. "Factor's hand. The floor's books open to you; the floor's enemies too. Don't drink at the Span with it in your pocket; Lazlo's fond of the porters."

decision.text: The Grand Factor made you a factor's hand for breaking the porters' strike.

odile.text: The pen stops for the second time. "Does she." Something old crosses her face and is filed. "Her tab is paid. Tell her it will go on being paid. Tell her — " She stops. "Tell her nothing. She hears everything anyway." Then, drier: "Whatever she told you about me is true, and whatever she told you about herself is a trade."

contract.text: "The floor pays ninety for lot four. The clerk handles it; I don't touch paper that small." She goes back to the pen. "Unless you were going to ask me to tear it up, in which case: not at that price."

fight.text: She has not moved from the desk. "You'll find the guild is credit, and I am the guild. Go on, then."

intro.text: The captain of the deck guard stands mid-span where he can see both ramps and the planks, and does not stop seeing them to talk to you. "Dent. Weapons stay down on the deck. Trouble goes in the river. The ninth span fell on its own; everything since, somebody pushed."

options.text: The block on the east bank.
Why hasn't the guild mended the span?

again.text: "Captain." His eyes are on the ramps.

strike.text: "Voss is a decent man with ruined knees and the guild will starve him anyway, because it has paper that says it can." He does not lower his voice. "I keep the deck. I don't keep the ramp. That's Esk's, and I thank the river for it."

block.text: "Fen sells debt. Somebody has to; the guild is credit and credit has to go somewhere when it goes bad." He watches a porter not carrying. "He hates it, which is why he's good at it. The ones who like it get careless."

span.text: "Two Tolls of planks against twelve a head to cross one at a time, slow, in sight of the guard." He almost smiles. "The guild doesn't mend things that pay better broken."

text.text: TODAY'S LOTS, in chalk. Lot four has a line through it.
TODAY'S LOTS, in chalk. 1 — PORTER, 40, SUM 31. 2 — COOK, 55, SUM 19. 3 — CLERK, 23, SUM 70. 4 — CALLOWAY, S., 19, SUM 58 AND INTEREST. 5 — MECHANIC, 48, SUM 44. Under the fourth, smaller: OPENS 60.

passives.text: Calloway. Wren's name. The Sallow is not so large that it is a common one.

intro.text: The auctioneer is young for the voice: a bright, carrying, cheerful voice that does not reach his eyes. "Lots at nine, settled by six, no credit, the guild is credit. Lot four's young, if that's what you came for. Everyone's come for lot four today. I open at sixty."

passives.text: His hands are shaking very slightly, and he keeps them on the counter so they don't show. He has looked at the cage exactly once.

options.text: (Let it go. Someone else will buy her.)

lot7.text: "Lot seven. Bexley, forty-one, a mechanic, forty-eight and interest. Signed for parts he fitted to a truck that then left without him." The voice, and under it: "Nobody comes for mechanics. He's been on the board since spring." He looks at you properly for the first time. "Seventy opens it. There is nobody to bid against you. There never is."

options.text: Nobody's bidding. Fifty, and your board is a card shorter.

lot7_low.text: "Fifty." He writes it in the voice that says sums. "Going — gone, to the stranger at fifty, and the guild can take the twenty out of my cheer." The paper comes across.

lot7_firm.text: "Seventy opens it. The guild counts what I open at, not what I close at."

lot7_sold.text: "Lot seven." The thumb-print on the paper is a working man's, broad and oil-dark. "He's wherever the guild has him working till the paper says otherwise. Whoever you're buying for — " He stops himself. "I say the sums."

four.text: "Sable Calloway, nineteen, fifty-eight and interest. Her brother's debt, if you want the story — he signed and ran, and the paper doesn't care who signed." The voice does not change. "Service until cleared. Most buyers want a cook or a carrier. Some want nineteen." He looks at the counter. "I say the sums. I don't say the rest."

bid.text: "Sixty from the stranger." The voice rises and the crowd leans. "Seventy from the back. Eighty — the gentleman in the coat, thank you, eighty." He looks at you. He is very slightly, under the voice, on your side.

options.text: (Talk the room down.) The coat bought lot two for a cook. He doesn't want a girl, he wants to be seen.

bid_low.text: The coat colours, and finds he has business elsewhere, and the back goes quiet. "Seventy, then. Going — gone, to the stranger at seventy." The hammer is a tin cup on the counter.

bid_high.text: "Ninety from the coat." He will not look at you. "Against you, stranger."

sold.text: "Sold." The contract comes across the counter with a thumb-print already on it that is not yours. "She's yours till it clears. The cage key's on the paper. I don't ask what for." Very quietly, under the voice: "Please don't make me wish I had."

hate_ok.text: The voice stops. What is left is a man of thirty with shaking hands. "Every day. Every lot." He looks at the cage, the second time. "I can't lose a lot in daylight; the guild counts. But the box isn't counted till nine, and I lock it badly, and I sleep by the fire on the east bank." He does not say anything else. He does not need to.

hate_no.text: The voice does not even flicker. "Everybody hates it, friend. I'm paid to say the sums." He turns to the crowd. "Lot four, sixty, do I hear sixty."

night_help.text: He is by the fire on the east bank, awake, not looking at the block. "Box is open. Paper's on top. The cage key's under it." He looks into the fire. "If anyone asks, you stole it, and I'll say so with my whole chest."

took.text: "Lot four, stolen in the night," he says to the fire, in the voice, and then not in it: "Thank you."

let_go.text: "Lot four, sixty — seventy — ninety to the gentleman in the coat, going, gone." The cup on the counter. The crowd moves to lot five. Somebody opens the cage.

off.text: Off the block he is somebody else: smaller, by the fire, with a cup. "Lots at nine. I don't sell at night; it's the one rule I made myself."

text.text: "Lot four, stolen, lost, mislaid — I've said all three to the guild and they wrote down the one they liked." He almost smiles. "Lot seven's a mechanic. Nobody comes for mechanics."
"Lot eight. A carrier, thirty." The voice is back, and the board is one card shorter.
"Lot seven. A mechanic, forty-eight." The voice is back.

intro.text: A young woman on a cot in a cage, knees up, who looks at you the way the lots look at the crowd: as a sum. "Sixty. I heard him. If you've sixty, don't stand there being sorry about it."

passives.text: A burn scar on the inside of her left forearm, old, the shape of a hand that grabbed. Wren has one like it, on the right.

options.text: You've a sister. A scout, with the Dogs.

name.text: "Sable. Calloway, if the paper wants it. My brother signed for a bike and rode it away and the paper doesn't care who signed." She looks at the chalk board. "I had a sister. Everyone had a sister once."

wren.text: Wren has not said a word since the block came in sight. Now she steps up to the cage and says, "Sable," and the girl on the cot looks up and says nothing at all for a long time, and then, "You left," and Wren says, "I know," and that is all either of them can manage.

sister.text: Something goes across her face and is put away. "Wren." Not a question. "Is she alive?" You tell her. "Then she can come and buy me herself." But she has turned so you cannot see her eyes.

text.text: You hold her paper. Wren is looking at you, not at her sister.
You hold her paper. She has seen the thumb-print on it and has stopped looking at you as a sum and started looking at you as weather.

options.text: (Give her the contract.) It's yours. Tear it.

decision.text: You put Sable Calloway's debt contract in her own hands at the Ninebridge block.

options.text: (Keep it.) You work for me until it clears.

freed.text: She tears it in half and in half again, slowly, as if it might be a trick, and then she is standing outside the cage with four pieces of paper in her fist and nowhere to put them. "I'm going west," she says. "To Shale. There was a sister." She does not thank you; she has decided not to. Then, at the ramp, she does, without turning round.

kept.text: She stands up off the cot and folds the blanket and does not look at you. "Where do you sleep? I'll keep it." Her voice is level. Wren, if she is here, has walked away down the deck and will not be found until morning.

intro.text: "Guns, cells, and things that were somebody's." A broad woman behind a counter of oiled steel, a machine pistol slung and a boxed something under the counter she does not mention. "Guild price on the sign; your price on your face."

chrome.text: "Chrome. Concern-made, sealed, a leg that doesn't tire. I don't fit it; the Sink has people for that, or the Mender in Shale if you're going back." She does not open the box. "Ask when you've the coin. Everyone asks before."

intro.text: "Water, jerky, tins. Fruit from Openfield when the Choir sends it, and they haven't — blight, they say, or the guild says it for them." An old man with a goatee and a tin cup. "Eat something. You look like a forecast."

look.text: Guild paper, wax, the half-moon. On the outside: LOT 3 — NINEBRIDGE — DAY 2. Odile said the seal is the product. Opened, it is only news.

read.text: NINEBRIDGE — PORTERS' STOPPAGE — ENDS THIRD DAY, STRAPS ON, TERMS UNCHANGED. Dated the day before the porters sat down. The hand is not the clerk's; it is nobody's — too even, every letter the same.

sealed.text: Oilcloth, wax, the guild's half-moon. Lighter than it should be. The clerk at Tollhouse 9 said: opened, the bearer owes a sum nobody has.

decision.text: You broke the seal on the guild's packet and read it.

opened.text: One sheet. SHALE — WATER — 0.62 — and a date a month after you stood at Dry Wells, and a sum, and no signature, in a hand too even to be a hand. A schedule for a town's thirst, sold in advance to whoever wanted to know.

day.text: The well: a wheel on a timber frame over a shaft, a pipe to two stone troughs, north and south. The north trough feeds the field rows; the south, the halls. Moss on the south trough. The north one is clean as a plate.

passives.text: Clean because it is scoured — nothing grows in it. There is a bitter smell off the north water that the south water does not have.

mods.why: you know which trough to test

options.text: (Read the ground round the north trough.)

test_ok.text: Iodine from the healer's shelf, a tin cup, patience. The south trough stays brown. The north goes the grey-green of a thing that should not be drunk: a metal salt, dosed, not leached. The glass did not do this. Someone did, at the north trough, at night.

test_no.text: Both troughs taste of stone. Without a reagent you cannot say more than the Elder says: something is wrong with the water and the rows.

tracks_ok.text: One set of boots comes to the north trough every night — the dust is beaten flat in a line nobody else walks — and goes back west, not to the halls but to the small hut past the seed store. A man's boots, heavy on the left. The Elder's son walks like that.

tracks_no.text: Forty people drink here. The ground is a page everyone has written on.

night.text: The well in the dark. The windpump creaks over the burial ground; the halls are shut. The north trough is a black mouth.

options.text: (Wait in the dark by the north trough.)

wait_no.text: An hour, and cold, and your boot finds the bucket. Somewhere a lantern that was coming toward the well goes out and does not come back tonight.

caught_well.text: A lantern, hooded. A man with a pouch, kneeling at the north trough, shaking something into the water with the care of a man salting bread. He does not hear you until you are beside him. Tobias Mason looks up, and does not run, and says, very tired, "Don't tell him. Let me tell you why first."

why.text: He takes a paper from his shirt, worn soft as cloth. OPENFIELD — HARVEST ABOVE PLAN — THE LONG NIGHT — BURNS. "The guild sells these. I bought one with a year's seed money. If we grow, we burn: that's what the city's machine has written for us, and the guild knows it, and my father sings." He puts it away. "Every third row. Enough to stay small. Nobody dies of it." He does not look at the sick hall when he says that.

options.text: Your father hears it from you, tonight, or from me in the morning.
Stop. Give me the pouch and the paper. I keep both, and your father keeps his son.
Your sister keeps a door for people who break forecasts. Let's see what she thinks of how you did it.

decision.text: You drew on Tobias Mason at Openfield's well.

exposed.text: He goes grey in the lantern light and nods, once, the way his father nods. "Tonight, then." He walks to the Elder's house with the pouch in his hand and does not look back, and the light in that window burns until dawn.

mercy.text: He gives you the pouch, and the paper, and stands there with his hands empty like a man who has put down something heavier than either. "The north rows will come back in a month," he says. "If we burn, you'll know why." He goes to bed. You stand at the well a while.

unwritten.text: He looks at the common hall, where the hatch is, and something in him that has been very tired for a year gives up arguing. "Petra." Not a question. He walks there himself. The hatch closes on both of them and the lantern stays on the deck.

clean.text: The well. Both troughs run brown and ordinary now, and the north rows have put out new leaves at the base, small and greedy.

read.text: The notice post. Chalk, in a careful hand: WATER FROM THE SOUTH TROUGH ONLY. SICK HALL: ASK IMRE. SKY-SONG AT DUSK. And a guild paper nailed under it, wax seal and half-moon: THE EXCHANGE AT NINEBRIDGE WILL BUY OPENFIELD'S HARVEST IN ADVANCE AT A FUTURE'S PRICE. ASK FOR VAIL. Somebody has drawn a half-sun over the half-moon.

A post with a sign on it: half a sun, no ground under it, painted and repainted until the wood under the paint is a different shape. Round it, benches and a fire that is kept in all night. There is nothing else to the shrine. The sky is the rest.
The seed tally, in Doria's hand: crates at dusk, crates at dawn, a line between. Fourteen, thirteen. Thirteen, twelve. Twelve, eleven. Every night for a week, one, like a clock.

passives.text: One crate, every night, never two, never a broken lock: that is not a thief grabbing. That is someone with a key, filling an order.

night.text: The store in the dark, the crates in their rows, the tally pale on the table.

seen.text: An hour past midnight the door opens on a key and Hollin Brannock, the yard hand from the Sump, lifts a crate onto his shoulder as if it were his, and goes out east along the lane toward the guild buyer's tent. He does not hurry. Nobody hurries who has done a thing six times.

seen_no.text: A shelf board creaks under your hand. Footsteps outside stop, and go away, and nothing walks tonight.

hatch.text: A hatch in the hall floor at the far west end, iron, with a ring and no lock you can see. Someone has swept round it, carefully, so that the sweeping shows.

locked.text: The ring turns and the hatch does not. Bolted from below, and below there is somebody who has stopped breathing to listen.

opens.text: A bolt goes back under the floor. The hatch lifts on its own, and under it is a ladder and a lamp and Petra Mason's face, looking up, not surprised.

inside.text: A cellar cut into the glass, dry and cold. Grey scarves on pegs. No mirror, no drawing, no photograph of anyone; on the wall a board with twelve pins in it and a road between them, like the map in your pack, except that here the names are written plain. Petra waits until you have seen that. "Hollis Dray," she says. "The man who died at your door. He was ours. He took that list out of the city's tower so the people on it would know, and the guild shot him for it on the highway, and he walked to you anyway." She lets it sit. "We are the Unwritten. We keep no likeness. The city's machine makes its forecasts from faces; a face it has never seen, it cannot write. That is the whole of our religion, and it is not a kind one."

decision.text: Petra Mason showed you the cellar under Openfield and told you the stranger's name.

options.text: There's a photograph of me. Older. In a city.

photo.text: She does not ask to see it. "Then the machine has your face, and has written you, and that is what it wrote. Hollis carried it to you so you would know what they want you to become." She looks at the board. "You are a pin on this. So is my father. So is a boy called Jonah in Shale, if he is still alive." A beat. "Keep it covered. Don't let the guild see it. And don't ask me yet to burn it; you're not ready to hear what I'd say."

options.text: Not a kind one, you said.

kill.text: "Some of us break a forecast by killing the person it is about." She says it like weather. "If the machine says a man rises, and he is dead, the machine was wrong, and the Plan slips a notch. I don't do it. Some of us do. I won't tell you which, and you should not tell anyone on that board that you have been down here." She turns the lamp down. "When Openfield has been through its night, come and ask me what we are for. Not before."

again.text: The cellar. The scarves, the board, the twelve pins. Petra is not here; the lamp is lit anyway, which is how the Unwritten say *welcome*.

look.text: A fresh cairn, small. The stones are still the colour of the ground they came from. No name — the Choir cuts none — but somebody has left a child's cup on top, the kind with a chipped lip.

read.text: A sign at the burial ground's edge: UNDER THE OPEN SKY. NO NAMES. NO LIKENESS. WHAT IS NOT WRITTEN IS FREE. Rows of cairns under a windpump that turns for no one.

look.text: A bench of planks in the son's hut, with tools on it, and a crate under it pushed back further than tools need. The lamp beside it has been trimmed so often the wick is a stub.

A windpump over the burial ground with no pipe under it any more, turning because the wind says so. The Choir left it standing because the dead like a sound, Petra says, and because it is the tallest thing in the glass and the city can see it from the towers.

read.text: OPENFIELD — HARVEST ABOVE PLAN — THE LONG NIGHT — BURNS. Guild paper, seal long broken, the fold worn through. It was under the bench in Tobias Mason's hut with a pouch of grey salt and a bottle of iodine to wash his hands after.

intro.text: An old man with a farmer's hands and a grey scarf, who has been counting rows so long he counts you too, from habit. "Elder Mason. Sit, friend; nobody here will ask you to sing." He looks past you at the fields. "You'll have seen the third rows. Everyone sees them. Nobody can tell me why."

text.text: "The rows are coming back." He says it to the fields, not to you. "Thank you is a small word. I'll say it anyway."

blight.text: "Every third row. Leaves curl, the root goes soft, it smells sweet. We pull it, we burn it, it comes again in the same rows, never the rows between." He turns his hands over. "Forty years in the glass and I have never seen blight that could count. Imre says the sick in the hall didn't catch it off the plants. Benedek says he saw a light at the well, which Benedek says about most things." He looks at you. "You came up the lane like someone who finds things out. Find this out. I'll feed you and I'll owe you, and the Choir pays its debts under the sky."

sick.text: "Three in the hall. A child. Shaking hands, bad stomachs, no fever. Imre boils everything now and it's stopped, mostly." He does not say what he thinks that means. He has decided not to think it.

word.text: He is quiet for a while. "Not me. I'm a farmer; I don't keep that kind of door." He looks toward the shrine, where his daughter is. "My daughter keeps it. Say it to her, not to me, and not where anyone from the bridge can hear."

seed.text: "She did. Ninety years in the cold under the Cistern and it came up in nine days in the north rows." His face changes. "The north rows." He looks at the fields and the thing he will not think about gets closer. "Tomato and millet. Dying first, with the rest."

guild.text: "Vail. He wants to buy the harvest before it's grown, at a price that would feed us through two winters, and the guild would carry the risk." He almost smiles. "I asked him what the guild knows about my fields that I don't. He said *the future*, and smiled, and I have not slept well since."

son.text: He does not say *no*. That is the worst of it: he does not say no, he sits down on the bench by the well and looks at his hands for a long time, and then he says, "Show me," and you do, and he reads the paper his son bought with a year's seed money, and reads it again. "Burns," he says. "If we grow." He folds it. "He thought he was keeping us. He was." He stands up, old. "Fetch him to me. I'll do the rest myself."

son_done.text: What the Elder says to his son is said in the house with the door shut. When it opens, Tobias walks to the track with a pack and does not look at the fields, and his father stands at the well until the lamp-post comes on, and then goes to the shrine and sits with the fire and does not sing.

after_exposed.text: He is at the well, or the shrine, or in the rows, the way he always was, and he speaks to you kindly, and there is a place behind his eyes where his son was and the door to it is shut. "The rows are coming back," he says. "Thank you is a small word."

options.text: Brother Ash. I'm going east. I'd take him.
Petra says the Choir's door is a burial.

ash.text: "Ash came to us with a shotgun and a thing he would not say, and dug for a year before he'd sing. He's the best of us now, which he'd deny." The Elder looks at the burial ground. "He asked me yesterday whether he should go with you. I said the sky would tell him. The sky told him yes, apparently; it usually agrees with him." He nods. "Take him. Bring him back, or don't, but don't waste him."

rite.text: "It is. We bury what we lost under the sky, and say its name once, and never cut it in stone. Then you're ours, as much as anyone is anyone's." He looks at you. "Everyone has someone. Petra will say the words. Go when you're ready; the sky waits."

grief.text: The Elder is at the burial ground, where the newest cairn is, and does not turn round when you come, and will not, and the Choir has stopped singing at dusk for a month.

intro.text: A woman by the shrine fire with a grey scarf up to her eyes and a machete she does not pretend not to have. "Don't look at me long. Don't describe me to anyone. That's not rudeness; it's the religion." She looks at you, though, carefully, and then at the sky, as if checking you against it. "Petra. The Elder's. You came from the bridge; you smell of its paper."

options.text: Your father says you keep a door.
The Choir's door is a burial, your father says.

text.text: "My brother is below, being argued with. He may be ours by spring. He may be nothing." She feeds the fire. "You did a harder thing than telling my father. I noticed."
"You've seen the board. Don't tell me what you think of it yet."
"The sky's still up."

choir.text: "People who decided the sky was the only thing left worth praying to, because it was the only thing that hadn't been written." She says *written* like a curse. "We farm. We heal. We bury without names. The city's machine keeps a face for everyone it has seen; we try to give it nothing to keep."

word.text: She goes very still, and then she does a strange thing: she pulls the scarf down and lets you see her whole face, once, the way you would show a wound. "Then he reached you. Then it was worth it." The scarf goes up. "The hatch under the common hall. Say that to the iron. Come alone."

door.text: "I keep several. Which one you get depends on what you bring." She looks at the fire. "Bring me the word a dying man said, or bring me a cairn you raised, and we'll see."

rite.text: "It is. Everyone has someone." She stands. "The burial ground, under the windpump. You raise the stones yourself; I say the words; you say a name once and never again. Then you're a sister of the Open Sky, or a brother, and the halls are yours from Shale to the city." She waits. "Who?"

options.text: The man who died at my door.

cairn.text: You carry stones from the glass-crust to the burial ground, one at a time, because that is the rule, and build them under the windpump while the sky goes from white to red. Petra says the words, which are short and not about anyone in particular. You say the name once. The wind takes it. She puts one stone from the cairn in your hand. "Sister," she says, or "brother," and the Choir at the shrine fire sings the sky-song, which has no words at all.

rows.text: "Blight." She says it the way her father does, and then, because she is not her father: "Blight that counts. Something is being done to us, and I don't know by whom, and I would like to." She looks toward the small hut past the store and does not look away quite fast enough.

dead.text: She is at the burial ground, at the newest cairn, with her scarf down, and she looks at you with nothing in her face at all. "Go east," she says. "Don't come back through here."

intro.text: A big, gaunt man digging in the burial ground with a shotgun leaned on a cairn and a grey scarf on a cord, who does not stop digging to look at you. "Friend." He gets another spade of glass-crust out. "There's a weight to a thing like a grave. People think it's the stones. It's the digging."

passives.text: Under the scarf, at the collarbone, the end of an old scar that is not a scar: a dog's head, burned off the way the stranger burned his mark. Rust Dog work.

text.text: "The rows are coming back." He leans on the spade. "You did that. There's a weight to that too, friend. A good one."
"Friend." The spade goes in.

grave.text: "Sem. Six. First the trough took." He does not stop. "The Choir says no names on the stones, so I say them while I dig. Sem, Sem, Sem. The soil doesn't mind." He looks up for the first time. "Somebody did that to the water. Soil forgives. I don't, yet. I'm working on it."

dog.text: The spade stops. "I was." He does not touch the scarf. "Before the Elder. Before the sky. A long time before I knew what a weight was." He looks at you to see what you will do with it. "I burned the mark off myself with a lamp. Took three nights. If you're going to use it, use it now; I'd rather carry it in daylight."

options.text: I'm not going to use it.

wren.text: Wren looks at the burned place under the scarf for a long time, and he lets her. "I don't know you," she says finally. "No," he says. "You were a child. I was with Kessler's old man." She says nothing. Then: "Dig, then." And he does, and she stands there, and neither of them explains anything to you.

join.text: He finishes the row of stones he is on, because you finish a row. Then he picks up the shotgun and puts the spade where the next person will find it. "The Elder said the sky would tell me. The sky doesn't talk, friend; that's the point of it. I'm coming because the thing that was done to the water came from the city, and I want to see the city." He touches the scarf. "I count things out loud too, sometimes. Different things from your sniper."

decision.text: Brother Ash of the Choir left Openfield's burial ground with you.

not_yet.text: "Ask the Elder. Or raise a cairn here, so I know what you carry." He goes back to the row. "I don't go east with a stranger. I've done that once."

refuse.text: He is digging a grave that is not Sem's, and he does not look up, and the shotgun is not leaned on the cairn; it is across his back. "Not with that on you, friend. Walk on."

waiting.text: "Well?" The spade is already put away.

text.text: "Soil's good here. Everything else is what it is."
"There's a weight to the road. Good one, so far."

camp.text: "Fire's honest. Say what you want to say to it and I'll listen in."

weight.text: He is quiet for long enough that you think he will not answer. "A place called the Gully. I'll tell you when we're nearer to it, because I'll have to, and because I'd rather you heard it from me than from somebody standing in it." He feeds the fire. "That's all tonight, friend. That was a lot."

sky.text: "No." He says it kindly. "That's what I like about it. Everything else out here answers, and most of what it says is written down somewhere by something that wants a thing from you. The sky wants nothing. It's the only honest thing I've met, bar soil." He looks at you. "And a couple of people. Rest, friend."

unwritten.text: He looks at the common hall, where the hatch is, and something that has been tired in him for a year stops arguing. "Petra." Not a question. He walks there himself. The hatch closes on both of them.

after_mercy.text: He hoes the rows that are coming back, and does not look at you, and the north trough runs brown and ordinary, and his father sings at dusk and does not know why his son will not.

intro.text: The sick hall smells of boiled water and iodine. The healer, a tall woman with a grey scarf tied back, looks at your hands before your face. "Sister Imre. "The hatch sends these every few months and never a note. Tell them the Choir thanks the sky, and I thank them, and I know the difference."

sick.text: "Shaking hands. Bad stomachs. A taste of pennies, the child says. No fever, no rash, nothing passing from one to the next." She folds a cloth. "All three drank from the north trough before I made the rule. That's as far as I can take it. I'm a healer; I'm not a well."

diag_no.text: Pale, shaking, frightened. It could be a dozen things. Imre has been through the dozen already.

heal.text: She works fast and talks to the wound, not to you. "The sky doesn't charge. I do, a little, in water: drink the south trough and not the north."

intro.text: The seed-keeper is a thin woman with ink on her fingers and a tally board she holds like a shield. "Doria. Keeper. Counted at dusk, counted at dawn, and every dawn there's one fewer." chaff.text: "Dead seed." She almost smiles. "Last year's, boiled and dried. Looks right, weighs right, grows nothing. Chaff with manners." She looks at the crates. "If the guild is buying our seed for somebody east, I would like that somebody to plant a field of nothing and wait a season for it."

chaff_done.text: Over the next nights the crates walk as before, and the guild's man pays as before, and on the seventh morning he leaves with six crates on a mule and a receipt, going east to a client who will plant a field of manners and wait. hollin.text: She does not look surprised; she looks tired. "Tell the Elder. I can't." She turns the tally over. "He'll give Hollin the night watch over the store he stole from. That's the Choir's way. It's worse than the track and he'll stay, which is the point."

who_no.text: "A light." He goes back to the rows. "I'm seventy-two. I see lights."

Kip, from the orchard, in a grey scarf two sizes too big, with dirt to the elbows and a face that has eaten every day for a month. "They feed us first. First!" Then, lower: "Hollin goes to the store at night. We don't say. We've been thieves; we know what the look is."

Mote, from the orchard, who has learned the sky-song and sings it under her breath while she works, all of it, wrong. "The Elder says the sky keeps no books." She considers that. "Kessler kept books. I like this better."
