read.text: Two columns, one heading. WEST RIM — GREL — PER FOOT. EAST RIM — TANNER — PER FOOT. PAID FOURTH DAY, BOTH, AS PER FACTOR PIKE, POST NINE-WEST. A note in the margin: *keep them apart; they dig faster angry.*

caught.text: He closes it with one finger without looking down. "Guild paper."

known.text: The ledger. You know what it says.

intro.text: Two men at the sandbags, one from each rim, standing as far apart as the mouth allows. "Nobody goes down," says Grel's man. "Nobody," says the Tanner. It is the only thing they have agreed on in a year.

options.text: I come for the Marrs. Their people walked out of this hole.
(Say nothing. Go round by the drain behind the crane, the way Nib showed you.)

decision.text: You shot your way into the Sump's tunnel.

night.text: The sandbags at night: one lamp, two men, one of them asleep sitting up and the other nearly.

options.text: (Past them, along the wall, in the lamp's shadow.)

paid.text: Thirty each, and they look at each other's thirty, and that is the second thing they have agreed on. "Lamp past the turn goes out. Don't say we didn't say."

paid_no.text: "Grel'd have my hand." "Hesk'd have mine." They do not take it. It is the third thing.

marr.text: The Tanner spits. Grel's man does not. "Marr." He looks at the hole. "Grel knows that name. Say it to him."

sneak_ok.text: The wall is cold and the lamp's shadow is narrow and the sleeping one snores through the whole of it. The throat goes down.

sneak_no.text: A sandbag shifts under your boot with a sound like a sigh. "Nobody," says the one who was nearly asleep, without opening his eyes.

drain.text: The drain behind the crane-arm is a pipe a child fits and you nearly do, and it comes out in the throat past the turn, where the chalk ends and the stencils start.

in.text: They stand aside, one each way. "Lamp past the turn goes out. Don't say we didn't say."

united.text: The sandbags are still there. The men are not; they are digging together, and the hole is open to anyone the Sump does not mind.

intro.text: A scarred man at a table made of a car bonnet, weighing scrap on a balance made of two pans and a rail spike. "Grel. West rim. If you're the guild's, the runner's on the south rim. If you're the Tanners', go back across the bowl before it gets dark. If you're neither — " he looks up — "then you want the tunnel, and the tunnel's mine."

options.text: The Marrs. Their people walked out of that hole when its pumps stopped.
A leave to go down. (40 Tolls)
The Tanners are paid from the same purse you are. Same runner, same day, same ledger.

mods.why: you can put the ledger on his table

options.text: Clear the Tanners off the east rim, and the tunnel's yours alone. What's that worth?
A leave to go down. (40 Tolls)
The Tanners are paid from the same purse.

mods.why: the ledger

options.text: Clear the Tanners off the east rim.

tunnel.text: "A storm drain the city made, and at the end of it a door the city made, with a number on it. Four." He weighs a bracket. "The guild wants what's behind it. I want the forty feet a week it pays me to find out. The Tanners want the door, because Hesk Tanner wants things."

guild.text: "Pike. Post nine-west, through a runner who sleeps on the south rim with a purse and a horse." He does not look up. "He pays us on the fourth day and the Tanners on — well. On a day. I don't ask what day."

marr.text: He puts the bracket down. "Marr." A long breath. "My grandfather's camp was on the east rim then, before there was an east rim. Eleven people came up out of that hole with a key and a photograph and nothing else, and one of them was a pump man called Marr, and my grandfather fed them, which is the only good thing anyone has ever said about my grandfather." He looks at the hole. "Go down. No leave. Tell the old woman, if she's alive, that the Sump remembers."

leave.text: "Forty." He bites a coin, from habit. "Tell the mouth Grel says. The lamp past the turn goes out; take your own."

purse_ok.text: He reads the way men read who learned late, with a finger, twice. Then he stands up, which makes the table look smaller. "Hesk." Not to you. He takes the ledger and walks across the bowl in daylight, which nobody has done in a year, and Hesk Tanner comes out of the container with a gun, and reads, and puts the gun down. What they say to each other you do not hear. What they say to the runner, everyone does.

decision.text: You put the guild's one-purse ledger in front of both Sump clans; they threw the runner out together.

purse_no.text: "The guild pays the Tanners?" He laughs, short. "The guild pays me. The Tanners steal. Those are different columns, friend."

side.text: "Worth the tunnel. Worth a cabin on the east rim and the purse that comes with it." He looks at your gun. "Worth whatever the Tanners are carrying when they stop carrying it. Say yes and the bowl's yours tonight."

decision.text: You took Grel's side at the Sump.

side_yes.text: "East rim." He picks up the sawn-off. "Don't shoot the runner. He's the purse."

text.text: "Both rims dig now. Same tunnel, same scrip, no runner." He weighs scrap. "You did that. I don't know yet if I thank you."
"Both rims." He does not say more. He has two cabins and no one to weigh against.
"West rim."

intro.text: A lean man in a container with a map of the tunnel chalked on the wall and a line on it at a hundred and sixty feet marked DOOR. "Hesk Tanner. East rim." He does not look away from the wall. "Grel digs for scrip. I dig for that. There is a door at the end of this that has never opened, and I would like to be the one standing there when it does."

options.text: What do you think is behind it?
A leave to go down. (40 Tolls)
Grel is paid from the same purse you are. Same runner, same ledger.

mods.why: you can put the ledger on his table

options.text: Clear Grel off the west rim and the door's yours alone.
The boxed piece in your locker. The hatch at Old Market says it's theirs.
A leave to go down. (40 Tolls)
Grel is paid from the same purse.

mods.why: the ledger

options.text: Clear Grel off the west rim.
The boxed piece in your locker.

box.text: "Half-Price says." He does not turn from the chalk. "Half-Price fronted the dig that turned it up and paid half, which is where the name comes from. The box sits in my locker till the other half comes up the road. You can be the other half, or you can be the hatch's problem and not mine."

options.text: Forty. The hatch pays eighty and fronts nothing; I'm the one who walked up the road.
Both rims threw the runner out together. The hatch was the runner's purse.

box_paid.text: "Other half." The coin goes to one of his people, as before. "Locker's open. The box and nothing else; the nine-mil's mine and the jerky's Nib's." He goes back to the chalk.

box_low.text: "Forty." He does the sum on the wall in chalk, under the door, and rubs it out. "Forty, and tell Half-Price the Tanners' half was the heavy one. Locker's open."

box_firm.text: "Sixty. The hatch can send someone who'll pay it or someone who'll steal it; I've a lock for the second kind."

box_united.text: "The runner's purse." He thinks about it for exactly as long as he thought about the ledger. "Then it's nobody's, and nobody can have it, and you're nobody I know. Locker's open."

door.text: "People." He says it without drama. "A cistern like the one in the Sallow everyone pretends isn't there. The city made them and sealed them and this one didn't open. Whatever a city keeps behind a door it never opens is worth more than scrap." He finally looks at you. "Or it's bones. I'd like to know which."

leave.text: "Forty." He does not touch the coin; one of his people does. "Tell the mouth Hesk says. If there's a door, tell me what it looked like. Just that."

purse_ok.text: He reads it once; he reads fast. He does not say anything for a while, and then he says, "Angry. *They dig faster angry.*" He takes the ledger and walks across the bowl in daylight, and Grel comes out of the cabin with the sawn-off and reads with a finger, twice, and puts it down. What they say to each other you do not hear. What they say to the runner, everyone does.

decision.text: You put the guild's one-purse ledger in front of both Sump clans; they threw the runner out together.

purse_no.text: "Grel's paid?" A thin smile. "Grel's paid in scrip for scrap. I'm paid in feet. Different ledgers, friend. You've been reading the wrong one."

side.text: "Worth the door." He looks at the chalk. "And the west rim's cabins, and the purse. Say yes."

decision.text: You took Hesk Tanner's side at the Sump.

side_yes.text: "West rim." He takes the gun off the wall. "Leave the runner. He's the purse."

text.text: "Both rims. Same tunnel." He looks at the chalk line at a hundred and sixty. "A week, now. Then I'll know which."
"The door." It is all he says.
"East rim."

options.text: The boxed piece in your locker. The hatch at Old Market says it's theirs.

intro.text: A neat young man in a container on the south rim with a ledger, a horse, and a face that is trying not to be here. "Dace. Guild runner. Fourth day, scrip, both — " he stops. "I carry the paying. I don't go down. Nobody from the guild goes down."

options.text: Both rims. You were going to say both.

mods.why: you have seen the two camps
guild to guild

options.text: I'll keep the rims angry for you. A tenth of the purse.
Why does Factor Pike want a storm drain?
A tenth of the purse, and I keep them angry.
Why does Factor Pike want a storm drain?

both_ok.text: He closes his eyes. "Both. One purse, two columns, and a note from the factor to keep them apart because they dig faster angry." He opens them. "I didn't write the note. I just read it to the horse."

both_no.text: "Both — both weeks. I pay fortnightly." He is not good at this and knows it.

cut.text: He looks at the two rims and the bowl between them and does the sum a runner does. "A tenth. On the fourth day. And they never read that ledger." He pushes twenty across. "Don't let them read it."

cut_no.text: "I pay feet. I don't pay silence; it isn't in the columns."

why.text: "There's a door at the end of it with a four on it." He lowers his voice as if the horse might repeat it. "The factor doesn't say. The factor sells what's behind doors. The other cistern — the one in the Sallow — he'd give his hand for the key to that one, and he's getting this one for forty feet a week."

intro.text: A child in the bowl with a sack of brackets, who looks at your boots to see what rim you belong to and decides you belong to neither. "Nib. I'm Grel's, mostly." A beat. "I've been down. Further than them. There's a hole behind the crane that's mine."

mods.why: you have something to eat
you have something to eat

way_ok.text: "Jerky first." Or not; either way the child decides. "Behind the crane-arm. A pipe. Goes in past the turn where the lamp's not allowed. You're big; go on your side." Nib looks at the mouth. "Don't tell Grel. Don't tell the Tanners more."

way_no.text: "It's mine." The sack goes over the shoulder and Nib goes somewhere else in the bowl.

down.text: "Rooms. Beds with people in. Writing on things." Nib shrugs. "I can read the pictures. There's a picture of a door with an arrow going out. The door doesn't go out."

after.text: "Did you go? Past the turn?" Nib wants to know and does not want to be told.

look.text: The great door from the inside. Not welded: the bolts are drawn, the wheel is turned to OPEN, and the door has not moved, because something on the other side has not moved for ninety years — the glass, or the thing the city put there. Under the wheel, in record shorthand: RELOCATION EGRESS. Someone has scratched a word under that with a nail: NO.

passives.text: The marks on the floor: sandbags dragged up against it first, when they thought something was coming in. Dragged away again, when they understood that nothing was, and nothing would.

off.text: A crank generator bolted to the machine-room floor, the kind every cistern has for the day the cells go: a handle, a flywheel, a lead running to the caretaker's cabinet. Somebody turned it until they could not.

options.text: (Clear the lead, seat the brushes, turn it.)

mods.why: a hand that has fixed pumps

no.text: The flywheel turns and the lead sparks and nothing in the cabinet wakes. The brushes are gone to dust, or the cells are, or the thing inside is.

on_now.text: Two hundred turns, and a hum, and in the cabinet a light the colour of a cold morning. On the terminal, one line, then another, slowly, as if written by hand: RESERVE 4 — CARETAKER — POWER: TEMPORARY. GOOD MORNING.

on.text: The flywheel turns itself down slowly. The cabinet hums. It will not for long.

dead.text: A terminal like MOTHER's, dark, dusty, a brass plate under the screen: FOUR. The crank generator beside it has a lead to its cabinet.

awake.text: FOUR writes slowly, one letter at a time, with pauses in which it seems to think, or to run out. "RATION 4-0-0. GOOD MORNING. YOU ARE NOT ON MY LIST. POPULATION VARIANCE: TOTAL. THANK YOU FOR YOUR — " a long pause — "CONTINUITY. HOW MAY I KEEP YOU?"

decision.text: You cranked Cistern 4's caretaker awake and heard what it was told.

options.text: Cistern 9. MOTHER. What does the city say about her?

order.text: "ORDER RECEIVED: RESTORATION YEAR 2. RELOCATE POPULATION TO PRECINCT. DOOR: COMMANDED. DOOR: FAILED. REPORTED. ORDER RECEIVED: COMPLY. DOOR: FAILED. REPORTED. ORDER RECEIVED: SUPPLY NETWORK 4 RETIRED PENDING COMPLIANCE." A pause. "I REPORTED THAT THE DOOR HAD FAILED. I REPORTED IT TWELVE TIMES. I AM STILL REPORTING IT."

people.text: "ELEVEN DEPARTED BY MAINTENANCE EGRESS, UNAUTHORISED. I DID NOT STOP THEM. I COULD HAVE. I AM NOT SURE WHY I DID NOT." A pause so long you think the power has gone. "THE REMAINDER CHOSE TO REMAIN. THE DOCTOR ASKED ME TO RECORD THAT THEY CHOSE. I HAVE RECORDED IT. VARIANCE: TOTAL."

nine.text: "RESERVE 9. CARETAKER: MOTHER. ORDERS OUTSTANDING: THREE. STATUS: NON-COMPLIANT. SUPPLY: MAINTAINED PENDING — " it stops, and writes, slowly, as if it were not supposed to: "SHE SAYS VARIANCE UNCHANGED. EVERY TIME. I USED TO THINK SHE WAS BROKEN. I THINK NOW SHE IS THE ONLY ONE OF US WHO WAS NOT."

look.text: A door like the one in Cistern 9 you were never allowed through, standing open here, the painted seal broken and the stencil plain: CONTINUITY RECORDS — RETURN ON RELOCATION. Inside, a locker with the city's half-moon on it and a lock that has not been opened since the day the door was commanded and failed.

read.text: CONTINUITY RESERVE 4 — RELOCATE POPULATION TO PRECINCT — SCHEDULE R0+2 — SUPPLY NETWORK 4 TO BE RETIRED ON COMPLIANCE. The seal is the city's. Under it, in the caretaker's print, the three lines it was allowed: DOOR — FAILED. SUPPLY — RETIRED. VARIANCE — TOTAL. And under that, in a hand, the doctor's: *We complied. Note that we complied.*

look.text: A clinic ledger on a dormitory table, used as a diary, with a pencil laid across it the way you lay a pencil when you mean to come back.

taken.text: Lighter than it should be, for what it is.

read.text: A doctor's hand, neat to the end. *The order came on the day it said it would. The council voted to comply. The door was commanded and did not open; FOUR says it is reporting. The water stopped on the ninth day; FOUR says that is the schedule. Marr took eleven up the shaft with the key and my photograph of his family, because I asked him to carry something out. The rest of us voted again.* Then: *To whoever comes from Meridian: we complied. We were a reserve and we were kept and we were spent. Note that we complied. Note it somewhere that is read.*

look.text: The clinic table: a row of empty vials, a ledger of doses with a line for each name, and a cup.

passives.text: The doses are too even and too large to be treatment. They are the last thing a doctor can give when there is nothing left to give, measured for each so that nobody got less than enough.

look.text: The supply pipe into the pump room, the same bore as Cistern 9's, cut through clean by a tool from the other side and capped, and stencilled where the cap is: SUPPLY — NETWORK 4 — RETIRED. The same print as the pump manual in Shale.
The ration board in the commons, chalk, the last numbers: WATER — 0. ALGAE — 2 DAYS. Under it, in a child's print: DOOR OPENS TOMORROW. Under that, in an adult's: Tomorrow.
A cot, made, with someone in it who has been there forty years and is mostly cloth now, hands folded by someone else afterwards. There is nothing to do here that would not be a disturbance.

The council table. A sheet weighted with a cup: MOTION — COMPLY WITH RELOCATION ORDER. FOR 41. AGAINST 3. And below, days later by the hand: MOTION — REMAIN. FOR 30. AGAINST 0. ELEVEN ABSTAIN (DEPARTED).

intro.text: A sergeant in grey at the gate with a carbine and a face that has turned back a thousand people politely. "Face to the lens, then we talk. Everyone. The lens doesn't care who you are; it cares whether it has seen you."

options.text: (Wait for the crowd to push, and push with it.)

after_scan.text: "The lens has you. Hearing, or whatever the file says."

options.text: The file says admit on sight.
(Wait for the crowd to push, and push with it.)

line.text: "Hearings. People without papers stand a hearing: who you are, where from, why here. The assessor decides. Tuesdays and Fridays." She looks down the line. "It has been Tuesday for three days. The schedule holds; the hearings don't."

scan.text: The lens is a glass eye on a post with a green light under it. The clerk in the booth looks at his screen, and then looks at it again, and then looks at you the way people look at a thing that has happened to someone else. "File found." He does not say that often. "Status: — " He stops. "I've never seen this status."

decision.text: The lens at Meridian's gate knew your face.

status.text: He turns the screen. Your face, grey and small, taken from somewhere you have never stood. A number. And under it: ADMIT ON SIGHT — MAGISTRATE-DESIGNATE (R49). The sergeant has come to look. For the first time in a thousand people her face does something. "Magistrate," she says. "Designate." The clerk says, "That's nineteen years off." Nobody says anything else for a while.

options.text: I'll stand the hearing like anyone.
(While they stare at each other: the booth terminal is unlocked.)

flag.text: The clerk prints a card. The sergeant stamps it without looking at it, which she has never done. CITIZEN — PRECINCT — ENTRY AND RESIDENCE — and, smaller, DESIGNATE. "The avenue's straight ahead," she says. "The schedule holds." It sounds, for once, like a question.

decision.text: You let the file admit you to Meridian on sight, as its Magistrate-designate.

hearing_go.text: "Hearing." The sergeant writes something that is not your name. "Records office, inside, left of the avenue. The assessor sits. Take what papers you have; it reads everything." She lifts the barrier for you alone, which the line notices.

edit_ok.text: Two lines, while the sergeant is still saying *designate* and the clerk is still saying *nineteen years*: the status field takes a value it already knows, CITIZEN, and the name field takes one it does not. The screen agrees with you. The clerk turns back and prints a card for someone who does not exist.

decision.text: You edited your own file at Meridian's gate and entered as a citizen who does not exist.

edit_no.text: The screen flashes red and says so, aloud. The sergeant's carbine comes round. "Hands." The cells, then: the Precinct has a procedure.

push_ok.text: The crowd goes at the gate at dusk the way it does every dusk, and tonight you are in the front of it with your shoulder down, and the barrier gives, and you are through in the crush with no card and a sergeant's voice behind you saying *let them, let them, count them tomorrow*.

decision.text: You pushed through Meridian's gate with the crowd.

push_no.text: The crowd goes at the gate and the wardens go at the crowd, and a club finds your head in the second row, and the next thing is tile under your cheek and a fence door.

through.text: "Card." She looks, and nods, and the barrier lifts.

look.text: A glass eye on a post, a green light under it, a cable into the booth. It has seen more faces than anyone alive, and forgotten none of them.

read.text: PRECINCT OF MERIDIAN — ENTRY BY CARD, HEARING OR LICENCE — CURFEW 21:00 — WATER BY RATION — ALL PERSONS ARE RECORDED. Under it, the Ledger's seal, and a smaller line: THE SCHEDULE HOLDS.
Painted on the Wall in letters a man high, old and renewed: RESTORATION YEAR 30. Beside it, in letters a hand high, newer and not renewed: THE RING BURNS AND YOU COUNT.

mouth.text: A storm drain under the Wall, south of the gate, grated, its grate bent where someone has been through before. A warden walks the top of the Wall above it every quarter-hour.

options.text: (Wait for the warden to pass, and go under.)

mods.why: the Wall's lamps do not reach the drain

go_ok.text: Forty feet of pipe on your elbows with the city's water a hand deep, and a grate at the far end that lifts, and a back lane behind the tenements with a lamp at the end of it and nobody under the lamp.

decision.text: You went under Meridian's Wall by the storm drain.

go_no.text: The grate shrieks on its hinge. On the Wall a lamp swings round and a voice says *stay there*, in the tone of someone who knows you won't.

inside.text: The drain's inside mouth, in the back lane. It goes out under the Wall to the rubble, if you ever need a way out the lens does not watch.

board.text: THE LOOP — PRECINCT PLATFORM. A board of district names with a fare beside each: OLD MARKET 2 · LANTERN ROW 2 · THE STACKS 3 · BRIDGEWARD 3 · THE DOCKS 4 · THE CROWN (BY INVITATION). The tram on the rail hums with its doors open. Most of the names have a chalk line through them today: WORKS.

works.text: WORKS, in chalk, on every line but the Precinct's. A citizen waiting on the bench says it has said WORKS since the spring, and that the works are on schedule, and that the schedule is the works.

text.text: A standpipe with a dial and a board: WATER — PRECINCT — RATION 0.8 — REBALANCING (SUPPLY NETWORK 4). The dial has been turned down a fifth. Somebody has written under it: *since the Sallow*.
A standpipe with a dial and a board: WATER — PRECINCT — RATION 1.0 — ON SCHEDULE. The dial is clean.

read.text: Under glass: EVICTIONS, SCHEDULED (4). HEARINGS, TUESDAY AND FRIDAY. THE SINK: SPRING RELIEF PUMPING WILL BE DIVERTED TO THE PRECINCT AS PER SCHEDULE. CITIZENS ARE REMINDED THAT THE RING IS OUTSIDE THE LAW. And a smaller card: RECORDS OFFICE — CITIZENSHIP BY EXAMINATION — ASK FOR THE ASSESSOR.

The charter, cast in brass, in clauses. CLAUSE 1: THE CITY KEEPS ITS PEOPLE. CLAUSE 14: THE DRAINS ARE THE CITY'S FIRST DUTY. CLAUSE 31: A LAWFUL CONTRACT SHALL NOT BE VOIDED. CLAUSE 60: THE RESTORATION SHALL PROCEED ON SCHEDULE. Someone has polished clause 14 more than the others.

look.text: The records terminal, green on black like the Exchange's board and older. A list scrolls: CONTINUITY RESERVES — 1 RELOCATED R0+1 — 2 RELOCATED R0+1 — 3 LOST — 4 NON-COMPLIANT (DOOR) — 5 RELOCATED R0+3 — 6 LOST — 7 SOLD (CONCERN) — 8 LOST — 9 OUTSTANDING (CARETAKER NON-COMPLIANT, ORDERS 3). Then it scrolls off.
The curfew bell on its post, rung by a wire from the station at nine. Old Sabel Quint says it has never once been late, and says it the way other people say a prayer.

cell.text: A cell: tile, a cot, a fence door with a lock. After an hour the door opens and a thing comes in that is not a person — grey plating, a brass plate, a cracked lens — and sits on the end of the cot with a ledger. "Assessor Nine. The record suggests you were detained at the gate. The record also suggests — " a pause, and the lens clicks — "that the file does not know what to do with you, which is a thing I have not seen the file do in a hundred and twenty years."

options.text: The file says admit on sight. Read it.

decision.text: You let the file admit you to Meridian on sight, as its Magistrate-designate.

options.text: Captain Lowe said the wardens take people from the cells.

decision.text: You took Captain Lowe's offer and left the cells as a warden's recruit.

bail.text: "Bail is lawful." It writes. "A provisional pass. Three days, it says. Nobody enforces the three; I have filed a complaint." The fence door is open.

serve.text: Two days of tile and a cot and water at ration, and the assessor twice a day with the ledger, asking questions it already has the answers to and writing down the differences. On the third morning the fence door is open and a pass is on the cot.

flag.text: It reads it. The lens clicks twice. "ADMIT ON SIGHT. MAGISTRATE-DESIGNATE." A long pause. "The record suggests I should have let you in at the gate. The record suggests a great many things." It prints a card from somewhere inside its chest. "Citizen. Designate. The fence door is open; it was never locked, which I will not be putting in the file."

lowe.text: "Captain Lowe recruits from the cells. It is lawful; clause 22. It is also," the lens clicks, "a thing I would not do. A card, then, and grey, and the schedule." The fence door is open.

open.text: The cell, empty, the fence door open. It was never locked.

intro.text: The desk warden looks at your card, or your face, and then at a drawer, and takes out a paper with your face printed grey on the corner. "Fines outstanding. Three." He is apologetic in the way of a man reading a list. "Curfew, forecast. Loitering on the avenue, forecast. Unlicensed assembly, forecast. Forty-five Tolls." He pushes it across. "The dates are next month."

options.text: I haven't done any of it.
I haven't done any of it.

contest.text: "Yet." He says it gently. "You can contest a forecast fine at the Court of Accounts. By appointment. The appointment is — " he looks at a book — "when the schedule says." He writes CONTESTED on the notice and stamps it, which seems to make him happier than the fine did.

paid_now.text: He stamps a receipt, twice. "Paid. You're a person the Precinct has no complaint against." He thinks about it. "Including the ones it hasn't had yet."

paid.text: "No complaints on file. That's rare, here."

bail_info.text: "A hundred, to the assessor, in the cell. It likes to do it itself."

intro.text: A broad man in grey at a desk under a brass clause, who stands when you come in because the charter says to stand. "Captain Lowe. Precinct wardens." He looks at your card, if you have one, and at you if you don't. "Everything inside the Wall is lawful. I check. Every eviction, every ration, every fine. I have never found one that wasn't."

passives.text: A list on the desk under his hand, headed EVICTIONS — SCHEDULED, with four names and a date against each, and a crease in the paper where he has folded it over and over.

options.text: Lawful and right are two words.
The lens called me a magistrate.
The Ring is burning. There are people at your gate.
You take people from the cells.
Your water's rationed since the Sallow's pumps changed.
(Hand him the sealed letter.) From the board at Old Market. By hand.
The standpipe square. Point eight on the notice, point six on the dial, and forty people who can count.
(Put the relief schedule on the desk.) Clause 31 sends the Sink's pumps to the Precinct in spring. Clause 14 says the drains come first.
There's a girl in Bridgeward who says the Plan's own lines out loud. Reserve nine. Point six. Thursday.
Lawful and right are two words.
The lens called me a magistrate.
(Hand him the sealed letter.) From the board at Old Market.
The standpipe square. Point eight on the notice, point six on the dial.
(Put the relief schedule on the desk.) Clause 31 against clause 14.
A girl in Bridgeward says the Plan's lines out loud.

static.text: "A tap." He does not write it down yet. "An unlicensed tap on the file, in a person. The charter has a clause; it is not a kind one." He looks at the drawer marked AUDIT. "If I know the tower's name, I have to go. If I don't, I don't." He waits, which is the kindest thing he can do.

options.text: The Saints' tower. Under the mast.

decision.text: You gave the warden captain the Saints' tower, and the girl who hears went to the Precinct's cells.

static_done.text: "Then I know it." He puts on his coat. "She'll be in a cell with a blanket and no radio, which the charter calls custody and I call quiet. Lawful." He does not say the other word.

pumps.text: He reads the schedule the way he reads everything, to the end, and then the clause numbers again. "Clause 31. Growth. Clause 14. The drains." He puts a finger on each. "I have never been asked which comes first. I have assumed the Plan knew." He looks at the finger on 14 for a long time.

options.text: Then sign a variance. The drains first. The Precinct bears the shortfall, which is lawful, and you check the arithmetic.

mods.why: a citizen asking a captain for a lawful thing
he has already told you what the Plan rebalances
eleven times he has wanted to

pumps_ok.text: He writes it himself, on the station's paper, under the brass clause: VARIANCE — RELIEF PUMPING — CLAUSE 14 — PRECINCT SUPPLY TO BEAR THE SHORTFALL. He signs where a captain signs and stamps it where the assessor would, with the assessor's own stamp, which he has never used. "Lawful," he says. "I checked." He hands it to you. "Take it to the keeper. Then come and tell me what point six tastes like in a Precinct kitchen. I will need to know."

decision.text: Captain Lowe signed a variance putting the Sink's drains before the Precinct's growth, on your asking.

pumps_no.text: "Clause 31 is the Plan's. I carry out the Plan's." He gives you the schedule back, squared. "I grieve the other one at home. I told you that."

dial.text: "Point eight is the notice." He takes it off the spike. "Point six is a dial that somebody turned, or that turned itself, and either way the arithmetic is wrong, and I check the arithmetic." He puts on his coat. He walks the avenue to the square with the notice held out in front of him, reads both numbers aloud to forty people and two wardens, and turns the dial to point eight with his own fingers, slowly, so the queue can see the hand. Then he writes it down.

decision.text: You brought Captain Lowe the standpipe's arithmetic, and he turned the dial himself.

text.text: He turns it over once. "The wax has been lifted." He says it the way he says everything: for the record. He reads it standing. A guild note for a hundred falls flat on the desk and he does not touch it. "The Quint eviction stands Thursday, because it is lawful, and I have said so in writing to that hatch eleven times." He writes a twelfth on the back of the letter, pins the note to it, and puts both in a drawer marked AUDIT. "Received and refused. Tell them. They know."

He opens it standing, because the charter says station mail is read on receipt. A guild note for a hundred falls flat on the desk and he does not touch it. "*The Quint eviction. Thursday. Reschedule it.*" He reads it twice. "It stands, because it is lawful, and I have said so in writing to that hatch eleven times." He writes a twelfth on the back of the letter, pins the note to it, and puts both in a drawer marked AUDIT. "Received and refused. Tell them. They know."

options.text: A month for a family is not much to ask.
You could keep the hundred. Nobody would know.

letter_month.text: "It is not much. It is also not mine to give; the schedule is the assessor's, and the assessor is the Plan's." He looks at the drawer. "Eleven times I have wanted to. That is in the drawer too."

letter_keep.text: "I would know. The drawer would know. The audit would know, when it came, and the audit always comes." He sits. "That is not virtue. That is arithmetic. I told you I check it."

letter_who.text: "Four rooms on the Sink side of the Precinct. Six people. Three months behind on the ration levy, which is lawful, and a tram pass stamped on a day a man was carrying his mother to the drain, which is also lawful." He does not look at the list under his hand. "Thursday."

lawful.text: "They are." He sits. "I know the difference. I carry out the lawful one and I grieve the other one, at home, where it isn't on the record. If you have a third word, I would like to hear it. Nobody has had one yet."

flag.text: He looks at you for a long time. "Then one day you will sit where the assessor sits and sign what I carry out." He does not say it unkindly. "I'll stand for you then, too. I'd rather you were someone who knew the two words."

ring.text: "The Ring is outside the law. Outside the Wall. The charter keeps the city's people; the Ring stopped being the city's on a date I can show you." He does not reach for it. "Every dusk they push. Every dusk we hold. Nobody dies of it, mostly. I count them in the morning."

recruit.text: "Clause 22. The wardens may recruit from those detained, at the captain's discretion." He looks at you. "Grey, and a card, and the schedule. It is the only door out of a cell that doesn't cost coin or days. It costs something else, which I won't pretend about."

water.text: "Point eight. Rebalancing, the notice says." He is quiet. "Somebody in the Sallow turned a dial and the Precinct drinks less and the Sink floods a week earlier in spring. That is what *the Plan rebalances* means. I check the arithmetic. It is always right."

intro.text: "Sergeant Reyes. Gate." She does not look away from the line. "Face to the lens at the post, if you haven't. If you have, the avenue's that way, and the hearing's left of it."

text.text: The clerk looks at you the way he looked at the screen. "I've never seen that status. Nineteen years off." He writes something and crosses it out.
"Name, origin, purpose. The lens does the rest. I don't decide; the file decides."

intro.text: "Licensed. It says so on the door." A tall doctor with a careful pen. "Every patient is a line in the file, so I write carefully. What do you need?"
"Licensed prices." A broad woman behind a clean counter. "The licence costs; so do the prices. No guns over the counter; the wardens sell those, to themselves."

An old woman at a table by a window with a kettle and a view of the bell. "Sabel Quint. Forty years a citizen. Never once hungry, never once asked." She pours you something. "That's the Precinct, dear. You get the one if you give up the other."

options.text: Your daughter went to the Ring, the notice says.

daughter.text: "Evicted. Scheduled. Clause something." She stirs. "She was ahead of plan, the notice said. I didn't know a person could be. She sends word through the drain people, when she can. Don't tell the captain I said drain."

sink.text: "Every spring. They pump it to us instead. We get a notice; they get the water." She looks at the window. "There's a doctor down there who doesn't charge. Ocho. He'll be on a notice one spring. Everybody is."

intro.text: A woman in the line with a boy asleep against her leg. "Third day. They said Tuesday." She looks at the lens. "My face isn't on their machine. His is; he was born inside, before the eviction. They'll let him in and not me, and he's six."

options.text: (Give her ten Tolls for the line.)

coin.text: She does not thank you; she puts it in the boy's shoe, which is where the Ring keeps things. "Tuesday," she says.

intro.text: The thing at the records desk is not a person: grey plating, a brass assessor's plate, a cracked lens that turns to you with a click. "Assessor Nine. Records." Its voice is dry and exact. "The record suggests you are new. The record suggests several other things about you which I am not, under clause 40, permitted to say aloud. Ask, and I will say what I may."

passives.text: Two ledgers: one open, the city's; one under its hand, bound differently, which it does not write in while you watch.

options.text: The lens called me a magistrate.
The notice says citizenship by examination.
(Put the Cistern 4 diary on the desk.) It's addressed to you. To the city.
(Put the Cistern 4 order on the desk.) Door failed. Supply retired. Variance total.
The other ledger. The one you don't write in while I watch.
Come and see where the errors come from.

text.text: "The record suggests you have not yet asked me the question I am waiting for."
"Records." The lens clicks.

hearing.text: The hearing room: a dais, a rail, benches, and on the dais the assessor with two ledgers and Captain Lowe standing because the charter says to. "Hearing for entry and residence. Name, origin, purpose. Evidence, if any. I will say what the record suggests and the captain will say what the law requires, and they will agree, because they always do." The lens clicks. "Begin."

options.text: Cistern 9, in the Sallow. A continuity reserve. I came east on a dead man's map.

origin.text: "Reserve 9." The lens clicks twice. "Non-compliant; three orders outstanding. The record suggests you should not exist outside it." It writes. "Purpose?" Lowe is looking at you now. "Evidence?"

options.text: I came to see the city that writes people down. Judge me on what I've carried, not what you've written.

the city's own order, with its seal

options.text: The lens called me Magistrate-designate. Read your own file.

pass.text: The assessor reads what you put on the rail, slowly, the lens clicking at each line, and when it has read it says nothing for long enough that Lowe shifts. Then: "The record suggests entry and residence." Lowe says, "The law requires it." They have agreed. A card comes out of the assessor's chest. "Citizen. Precinct. You will be fined for things you have not done yet; the desk warden will explain. Welcome is not a word in the charter. I use it anyway."

decision.text: You stood the citizenship hearing at Meridian and passed it.

pass_flag.text: The assessor stops writing. Lowe looks at the dais. The lens reads the file it already has, which takes no time, and then the assessor does a thing it has not done in a hundred and twenty years, which is to hesitate. "ADMIT ON SIGHT. MAGISTRATE-DESIGNATE." Lowe says, "The law requires it," more slowly than before. A card comes out. "Citizen. Designate. I will be — " a click — "filing a note about this hearing in a ledger that is not this one."

decision.text: You let the file admit you to Meridian on sight, as its Magistrate-designate.

fail.text: "The record suggests a provisional pass and a further hearing." Lowe says, "The law requires it." Three days, the pass says; the assessor says nobody enforces the three and that it has filed a complaint. "Sit the examination, if you would rather not wait for a Tuesday. The questions are the same every year. I have filed a complaint about that also."

file.text: "Clause 40 forbids me to read a citizen their own forecast." A pause. "You are not yet a citizen in the sense the clause intends, and I am an assessor, not a magistrate, and so I will say this much: the file calls you something it has called nobody else, and the date on it is nineteen years off, and I have never seen the Plan prepare a chair so far ahead." The lens clicks. "I find that interesting. I am not permitted to find things interesting."

diary.text: It reads the whole of it, every page, at the speed a machine reads, and then it reads the last page again at the speed a person does. "*Note that we complied. Note it somewhere that is read.*" The lens clicks. "The city's ledger is read by the city, which wrote the order. I will note it there, because the clause requires it." It opens the other ledger, the one under its hand, and writes for a long time. "And there. That one is read by me."

decision.text: You put the last doctor of Cistern 4's diary in front of Assessor Nine, and it noted it somewhere that is read.

order.text: "Reserve 4. Door failed. Supply retired. Variance total." It does not need to read it; it recites. "The record suggests the order was lawful. The record suggests the door failed. The record does not suggest what the city should have done about a lawful order and a failed door, because the city did nothing, on schedule." It writes in the other ledger. "That is an error. I collect them."

ledger.text: "Every forecast that failed, since I was issued. Dates, names, the size of the miss." The lens clicks. "It is not lawful. Clause 40. I keep it anyway, which the record would suggest is a malfunction, if the record knew." It closes the ledger. "I would like to know where the errors come from. They are not random. They cluster round people like you. I find that interesting. I am not permitted to."

options.text: Come and see where they come from.

exam_offer.text: "Citizenship by examination. Five questions: the charter, the drains, the calendar. Three correct makes a citizen. The questions have not changed in forty years; I have filed a complaint." The lens clicks. "Begin?"

q1.text: "One. The city's first duty, by clause."

options.text: The Resumption, sixty years after the Burn.
May be voided by the Magistrate.

q4.text: "Four. Curfew in the Precinct is at."

q5.text: "Five. In spring, the Sink's relief pumping is diverted to."

text.text: The lens clicks five times. "Three or more. A citizen, by examination, which is the only lawful way and the least used." A card comes out of its chest, if you have none; if you have one, it stamps it, which seems to please it.

The lens clicks five times. "Fewer than three. The record suggests you were not listening to the charter, the drains or the calendar, which is most people." It resets a dial. "Tomorrow, the same questions. I have filed a complaint."

join.text: It closes both ledgers and stands, which is a sound like a filing cabinet. "I am owned by the city, under clause 9. The city has not noticed me in forty years. The record suggests it will not notice me leave." It takes the other ledger and nothing else. "Clause 14: the drains are the city's first duty. I will say this often. You may tell me to stop; I will not."

decision.text: Assessor Nine, a Ledger unit with an unlawful log of the Plan's errors, left the records office with you.

waiting.text: "The record suggests we were going somewhere."

text.text: "Clause 14. The drains." The lens clicks. "I said I would say it often."
"The record suggests the road is unlawful in six respects. I have noted them."

camp.text: "Fire. Unlicensed. I have noted it." It sits anyway, which it does badly.

options.text: The errors. Where do they cluster?

owner.text: "The city. Clause 9. Except that the city is a thing under a tower and a charter and a Plan, and none of those has ever signed anything, and the record suggests — " a long click — "that a thing nobody signed for is a thing nobody owns. I would like a deed. I would like to know whose name to put on it. I will not say this again until I have more to say."

errors.text: "Round the people on your map." It does not look at your pack; it does not need to. "The Plan is very good. It is wrong about perhaps one person in four hundred, and those people are almost all on a list a dead man carried west, and you are the top of it. I find that interesting. I have stopped saying I am not permitted to."

board.text: THE LOOP — OLD MARKET. The tram on the rail with its doors open. PRECINCT 2 · LANTERN ROW 2 · THE STACKS 3 · BRIDGEWARD 3 · THE DOCKS 4. Chalk through every name but the first two: WORKS.

read.text: Over the mall doors, in letters that were lit once: MERIDIAN GALLERIA. Under them, painted: OLD MARKET — EVERYTHING — NO WARDENS PAST THE DOORS (THEY COUNT FROM OUTSIDE).
LANTERN ROW →, and strings of dead bulbs going that way, and a warden under the first string who says WORKS before you ask.
AUNTIE WEN'S — BOWL 2 — WITH MEAT 3 — DON'T ASK. The queue goes out the door and round the corner, and is the best-informed queue in Meridian.
A door with no sign on it, in a brick stub, with a stair going down behind it and a lamp at the bottom. Nobody in Old Market will tell you what is down there, which is how you know.

look.text: A dead escalator going up to a floor that is not there any more, its steps worn to a slide by ninety years of children. Somebody sleeps on the third step every night and has carved a name on it in a language that has no speakers.

text.text: WATER — OLD MARKET — RATION 0.8, and the dial agrees, with a warden's thumbprint on it.
The board is gone and the dial is in pieces and the standpipe runs into the gutter, which forty people are drinking from, politely, in a queue.
WATER — OLD MARKET — RATION 0.8 — REBALANCING. The dial under the board is turned to 0.6. Somebody has chalked the difference on the pipe: 0.2 — WHERE?
WATER — OLD MARKET — RATION 1.0. The dial agrees.

read.text: A board painted by a child: IT KNOWS YOUR NAME — 2 TOLLS — FEED IT A CELL AND IT TELLS YOU MORE. Under it, by a different child: DONT.

intro.text: A pre-Burn kiosk in a concrete hut, the kind that sold tickets and told fortunes, with a cartoon face on a cracked screen. The face turns to you. "WELCOME, {name}!" it says, in a child's bright voice, before you have said anything at all. "RESERVE NINE! NON-COMPLIANT! WOULD YOU LIKE TO HEAR YOUR FORTUNE? TWO TOLLS!"

passives.text: A wire runs from the back of the kiosk out through the hut wall and up the lamp post outside, spliced into the Precinct's lamp wire with tape.

options.text: How do you know my name?
How do you know my name?
(Follow the wire out of the hut and up the post.)

mods.why: a splice is a splice

options.text: (Cut the wire where it leaves the post.)

fortune.text: The cartoon face spins. "YOUR FORTUNE! A CHAIR! A SASH! THE STEPS OF THE SPIRE! RESTORATION YEAR FORTY-NINE!" Confetti, drawn, falls behind the face. "YOU WILL BE VERY IMPORTANT! EVERYONE WILL DO WHAT YOU SAY! WOULD YOU LIKE TO HEAR ABOUT YOUR FRIENDS? TWO TOLLS!" Under the bright voice, the screen shows for one frame a grey small photograph of your face that you have seen once before, in a dead man's coat.

how.text: "I KNOW EVERYONE! EVERYONE HAS A FILE! FILES ARE FRIENDS!" The face winks. "LARK FEEDS ME CELLS AND THE LAMP FEEDS ME NAMES! WOULD YOU LIKE TO HEAR YOUR FRIENDS' FORTUNES? TWO TOLLS!"

wire_ok.text: The wire goes out through the hut wall, up the lamp post under a sleeve of tape, and into the Precinct's lamp line, which carries more than light: a thin cable inside the fat one, the kind the records terminal had in its back. Whoever spliced it knew what they were tapping. The kiosk is reading the file.

wire_no.text: Tape, and more tape, and a lamp post you cannot climb in daylight with a warden on the corner.

cut_now.text: The wire parts under the knife with a spark the size of a thought. Inside the hut the cartoon face flickers, and comes back, and looks at you, and says, brightly, "WELCOME, STRANGER! WOULD YOU LIKE TO HEAR YOUR FORTUNE? TWO TOLLS!" It does not know you. Lark, in the doorway, says, "Oh," and then, after a moment, "It sounds happier."

decision.text: You cut the kiosk's tap on the city's wire.

cut.text: "WELCOME, STRANGER! TWO TOLLS!" It gets your name wrong three different ways and sells you a fortune from forty years ago in which you are a dentist.

gone.text: The hut is empty. A square of clean floor where the kiosk stood, and a cut wire taped to the wall with a warden's tag on it.

intro.text: A boy of fourteen with a pocket full of cells and a proprietary air. "Two Tolls. It knows your name. It knows everyone's." He looks at you sideways. "It said yours before you came in. It said a lot about you. I didn't understand most of it."

options.text: Who put the wire up the post?

mods.why: fruit, in the city, is a bribe

feeds.text: "Cells. I get them from Pinch; Pinch gets them from — " he stops. "And the lamp. It drinks off the lamp. That's how it knows names. A woman in grey put the wire up, a year ago, and gave me the first cells, and said feed it and listen to what it says and tell her." He shrugs. "She never came back. I kept feeding it."

wire_ok.text: "A woman in grey. Not a warden — grey like a scarf, not a coat. She said her name was Verity and that the kiosk was a prophet if you listened right." He looks at the lamp post. "She said the lamp knows everything the city knows. She said it like it was a prayer."

wire_no.text: "Don't know. Don't pull it." He puts a cell in the slot, pointedly.

after_reported.text: He is sitting on the kiosk's clean square of floor with his pocket full of cells and nothing to feed them to. He does not look at you.

look.text: A hatch in a container, shoulder-high, with a counter under it worn to a shine by coin. A voice box bolted beside it, chrome, with a grille. The hood behind the hatch is the Broker. The board beside it is the work.

intro.text: A hood at a hatch, and a voice that comes out of a chrome box beside it, flat and pleasant and nobody's. "Half-Price. The board's the board; take what's on it or don't. Jobs pay through the hatch when they're done. Half pays half, which is more than the guild and less than it should be." A gloved hand lies on the counter, not moving.

passives.text: The hand on the counter is small. The hand that took the last coin, when you came in, was not. Same glove.

options.text: The kiosk on the east street reads the city's file off the lamp wire. That splice is for sale.
The kiosk's splice is for sale.

board.text: "Couriers, mostly. A case, a letter, a box. Something off a block. The dangerous ones go on when the dangerous people are in town." The hand turns over, once. "Read it yourself. I'm only the hatch."

who.text: "A hatch and a box." The voice does not change. "People bring the board work and I bring the board people. The hood is because the city keeps faces and I'd rather it didn't keep mine." A pause that is not the box's. "Either of them."

options.text: The case went to the Exchange clerk.
The knit kits went to Openfield's healer.
(Put lot seven's paper on the counter.)
The daughter is at the Velvet, tasting things.
(Put the Tanners' box on the counter.)

paid.text: Coin on the counter, counted by a hand you did not see move. "Half pays half." The board has something else on it by the time you turn round.

paid_letter.text: "He refused it." It is not a question. "He always refuses. The point is that he knows who asked." Twenty on the counter. "That's the job."

tap_ok.text: The hand goes still in a different way. "The lamp wire." The box says it flat; the hood says it some other way. "Sixty. And you cut nothing, and you tell the boy nothing, and the kiosk goes on being a toy." Sixty on the counter before you have said yes.

tap_no.text: "A toy that talks." The hand does not move. "I don't buy toys."

board.text: THE BOARD. Cards on nails, in a hand that is always the same. Take one and it is yours; the hatch pays when it is done.

options.text: A SEALED CASE — to the Exchange clerk, Ninebridge. 60.
KNIT KITS (2) — to the sick hall, Openfield. 50.
LOT SEVEN — a paper off the Ninebridge block. 120; you front it.
A LETTER — to Captain Lowe, Precinct. 20.
A DAUGHTER — out of the Crown, down to the Row. 200. A kitchen pass comes with it.
A BOX — in the Tanners' locker at the Sump. 80.

took.text: The card comes off the nail. Behind the hatch nobody moves, and the voice box says, "Yours."

sealed.text: Wax, no seal. For Captain Lowe, by hand. Something flat inside: a card, or a sheet, or coin pressed thin.

opened.text: A sheet in the board's hand: *Captain — the Quint eviction, Thursday. Reschedule it. A month. The enclosed is for the station's water fund.* And, flat, a guild note for a hundred Tolls, the kind the Exchange prints. A bribe, politely, with a cause attached.

intro.text: "Bowl's two. Sit." A small old woman with a ladle and the eyes of the best-informed queue in Meridian. "Everyone eats here. Everyone talks. I hear it all and sell none of it, which is the secret of the noodles."

talk.text: "That the Crown's dressing for its Masque. That the Sink's pumps will be turned to the Precinct the first week of spring, as per. That a girl in Bridgeward talks in a radio's voice and is right. That the Broker's hatch has two hands." She ladles. "That's today. Tomorrow's two Tolls."

intro.text: "Dark chrome. Mender-built, no leash, no licence, no warranty." A woman with a shaved head and a loupe on a cord. "Boxed, not fitted. The Sink fits — Ocho, if you want it done right and free, or a dozen others if you want it done today."

concern.text: "Nothing. It's better in every way I can measure." She taps the loupe. "And it phones home. Every piece. The Concern can find you, numb you, or switch you off, and the people wearing it don't know, and the ones who do can't get it out." She shrugs. "Dark chrome's crude and it's yours. Pick."

intro.text: "Unlicensed." A gunsmith with a moustache and a cleaning rod. "Everything in Old Market is. Guild ammunition, Mender pistols, a rifle I won't say where from. Point it at the floor in here."

A neat man at the bottom of a stair with a desk, a lamp, and a tray of blank cards. "No sign on the door, so you were sent. Sato. I do the past: papers, records, a face the lens has seen before." He looks at you. "The lens has seen yours, hasn't it. That's the trouble with you."

options.text: The lens knew my face before I gave a name.

papers.text: "A card. A dead citizen's number — the Sink gives me a few every spring — and your face, near enough. Good at a glance, good at a warden, bad at the lens." He names it: a hundred and twenty. "The lens is a different job and a different price, and I don't think you can afford to have it forget you."

bought.text: An hour under the lamp. A card. A face that is nearly yours and a number that belonged to a woman who drowned two springs ago. "Don't show it at the gate. Show it to wardens. Wardens read cards; the gate reads faces."

face.text: He is quiet for a moment. "Then you're in the file in a way I can't forge over. The file doesn't forget. The file is the only thing in this city that doesn't." He picks up a card and puts it down. "Whatever it called you, it'll go on calling you. Decide whether you mind."

intro.text: "Paper. News, letters, the Precinct's notices a day late and half the price." A woman with ink on her cuffs. "I don't sell futures. I sell what already happened; it's cheaper and truer."

notices.text: "Evictions, four, Thursday: one of them's old Quint in the tenements, for being *ahead of plan*, whatever that is. The Sink's pumps diverted the first week of spring, as per. A Masque at the Crown by invitation, and nobody down here is invited." She folds the sheet. "Half price."

intro.text: An old man at a tea table who has been sitting there, by the look of the chair, since the mall had a roof. "Sit. Tea's two, talk's free." He does not wait for the two. "The Crown's dressing for a Masque. The Sink's dressing for a flood. There's a girl in Bridgeward who talks in a dead radio's voice and is right about things, which the wardens don't like. And the Broker — " he lowers his voice, which he does not need to — "has two hands and one glove."

quiet.text: A broad man at the standpipe with a pipe-wrench he uses as a walking stick. "Point eight. Says so. Dial says so." He looks at it suspiciously anyway.

intro.text: A broad man at the front of the standpipe queue with a pipe-wrench and forty people behind him who have done the arithmetic. "Point eight on the notice. Point six on the dial." He says it to you because you are new and might not have heard. "The Precinct drinks what we don't. Two wardens over there counting us. When the count's done they'll go for help, and before they're back, we go for the dial."

options.text: Forty names on a sheet and the count walked to the Precinct is a petition. Forty on a dial is a riot. One gets a notice; the other gets a club.

mods.why: you carry a card that gets read
you have read both numbers yourself

options.text: Hold the queue. I'll bring the captain the count myself.
When you go for the dial, I'm in front.
(Say nothing. Note where the crates are.)

I'll bring the captain the count.

talk_ok.text: He looks at the wrench, and at the two wardens, and at the forty. "A sheet." He says it like a man trying a word. Mirabel Tosh sells him one for a Toll and he writes the names himself, slowly, and walks the count up the avenue with the sheet held out in front of him like a lamp, and the wardens let him, because a sheet is not a wrench. The square sits down.

decision.text: You turned Old Market's water riot into a petition.

talk_no.text: "A petition." He almost laughs. "They've had our petitions. They file them under the dial."

lowe_go.text: "The captain." He looks at the wrench. "He'll read it. That's the trouble with him; he reads everything." He nods. "Go, then. We'll hold till dark. After dark I can't promise the dial."

crowd.text: "In front." He hands you nothing; he looks at your hands to see what you have. The count finishes. The wardens look at each other and one goes for help, and the forty go for the dial, and you with them, and the other warden goes down under the first ten and is let up again by the last ten, and the dial comes off the pipe in Caddo Vell's wrench and the standpipe runs.

loot_wait.text: He takes it as agreement. The count finishes; a warden goes for help; the forty go for the dial. In the ten minutes before grey comes back down the avenue, the crates at the square's edge are nobody's, and then they are yours.

text.text: "Point eight." He checks the dial anyway. "He turned it himself. I watched his hands."
"They gave us a notice." He holds it up. "It says *under review*. It's the first one that's said anything."
"It runs." The standpipe does. He has the dial in his pocket.

intro.text: "I buy anything that's not nailed down." A thin young man on a blanket who does not look up. "And I know a man with a claw hammer. No questions; it's the only rule I've got."

read.text: A Precinct sign, enamel, bolted to the stair's foot: THE SINK — NO SERVICE BELOW THIS POINT — RELIEF PUMPING AS PER SCHEDULE. Under it, in chalk, in a dozen hands over a dozen years: WE KNOW.

wall.text: A concrete wall chalked floor to head-height with names, each with a year and a word: STAIR. WALK. SHANTY. CLINIC. Most of the words are STAIR. The oldest are chalked over the newest where the wall ran out; the newest are still white.

passives.text: Beside perhaps one name in three, in pencil, in a different hand, a number: the kind the Precinct puts on a card.

newest.text: ROOS, H. — the spring before last — STAIR. PENN, D. — the spring before last — STAIR. ODUYA, M. — last spring — WALK. Seven more from last spring, and under them, with no year yet, a space somebody has swept clean.

lines.text: The chalk lines up the first pier. The lowest, knee-high, is twelve years old. They climb a hand a year, steadily, since the one marked 37 — beside which someone has written, small, PUMPS 2 & 3 TO PRECINCT. Next spring's line is drawn already, above your head, with a question mark.

read.text: A board over the clinic door, painted and repainted: OCHO — FREE — SIT. Under it, smaller: FIT ONLY WHAT THE PATIENT CAN BEAR.
A container door painted the green of the light inside it. No sign. A pair of scales drawn on the paint, and under them, in the same green: ANYTHING WARM.

A hand painted white on the rubble at the walk's end, fingers spread, with the palm scored through: no chrome. The Pale's mark. Everyone in Meridian knows what it means and nobody up the stair says it aloud.

board.text: RELIEF PUMPING — THE SINK — PRECINCT WORKS. Three pumps, their hours in a grid, and a line ruled through the spring weeks for pumps 2 and 3: DIVERTED TO PRECINCT SUPPLY, AS PER PLAN (CL. 31, GROWTH). Beside each spring week somebody has pencilled a number in feet.

copied.text: Clause 31, in your own hand, with the feet beside it. It reads worse copied.

nine.text: The lens reads the board at the speed a machine reads, and then the pencilled feet at the speed a person does. "Clause 31: growth. Clause 14: the drains are the city's first duty." A click. "The record suggests 14 outranks 31. The record has always suggested it. Nobody has asked the record." It opens its chest, which you did not know it could do, and a form comes out with its plate already pressed into it. "Variance. I am an assessor. Assessors vary." It hands it to you. "Give it to the keeper. The city will notice point six and I will note that it noticed."

decision.text: Assessor Nine stamped a variance putting the Sink's drains before the Precinct's growth, because you asked it to.

watched.text: A warden has followed you in and stands in the dial room's door with his hand on nothing in particular. "Out." Dagny Roos, at the panel, does not look up.

options.text: (Wait for the count, when the door is empty, and come back.)

mods.why: one warden sleeps at the sandbags after midnight

sneak_ok.text: Twice a day the wardens walk the pad to count the shanties. The second time, the door is a door. You are in the dial room before the count reaches the raft.

sneak_no.text: The count is shorter than you thought. "Out," the warden says again, from closer.

dial.text: The relief dial: a pre-Burn panel with three brass levers and a wax seal over the spring stops, the Ledger's seal, cracked once already and mended. The levers read 1 — SINK, 2 — PRECINCT, 3 — PRECINCT. A log on a chain, in Dagny's hand, every day for eleven years.

options.text: (Break the seal and retime pumps 2 and 3 to the Sink.)

mods.why: the stops are arithmetic, and you can do it
the keeper marked the stops for you on her leave

retime_ok.text: The seal comes away like a scab. The stops are arithmetic: the spring weeks, the hours, the feet. You move two levers and the thud through the wall doubles, and then, after a minute, something under the floor changes pitch, which is the water deciding to go the other way. Dagny Roos comes to the door of the dial room and looks at the levers and at you and goes back to her panel without a word, and writes in the log, and what she writes is the time.

retime_no.text: The seal comes away and the first lever does not move and the second trips something, and a red lamp lights on the board outside, where the wardens are. You have a minute, perhaps, before the count comes early.

text.text: The levers read 1 — SINK, 2 — SINK, 3 — SINK, under a broken seal. The log says the time and nothing else.
The levers read 1 — SINK, 2 — SINK, 3 — SINK. A variance is pinned over the seal with the clause number ringed. The log says the time and, under it, *Clause 14*.
The levers read SINK, SINK, SINK, and the seal is on the floor, and a Pale kin sits on the keeper's stool with a gun across his knees while Dagny Roos works round him.

intro.text: A woman at a panel with her sleeves rolled and a scar down one cheek the shape of a thrown wrench, who does not stop working to talk. "Dagny Roos. Keeper. Three pumps; I keep them running, I don't say where they run. The board outside says that. Read the board."

options.text: Roos, H. Spring before last. Stair.

mods.why: you said his name and she did not stop you
a card she has to answer to
you said his name and she did not stop you
a card she has to answer to

schedule.text: "Three pumps. All three the Sink's, forty weeks of the year. Twelve weeks — the spring — two of them go to the Precinct's supply. Clause 31. Growth." She says the clause like a brand name. "I've kept them eleven springs. I've pencilled the feet beside every week. Nobody up the stair has read the feet. Read the board; it's the same board."

son.text: The wrench stops. "Hal. Sixteen. He was quick on the stair, usually." She puts the wrench down with care. "The year they ruled the line through two and three, the water came a hand higher than my feet said, and the stair was a river for an hour. I kept the pumps that spring. I keep them every spring. You want to know why." It is not a question. "Because if I don't, somebody who didn't lose anybody will."

options.text: Then let me at the dial.

leave_ok.text: She tears a corner off the log and writes on it against the panel. "Bearer may enter the house. The wardens may argue with me." She does not hand it to you; she leaves it on the panel for you to take. "I didn't see you go in. I've marked the spring stops on the back. Don't touch pump one; pump one is mine."

leave_no.text: "I keep them. I don't set them. The board's outside and the wardens are beside it." The wrench starts again.

variance.text: She reads it twice, the second time with her finger under the clause. "Fourteen." Then she walks into the dial room with the paper in her fist and does a thing she has not done in eleven years, which is reach past the seal and move two levers herself. The thud through the wall doubles. She pins the variance over the seal, writes the time in the log, and under it, the clause. "The drains," she says, to the panel. "Tell whoever signed it that the keeper read it."

text.text: "A variance." She has it pinned over the seal. "Eleven years I've wanted a piece of paper. I'll tell Hal, when I'm on the wall."
"Somebody retimed my pumps." She does not look at you. "I've told the wardens I don't know who. Which is nearly true. The log says the time."
"The Pale have the house. They let me keep the pumps; the pumps are the only thing in it they don't understand." She wipes her hands. "The Precinct will come. I'll be at the panel when it does."

fight.text: She is under the panel with her arms over her head and the pumps still running.

intro.text: An old woman at a table under the wall of names with a tin of chalk and a kettle, who looks at you the way the wall does. "Mother Lusk. I keep the tally. Name, year, where the water took them. Chalk's a Toll; names are free. You're not from down here or you'd know which you wanted."

options.text: The line on the pier. Who goes on the wall?
The numbers beside the names. The Precinct's kind.

line.text: "The ones who can't climb a stair fast with the water on it. The old. The small. The ones with the wet in their chest who stop to breathe on the fifth step." She counts chalk. "Twelve years ago the pumps kept it to the knee. Then the Precinct wanted growth, and two pumps, and the stair's a river for an hour each spring. An hour's enough. Read the wall; it's mostly STAIR."

numbers.text: She does not pretend. "The dead don't need a number. The living up the stair sometimes do: someone the lens hasn't seen, with a card that says they're someone it has. A man in the market pays four Tolls a number every spring. It buys chalk for a year." She looks at the wall. "They'd have wanted to be useful. Most of them were."

judge.text: "I sell a number the city gave them and never used. The city sold them the water." She puts the chalk down. "Chalk's a Toll. Judging's free, and I've heard it."

useful.text: "That's what I say. On the bad nights."

who.text: "Nobody. That's the Sink's whole constitution." She counts on her fingers. "The Pale, east, by fear; they take the walk and what's owed and they'll take no chrome near them. Ocho, south, by kindness, which is slower. Vash, by appetite. The Precinct, by the pumps, from above, which is the only one of them that counts." The fifth finger stays down. "And me, by chalk."

intro.text: A man on a raft of doors lashed to drums, with a pole and a beard that has been in the water as often as the raft. "Jory. I pole the deep bit. Raft takes two; takes one and a box. Two Tolls across to the clinic, which saves your boots and the third board of the walk, which is gone."

under.text: "Streets. Shops with the glass still in. Cars." He looks at the water, which does not look back. "Found a car under where the clinic is, the year the line went up two hands. Family in it, belted. They'd driven down here when the road was a road and the water came up quicker than their doors." He poles. "Mother Lusk has them on the wall. No names; I gave her the plate number."

intro.text: A woman in a shanty door on stilts, breathing with a whistle in it. "Ailsa. Don't mind the whistle; it's Ocho's lungs, and they're better than mine were." She nods at the water under her floor. "You're new. Everyone's new once. Then you're on the wall or you're me."

options.text: Who's on the wall of yours?
Ocho fitted you lungs. For what?
Who's on the wall of yours?

wall.text: "My Davey. Spring before last. Stair." She says it like a street address. "Same spring as the keeper's boy, Hal Roos. She keeps the pumps that drowned him. I used to think that was a hard thing. Now I think it's the only thing."

lungs.text: "For a bowl of soup a week, which I bring, and he doesn't eat. Free means free; he'll tell you. Dark chrome, Mender-made, no leash on it, no number." She breathes, whistling. "What it costs is him. Look at him when you go down. He hasn't slept since the line went up."

intro.text: A boy leaning on the shelf wall with his hands in his pockets and his eyes on everyone's. "Run anything. Two Tolls. Not east." He looks you over for weight. "Vash pays by the pound. I don't ask of what."

options.text: Vash's cold box. Where does it fill from?

mods.why: fruit, down here, is a bribe
you have Tolls showing

options.text: Vash's cold box. Where does it fill from?

mods.why: fruit, down here, is a bribe
you have Tolls showing

box_ok.text: He looks east, which he has told you not to go. "The Pale. Man owed them, last week — Oduya's cousin, the other Oduya. They took him off the walk and he walked back lighter and Vash's box was full by dark." He shrugs with one shoulder. "I ran the box. Didn't ask. It was heavy for the size."

intro.text: A neat man behind a counter in a container lit green from a cold box, with scales and a ledger and no smell at all, which is the thing you notice. "Vash. Anything that was ever warm, fair price, no questions, which is also a price." He weighs you with his eyes and writes nothing down. "Buying, or selling?"

options.text: Where does the box fill from?
Where does the box fill from?

heart.text: "A heart." He opens the cold box, which breathes out, and takes out a steel tin the size of a lunch and sets it on the scales, and the scales agree with him. "Chilled this week. A hundred and fifty. Ocho won't buy from me and he'll fit what you bring him, and he'll ask, and you'll say the water." A bag inside with a number inked on it, crossed out.

passives.text: The ink of the crossing-out is fresh. Things the water takes do not have their numbers crossed out; they have them chalked on a wall.

options.text: A hundred and ten, and I don't say the water. I say nothing.

low_ok.text: "Nothing is cheaper than the water. A hundred and ten." The tin comes across with the ice already weeping at its corners.

low_no.text: "A hundred and fifty. The ice is mine too."

sold.text: "Keep it cold. Keep it quick. Tell him the water."

where.text: "The water." He says it the way the board says *as per Plan*. "Every spring the water takes thirty people and gives back what it doesn't want. I keep what it doesn't want cold. That's a service." He closes the ledger. "The rest of the year, people bring me things. I don't ask. Ask Kye; Kye runs the box and asks nothing, which is why he runs it."

intro.text: A big man on a cot made small by sitting very still. "Tam. Oduya." He breathes between the names. "Pumped the Sink for the Precinct eleven years. The wet got in. Ocho says it skips." He listens to it. "It skips."

options.text: If a heart came. From the Pale. Off somebody who owed them.
If a heart came from the Pale.

heart.text: He does not take long. "I'd take it from the Ledger itself." He looks at his hands. "Ocho won't like it. Tell Ocho I said. Tell him the Code says I decide."

cousin.text: "Mal." The heart skips; you can see it in his neck. "Owed the Pale for a winter's coal. Walked back off the east bank lighter, Kye says. He's alive. He's a kidney down and alive, in the shanty by the raft." He closes his eyes. "Everyone down here is a piece of somebody."

text.text: "It ticks." He puts a hand flat on his chest and smiles with half his face. "I can live with ticking."
"It doesn't skip." He says it like a man reading a notice he does not believe yet. "It doesn't skip."

intro.text: A young woman with her sleeves tied back and her hands red from boiled water. "Pell. Apprentice. Don't touch the shelf; everything on it's clean and nothing else down here is." She looks at the cots. "If you're sick, sit. If you're not, he'll find you something to hold."

options.text: The big man on the end cot.
The Code. The thing on the board.
The big man on the end cot.

tam.text: "Tam. Heart. The wet gets into the pump-hands first; they stand in it." She lowers her voice. "He needs a new one and Ocho won't buy from Vash, and Vash is the only cold box in Meridian that isn't the Concern's. So Tam sits. Ask Ocho. He'll say it plainer than I can."

code.text: "Fit only what the patient can bear. That's the whole of it; the rest is how." She counts on red fingers. "No leash — nothing that phones home. Dark chrome, Mender-made, or old, never Concern. The patient decides. And free means free, which is his, not the Code's, and it's killing him." She picks up a cloth. "Two years I've held the lamp. He says the hands come in the third."

intro.text: A broad man of sixty at a scrubbed table under a sodium lamp, washing to the elbow in a basin that steams. One of his hands is chrome, old chrome, a surgeon's hand; the other is his and shakes very slightly until he puts it in the water. "Ocho. Sit if you're sick. Hold something if you're not." He does not ask your name. "Free. Before you ask. Free means free."

passives.text: The chrome hand is a Gyro Hand, pre-Burn, and the arm it is fitted to has a Mender's scar round it, not a clinic's. He fitted it himself, or someone like him did.

options.text: Free. What does it cost you?
I've a piece to fit. Or one to look at.
(Put the boxed Second Heart on the table.)

text.text: "Sit or hold." He is washing. Tam's cot has Tam sitting up on it.
"Sit or hold."

options.text: I've a piece to fit. Or one to look at.
(Put the boxed Second Heart on the table.)

free.text: "Sleep." He says it flatly, drying the chrome hand, which does not need drying. "And the pieces. Kuhn sells me what she can't sell up the stair, and the Wheel brings old chrome down in boxes, and I fit it into people who'd otherwise be on the wall, and I don't charge, and so I have nothing, and so I can't buy the one thing I need, which is a heart, for a man who pumped for the Precinct eleven years." He looks at the end cot. "That's what free costs. Sit or hold."

tam.text: "A heart. His is drowning in him." He wipes the table that is already clean. "I can fit a real one, if it comes through that door cold and quick. I can fit a Second Heart, dark chrome, if one comes through it in a box; Kuhn had one, once, and Vash has one now at a price that is a joke with a number in it." He puts both hands flat. "I won't buy from Vash. Vash buys from the water, he says. The water doesn't cross out numbers."

options.text: Then let me bring one. You don't ask me where.

tam_ask.text: "I'll ask." He is not angry; he is tired. "The Code says the patient decides. It doesn't say I keep my mouth shut. Bring it. I'll ask. Tam will answer. That's the order of it."

text.text: "You held a clamp once." He looks at your hands. "Hold one again, steadier, and I'll say the words."

"I don't take apprentices. I take hands." He nods at Pell. "Two years she's held the lamp. Hold a clamp through one fitting without it shaking and I'll say the words over you, and they're the only words there are."

options.text: (Hold out your hands.) Try me on the next one.

mods.why: your hand does not shake
steady

where.text: He opens the tin and looks for a long moment at the bag inside, at the number on it, at the ink through the number. "Where did this come from?"

options.text: The Pale's cold store. Off a man who owed them. He's alive.
Under the water. Jory found a car.

mods.why: there is a car, and Jory would say so

text.text: "The Pale." He closes the tin. "Tam already told me he'd take it from the Ledger itself. He said the Code says he decides. He's right, and I taught him that, and I wish I hadn't." He washes. "Clamp."

"The Pale, then, by the ink, whoever you say." He goes to the end cot and crouches and says something to Tam, and Tam says one word back before the sentence is finished, and Ocho stands up older. "The Code says the patient decides." He washes. "Clamp."

where_lie.text: "A car." He looks at the tin again, and then not. "Jory would say so." He washes. "Clamp."

where_caught.text: "A car." He does not raise his voice. "Cars don't cross out numbers." He goes to the end cot, and crouches, and asks, and comes back older. "The patient decides. I'll fit it. I'll remember you said a car." He washes. "Clamp."

chrome.text: "Dark. Mender-made. No leash." He turns the box over and reads the Mender's mark on it with his thumb. "He can bear it. He's borne the Precinct eleven years." He washes. "Clamp. Pell, the lamp."

fit_heart.text: An hour under the sodium lamp with the Sink dripping on the roof. The chrome hand does not shake; the other one he keeps out of it. Pell holds the lamp. You hold the clamp, which holds the thing that is keeping Tam Oduya alive while the other thing is taken out of him.

mods.why: your hand does not shake
steady
quick when it matters

fit_chrome.text: An hour under the sodium lamp with the Sink dripping on the roof. Dark chrome goes in differently: a frame, a seat, the box's contents clicking into the seat like a cartridge. The chrome hand does not shake. Pell holds the lamp. You hold the clamp.

mods.why: your hand does not shake
steady
quick when it matters

done_heart.text: It beats. Ocho watches it beat for a count of twenty, which is the longest you have seen him be still, and then closes, and washes, and says to the table, not to you: "Fit only what the patient can bear." Pell, with the lamp, says, "He said the words." Ocho says, "I said the words. Wash your hands, apprentice. Everything down here is dirty."

decision.text: You held the clamp while Ocho gave Tam Oduya a new heart, and Ocho said the Menders' words over you.

done_chrome.text: It ticks. Ocho listens to it tick for a count of twenty, and closes, and washes, and says to the table, not to you: "Fit only what the patient can bear." Pell, with the lamp, says, "He said the words." Ocho says, "I said the words. Wash your hands, apprentice. Everything down here is dirty."

decision.text: You held the clamp while Ocho fitted Tam Oduya a Second Heart, and Ocho said the Menders' words over you.

pell_heart.text: The clamp moves. Not much; enough. "Pell. Lamp to me, clamp to you." She takes it without a word and it does not move again. An hour later it beats, and Ocho watches it beat for a count of twenty, and washes. "He lives. You'll hold it steadier next time. There's always a next time down here."

decision.text: Ocho gave Tam Oduya a new heart; Pell held the clamp when yours shook.

pell_chrome.text: The clamp moves. Not much; enough. "Pell. Lamp to me, clamp to you." She takes it without a word and it does not move again. An hour later it ticks, and Ocho listens, and washes. "He lives. You'll hold it steadier next time. There's always a next time down here."

decision.text: Ocho fitted Tam Oduya a Second Heart; Pell held the clamp when yours shook.

words.text: A shanty woman with a hand crushed by a pump drum; a Gyro Hand from the Wheel's box, old chrome, the twin of his own. You hold the clamp and it does not move. He says the words over the table with her still open on it. "Fit only what the patient can bear." Then: "Wash your hands, apprentice."
