decision.text: Ocho said the Menders' words over you at his table in the Sink.

shake.text: It moves. "Pell." She takes it. Afterwards he dries the chrome hand that does not need drying and says, "Next time," which down here is not a refusal.

intro.text: A woman in a container chair with skin the colour of the water and hair the colour of bone, who looks at your hands before your face. "You came past three of mine. Brave, or deaf." She does not get up. "Saskia Dray. The Pale. Show me your hands." You show her. "No chrome. Good. Keep it that way down here, or don't come down here."

options.text: The pumps. Spring. You want them.
There's a heart in your cold store with a number crossed out.
Call yours off the walk. I come and go.

mods.why: she has seen your hand
she has seen your eyes

options.text: The heart in your cold store.

mods.why: she has seen your hand
she has seen your eyes

pumps.text: "The pumps are ours by water. The Precinct has them by paper and two guns." She leans forward for the first time. "Twelve weeks a year they drown us for a number up the stair. I've nine kin who'll go down the walk with me and two who'll come back. That's the arithmetic. I've been waiting for someone to change it." She looks at your hands again. "You change arithmetic. I can see it on you."

options.text: There's paper that outranks their paper. Let me try it first.

paper.text: "Paper." She sits back. "Try it. When it doesn't work, I'm here. The water doesn't read."

seize.text: She stands. It is a different thing when she stands. "Then it's now." Three kin come off the fire without being called. "Two wardens, two guns, one door. Dagny stays alive; Dagny keeps the pumps. The rest is the walk's." She looks at you once more. "In front, you said."

decision.text: You went down the stilt-walk with the Pale to take the pump house from the Precinct.

won.text: The pump house, with the Precinct's lamps still on it and nobody's wardens at the door. Saskia Dray stands in it with her hand on a pump like a woman touching a horse. "Ours by water. Now by the walk too." Dagny Roos is at the panel, alive, not looking at anyone. Dray does not thank you; she gives you something better, which is a nod from the Pale. "Keep your hands. Come east any time."

held.text: "The house holds." She is on the pump pad now, most days, and the kin have moved the fire. "The Precinct will come. We'll be here. So will the water."

heart.text: "He owed. He paid. He's alive — we're not animals; we took what he had two of." No shame in it; it is a ledger. "The box is Vash's by dark. This one he hasn't had yet." She watches you want it. "Eighty, and you take it from the cold store yourself, and you tell Ocho whatever you like."

heart_paid.text: "The store's open. Take the tin and nothing else." She sits back down. "And tell Ocho it was the water. He likes the water."

heart_no.text: "Then sit with Tam while he drowns in his own chest and tell him about living men." She does not get up. "Go on. Clinic's south."

walk_ok.text: "Come and go." She says it to the kin, not to you, and they sit back down. "You've a face the water hasn't had. Keep it out of my cold store."

walk_no.text: "No." The kin do not sit down. "Walk ends at the sandbags. It always did."

scald.text: "Before the Burn finished burning, the city's chrome all woke up at once and did what it was told, and what it was told was *hold still*. Everyone with a leash in them stood in the street and held still and the fire came." She does not blink. "Our grandparents watched. We don't forget. No chrome, ever, and nobody with chrome among us, and we take it out of people who owe us, which is the same rule from the other end."

board.text: THE LOOP — LANTERN ROW. The tram with its doors open and a tube over the board, pink. PRECINCT 2 · OLD MARKET 2 · THE STACKS 3 · BRIDGEWARD 3 · THE DOCKS 4. Chalk through the last three, and under it in a different chalk: SOON.

read.text: THE COINAGE, in gold tube over a brick door, and a hand painted under it with the palm scored through — the Pale's mark — and over that, in gold paint, a coin. The Gilt's answer.
A green tube and no name. Through the door, tables, and the sound Dust makes when it is being lost by people who can afford it.
THE VELVET, in pink, with the T burned out so that it reads THE VELVE. Nobody has fixed it in a year; it is said with the T anyway. A queue, orderly, under the tube.
A violet tube over a container door: THE LANTERN — REVERIES BY THE HOUR — YOURS OR BETTER. Smaller, under it: WE DO NOT BUY FROM THE DROWNED.
WORKS. A chain across the street east and two Gilt on the chain. Behind them the tubes are dark all the way to Bridgeward, which is where the chain is really about.
LANTERN ROW, in every colour, on a board that was once a tram timetable. Under it, in warden stencil: NO WARDEN SERVICE. Under that, in chalk: GOOD.

A tide mark on the canal wall with a date beside it, and the water a foot below it. The canal was a street; the Sink's pumps found it. It runs warm and it throws the tubes back at you, pink and cyan, all night.

look.text: Shay's boat: a flat hull of doors with a pole and a lantern, tied at the quay. Two Tolls, the board says, and a hand painted pointing across.

card.text: TONIGHT'S CARD, in chalk on a post: TEAGUE v. DOUBT — house pays two to one. ANVIL v. ALL COMERS — thirty to enter, ninety standing. HANDS AND IRON. GUNS WITH MAB. Under it, older: NOBODY HAS STOOD SINCE SPRING.

passives.text: The chalk under DOUBT has been rubbed out and written again tonight, and the odds beside it moved a notch the house's way.

intro.text: A woman with a slate, a stool, a cash-box and a revolver she does not need to touch. "Mab Corrigan. The pit's mine, the floor's washed, the odds are chalk. Undercard's twenty, two to one. The comer's thirty to enter and ninety if you're standing at the end." She looks you up and down the way a scale would. "Nobody's standing."

options.text: What would the house pay for the comer to fall in the second?
What would the house pay for the comer to fall in the second?

under.text: "Teague or Doubt." She has the slip written before you answer; she writes both and tears one.

bell.text: An hour, and the bell. Teague is the small one and fights like it, in and out; Doubt is the big one and fights like a man with somewhere to be. In the second, Doubt walks onto a left that a child would have seen coming and goes down, carefully, like a man checking the floor for coins. The crowd knows. The crowd always knows. The house pays anyway.

collected.text: "Forty." Counted onto the slate, not into your hand; you pick it up yourself. "The small one. Everyone says the small one, after."

torn.text: "Doubt." She almost smiles. "Nobody's ever sure why."

comer.text: "Anvil's in the ring. Hands and iron only — leave the guns with me; you get them back, you always do." She holds out the cash-box lid. "Thirty."

comer_go.text: "Go and stand in front of him. He'll do the rest." The slate: COMER — 3 TO 1. Somebody in the crowd has already bet against you.

dive.text: She does not look up from the slate. "Sixty. After. From me. And nobody says." The chalk does not stop. "Anvil knows. Anvil doesn't mind. Anvil's been in the second since spring."

dive_done.text: "The second. Not the first; the first's an insult. Not the third; the third's a crime." She writes nothing down.

text.text: The slate is still up. COMER — STANDING. She looks at you for a long moment over it. "You had a deal." The cash-box opens anyway. "Ninety. The deal was sixty and I don't pay men who don't fall. Take the ninety and don't come to me for a deal again."

The slate is still up. COMER — STANDING. The crowd is the loudest it has been all year and most of it is losing money. "Standing." She opens the cash-box. "Ninety. And this." A brass token, pit-stamped. "The Skirts' pits honour it, and the Crown's, if you ever stand in one of those."

decision.text: You stood in Lantern Row's pit against Anvil and were standing at the end.

news.text: a comer stood against Anvil in Lantern Row's pit and was standing at the end

text.text: "The second." She says it like a date. "Sixty." Counted onto the slate. "That's a deal kept, which on this row is rarer than standing."
"Anvil." She wipes the slate. "Thirty's chalk. There's tomorrow; there's always tomorrow, down here."

decision.text: You took a dive in Lantern Row's pit for the house's sixty.

intro.text: A man in the ring with his hands wrapped and bolt knuckles on the wraps, standing the way a wall stands. "Anvil. You're not on the card." He does not look at you long. "Mab's thirty. Then you're on it."

ready.text: "You paid Mab." He rolls his shoulders once. "Hands and iron. I don't go for the head unless you do. Floor's washed; try not to be the reason it needs washing." The crowd leans in over the chain.

stood.text: "Standing." He says it with something that is nearly respect and nearly relief. "Nobody's done that since spring. The spring one was me." He unwraps a hand. "Mab's got your purse. Go and get it before she thinks of a reason."

floored.text: "Floor's clean." He means it kindly. "You cleaned it. Thirty gets you another go; the second go is the one that counts, most of them."

intro.text: A small fighter wrapping her hands with the care of someone who has broken them before. "Teague. I'm the small one. Bet on the small one; the big one's got somewhere to be." She looks at Doubt across the ring, and at Mab's shack, and back at her hands.

doubt.text: "Mab's shack, after. With a slip in his hand and a limp he hasn't got." She ties off the wrap. "Everyone on the Row knows. Everyone bets anyway. That's the Row."

intro.text: A big man with a beard and bolt knuckles, looking at the pit floor as if it owed him. "Doubt. They call me Doubt. Nobody's sure why." He does not look at Teague. "Second round. Could go either way."

passives.text: He is counting something on his fingers inside his coat, and it is not rounds.

intro.text: A woman at a desk between three cots with headsets on hooks over them, and a locker behind her with a violet tube on it. "Ysolde Marr. The Lantern. Yours or better." She taps the hooks. "A Summer in the Crown. The Race. Five an hour, either. And the evidence shelf, which isn't for sale, and which you'll ask about anyway."

options.text: A Summer in the Crown. (5 Tolls)
A Summer in the Crown. (5 Tolls)

what.text: "A day someone had, on a reel, through a headset. The Crown records art. The Row records whatever sells. Wardens record for evidence." She shrugs. "Some people live in them. I don't sell to those; look at the cots after and you'd stop too."

shelf.text: She takes a reel off the locker shelf with two fingers, the way you hold something that is not yours. "A Rustmouth brought it off a warden's shelf. A man sat on that cot a season ago and paid me to record his last day in the city, start to end, and left before dawn. No face in it; he was a Choir man, they keep no likeness. The wardens wanted it for who he met." She puts it down between you. "Two hundred. Because wardens."

who.text: "I didn't watch it. I never watch the shelf." She means it. "Buy it and tell me, or don't."

trade.text: "A memory of yours." She looks at you properly for the first time. "The Cistern. Nobody up here has one of a cistern; nobody up here has been in one. An hour on the cot and the reel's yours." A pause. "It's not a copy. It's yours; you'll still have it. People say it feels thinner after. People say a lot."

decision.text: You sold a reverie of the Cistern to the Lantern, for the stranger's day.

reel.text: "Jack in here or don't jack in at all; the reel's keyed to my cots." She hangs a headset on the nearest hook. "I won't watch. I never watch the shelf."

garden.text: Light. Real light, through a dome, on leaves that are green all the way through. You are carrying a tray; the hands are not yours and they are steady. A woman in grey silk at a glass table does not look at you as she takes a cup, and beyond her, over the parapet, the whole city lies in haze like something spilled. The air has no taste at all. You stand there a long time, holding the tray, and nobody asks you to stop.

city.text: From up here the Precinct is a grid and Old Market is a stain and the canal is a bright thread, and you cannot see the Sink at all, which is the point of up here. The woman says, to nobody, "Bring the next one." The reel ends on the tray going back through a door.

line.text: Engine. Dust. A buggy of welded doors with a wheel in your hands that fights you, and six others beside you on a ring road of cracked concrete outside the Wall with the towers behind, and a flag. The flag drops. For four minutes you are faster than anyone you have ever been, and then a wheel comes off something ahead and it is not yours, and the reel ends in the roar, which the crowd at the Dead Ring makes when somebody does not get up.

stair.text: A stair. Concrete, lit every landing by a tube that is the city's, not the Row's: white, steady, counted. The hands are not yours; they are older and the knuckles are scarred, and one of them is pressed flat against the coat over the ribs where something flat and square is carried. Breath, going down. Nobody on the stair. The reel is a season old and the man whose eyes these are is still alive in it, for the length of the reel.

options.text: (Look down, at what the hand is pressing flat.)

count.text: Landings. Under the breath, a number at each: "— ninety-one. Ninety. Eighty-nine —" It goes on a long time. There is only one house in Meridian with that many floors above a stair, and it has the city's own tubes on its landings.

options.text: (Look down, at what the hand is pressing flat.)

count_no.text: Breath, and the stair, and a number you cannot catch.

options.text: (Look down, at what the hand is pressing flat.)

bundle.text: On a landing he stops and takes it out, to check it, the way you check a thing you have stolen. A bundle of photographs in a cloth, each a face, each with a line of cipher under it; and a sheet, the same cipher, twelve lines long. He fans them once with his thumb. The fourth face is yours, older, grey at the temples, and you feel the hand that is not yours stop, and feel — through a season and a reel — the man decide something. He puts them back against his ribs.

bundle_no.text: The hand stays flat. Whatever is under it stays under it.

row.text: Then night, and tubes, pink and violet, and this cot, from the inside: the headset coming down over eyes that are not yours and a woman's voice — Ysolde's, a season younger — saying "Start to end?" and his, the first time you have heard it, saying "Start to end. If I don't come back, somebody should have seen it." Then a bowl of Auntie Wen's noodles, eaten standing. Then the gate.

options.text: (The gate. Look at who is looking.)

gate.text: Dawn at the Wall, the gate the size of a door, the lens. He does not look at the lens; he looks past it, west, at the road, and at a rider on the road who is not going anywhere: a long coat, a guild rifle across the saddle, a brand on the saddle's leather you have seen on a gatepost at Tollhouse 9. The rider is waiting. The man whose eyes these are sees that the rider is waiting, and goes west anyway, and the reel ends on the first step.

gate_no.text: Dawn, the Wall, the road west. Somebody on it. The reel ends on the first step.

wake.text: The cot. The violet tube. Ysolde at her desk with her back to you, not watching, as promised. Your own hands, which shake, a little, which his did not.

decision.text: You lived the stranger's last day in the city, through his eyes, on a cot in the Lantern.

intro.text: A boy of twenty-two on a bar stool with gold in his hair and gold at his wrist, which is a watch, and gold behind his left eye, which is not. "Pip Aldous. Gilt." He says it like a family name, which it has replaced. "You're not Row and you're not Crown. That makes you trade. Chrome, coin or trouble?"

options.text: Trouble. What kind do you pay for?
(Put the Rustmouths' toll ledger on the bar.) Warden-stamped. Out of their box.
(Put the Rustmouths' toll ledger on the bar.)

gilt.text: "Crown kids who came down the Loop and didn't go back up." He turns the watch. "We fence what the Crown loses and fit what the Concern won't licence, and we wear it where the wardens can see, which they can't, because there aren't any. Mother thinks I'm at a salon."

chain.text: "Bridgeward's a Rustmouth street. Was. Is." He shrugs the eye. "The chain says works and means ours, and the Rustmouths have a chain at their end that says the same. Between the chains it's dark. Nobody walks it. When somebody does, it'll be a war or a wedding."

run.text: "The kind the wardens want back." He finishes the glass. "Bring me a thing with a warden's tag on it and I'll give you a name to say at the chain. Runner. It's a start. Everything on this row's a start."

ledger.text: He turns it over and finds the warden's stamp and laughs, once, gold. "That's the thing. That's exactly the thing." He puts it under the bar. "Runner. Say it at the chain; Jax will know what it means, because I'll tell him." He pours you something that costs more than the bar. "Welcome to the Gilt. Don't die before I've got the use of you."

decision.text: You brought Pip Aldous the Rustmouths' warden-stamped ledger and became a Gilt runner.

pale.text: He looks at your hands and then does not look at you at all. "Pale." The stool turns. "We don't trade with the hand. Drink, if you like. Then go."

intro.text: A dealer at the middle table with a deck she does not look at. "Dust. Ten the hand, thirty the high table. The house wins. I'm the house." She fans the deck without looking at that either. "Sit."

options.text: A Crown boy lost a chit here.

chit.text: "Lorne." She taps the cage behind her without turning. "A Masque chit, House Lorne, one guest. In the cage, with the rest of what the Crown loses when it comes down to feel something." She looks at you for the first time. "A hundred. Or win it; the house plays for it, high table, once."

options.text: The high table. For the chit.

chit_got.text: "House Lorne." She slides it across. "Wear something. They'll know you're not Lorne; they won't care, if you wear something."

intro.text: A woman behind a long counter in a room that is warmer than the Row and smells of oil and oranges, who has seen everyone who has ever come through the door and let most of them in. "The Velvet. Madame Oyelaran; the Madame does, if you're shy. Company, conversation, the hour. In that order, if you're wise." She takes you in. "You're not shy. You're tired."

options.text: Dress me for the Masque. (60 Tolls)
You dress the Crown's girls, they say.
Dress me for the Masque. (60 Tolls)

hour.text: An hour in a warm room with the door shut and somebody who asks nothing and listens to everything, and a bath that is actually hot, which in Meridian is the rarer thing. You come out slower and better.

dress.text: An hour in the back room with pins in her mouth. Bottle-green, Crown-plain, nothing on it that says the Row; and then she walks you across the room three times until the clothes do the talking. "They check whether you look like you belong. That is the only thing they check. Wear it up the car; walk past the sergeant; don't look at the lens, the lens is for people who are worried."

crown.text: "I dress them and I send them up the Loop, and at the Masque they are the Crown's and in here they are mine, and they tell me everything, because nobody up there listens." She folds a cloth. "Vane's Masque is this season. The chits are paper; House Lorne's boy lost his at the hall. If you ever need to be at a Masque, come to me first. I'll make you look like you belong, which is the only thing they check."

row.text: "Nobody, and the Gilt think it's them, and Mab thinks it's money, and Perrin thinks it's the tubes." She smiles. "It's the canal. Everything on this row is here because the water came and the wardens didn't."

intro.text: A boy in a coat that cost more than the bar, leaning on it. "Lorne. House Lorne." He is drunk in the careful way of someone who has only recently learned how. "I lost it. The chit. At the hall, on a hand I was *sure* of. Mother will see. Mother sees everything from up there; it's what up there is for."

options.text: Why come down here at all?

chit.text: "The Masque. Vane's. House Lorne, one guest, which was going to be —" he waves at the Row — "somebody from down here, to see their faces. Now it's in Dolour's cage with my dignity." He drinks. "She'd sell it. She'd sell her mother."

why.text: "Because it's real." He says it like a man who has just found the word. "Up there nothing hurts and nothing tastes and nobody loses. Down here Doubt went down in the second and I *felt* it." He looks at his glass. "I'm going to be very ill and it's going to be wonderful."

intro.text: A boatman with a pole and a lantern on a hull made of doors. "Shay. Two across, either way. Bridge is free and further, and the bridge has Kit on it."

options.text: Where does the canal come from?
Where does the canal come from?

canal.text: "The Sink. Pumps push it up through the old storm line and it comes out here warm, because the Precinct's pipes run alongside." He poles. "Spring, it comes up a foot. The Sink goes under and we get a foot. Everything on this row is somebody else's water."

intro.text: An old man with a pole with a hook on it and a bag of tubes, walking the towpath lighting what will light. "Perrin. Lit the first tube on this row. Pink. Still pink; look." He points with the hook. "Everything that's lit is mine. Everything that's dark is the Gilt's, or dead."

options.text: A stranger on the card, they say. A season ago.

row.text: "Canal was a street. Water came up the year the Sink's pumps went to the Precinct, and the wardens drew the line at the water and said *no service below*, and the first night nobody came to count us, somebody put a tube up." He taps his chest. "Pink. Then a bar, then the pit, then the Velvet, then everything. Lawless is just a word for *the water came and they didn't*."

stranger.text: "A Choir man, hood up, sat in the Lantern a season back and paid Ysolde to record his day, start to end, which nobody does; people record the good hour, not the day." He lights a tube; it comes on cyan. "Wardens took the reel off her a week later. Rustmouths took it off the wardens. It's back on her shelf. She won't watch it. I would, if I had the Tolls, and I don't, and I'm not sure I would."

intro.text: A girl of seventeen leaning on a lamp post as if she were holding it up, who falls into step beside you before you have decided to walk. "Lost? You look lost. Two Tolls and you're not." She is very close, briefly, and then not.

passives.text: A hand in your coat, out again, five Tolls lighter. She is already three steps off and not looking back.

options.text: The five you took. Hand it back.

back.text: She stops, considers running, considers you, and hands it back with a bow that is nearly real. "Mostly nobody notices. You're not mostly." She grins. "Keep your hand on it on the bridge."

guide.text: "Pit's south, Mab's the woman with the slate. Hall's the green tube; the dealer's the house. The Velvet's the pink one, and the queue's the queue. The Lantern's the violet one at the end, and don't buy the shelf." She counts on her fingers. "Gilt are the gold ones. Don't take their coin; it's counted."

board.text: THE LOOP — THE STACKS. A board under Block Eight's face: PRECINCT 3 · OLD MARKET 3 · LANTERN ROW 3 · BRIDGEWARD 3 · THE DOCKS 4. Somebody has written under it, in the careful hand of a committee: RESIDENTS HALF FARE — ASK THE DRIVER. There is no driver.

read.text: BLOCK SEVEN, in letters a floor high that were white once. Under them, in a hundred hands: floor numbers, names, a chalked list of who owes whom water, and RING THE BELL FOR THE COMMITTEE with no bell.

The lift yard: the shaft's foot behind a grille, a motor the size of a room with its casing off, and cables going up into the dark. On the motor, in Plan stencil: SERVICE AS PER SCHEDULE. On the grille, in chalk: THE SCHEDULE IS NEVER.
THE STAIR. FLOORS 1–40. A chalk tally of how many steps, which someone has corrected three times. Under it: IF YOU SIT DOWN ON NINE, YOU LIVE ON NINE.
The stair cage. Down: nine floors to the lobby and the Loop. Up: the roof, the tank, and whoever is standing by it today.
THE TANK — BLOCK SEVEN — FILLS 23:00–05:00 FROM PRECINCT MAIN (CL. 14). Under it, chalked and rubbed and chalked: TWELVE 02–05. NINE: WHAT'S LEFT. A keeper's log hangs from the valve on a chain.

Beds of real dirt, carried up nine — forty — floors in buckets over thirty years, with things growing in them that have names: tomatoes, once; beans; greens; a tree the height of a child. The dirt is dry to the knuckle at noon.

Trays under a scrap awning, stacked, each with a tube running to it and a green so even it looks printed. A pump, humming. A crate stencilled with a word that is also a company: NUTRIENT — CONCERN AGRONOMY. Nobody up here says the word aloud.

panel.text: A lift panel with a cracked screen that still lights: BLOCK SEVEN — LIFT SERVICE: AS PER SCHEDULE. Under it, a schedule, in the Plan's own font: 02:00 — SYSTEM CHECK. No other line. The lifts have checked themselves every night at two for forty years and carried nobody.

passives.text: The check draws the block's whole power for three minutes — which is why the pumps on the roof run at two: that is when the main is live.

board.text: THE FLOOR BOARD. Notices in a dozen hands: NINE — WATER TUESDAYS. TWELVE — TRAYS, DO NOT TOUCH. ROOF — COMMITTEE PENDING (this one is old). 9-14 — EMPTY — SEE HESTER. FOUND: ONE CHILD, FLOOR 22, CLAIM AT LAUNDRY.

NINE'S BOARD. A rota for the beds, a rota for the laundry, a line that says THE ROOF IS NINE'S BY RIGHT OF DIRT and under it, in a different chalk, THE TANK IS WHOEVER'S AWAKE. Mama Deel has signed the first. Nobody has signed the second.

intro.text: A woman at a desk in a wooden office inside a concrete hall, with a ledger of floors and a face that has chaired a thousand meetings and won most of them by outlasting them. "Hester Quill. Committee, Block Seven, floor nine, and the lobby when nobody else will." She does not ask what you want; she looks at the ledger. "You want a flat or you want the roof. Everyone who comes in here wants one of the two."

options.text: The roof. Nine's dry and Twelve's pumping.
The Twelves want the committee to let the trays have the tank. I'm here to say they should.

mods.why: the trays' ledger says what sixty people eat

options.text: A schedule. Nine has the tank from five to two; Twelve from two to five. Oskar keeps it; the committee signs it.

decision.text: You brokered the Stacks' roof: a water schedule between the beds and the trays, signed by the committee.

options.text: The Twelves want the tank for the trays. They should have it.

mods.why: the trays' ledger says what sixty people eat

options.text: A schedule: five to two for Nine, two to five for Twelve. Oskar keeps it; you sign it.

decision.text: You brokered the Stacks' roof: a water schedule between the beds and the trays, signed by the committee.

flat.text: "9-14. Two rooms, a stove, a bed the Marrs left, a window on the canyon. Key money's two hundred and fifty, which is the committee's, which is the floor's, which is water for a month." She turns the ledger round. "Or the roof. Settle the roof so Nine isn't dry at six, and the committee will give you the flat for the settling. That's the other price. People think it's the cheaper one."

decision.text: You paid Block Seven's committee key money for flat 9-14.

options.text: The roof, then. I'll settle it.

key.text: A key on a string, brass, worn to gold at the bow. "Nine. Fourteen. The stove draws if you open the window first." She writes your name in the ledger, and under it, FLOOR NINE, and that is apparently all there is to it.

earn.text: "Oskar has the log. Lio has the pump. Mama Deel has the dirt and Ren has a jerry-can he thinks I don't know about." She does not look up. "Come back with the roof settled and 9-14 is yours. Come back with it burned and we will have a different conversation."

roof.text: "The tank fills off the Precinct main at night, which is the only time the main is live down here, and the Twelves pump it into trays from two to five, and Nine's beds get what the trays leave, which is a wet floor." She closes the ledger. "The committee could vote the tank. The committee has been going to vote the tank for three springs. The Twelves feed sixty. Nine feeds nine, and the nine are old, and the dirt is thirty years of buckets. You see the problem. Everyone sees the problem."

twelves_ok.text: She listens to the whole of it, which is her gift. "Sixty." She writes it. "Mama Deel will not forgive the committee. The committee will survive that; it survives everything." She signs something. "The tank is the trays'. Nine can carry buckets from the laundry, the way we carried the dirt."

decision.text: You argued the Stacks' committee into giving the roof tank to the Twelves' trays.

twelves_no.text: "Sixty." She does not write it. "And nine, who are old, and a tree the height of a child. No."

shared.text: She reads it twice and writes it once, in the ledger, in capitals, and signs it, and dates it. "Three springs." She looks at the page as if it might disagree. "Oskar keeps it. Lio keeps to it or the committee stops signing Twelve's water for the laundry." Then, almost as an afterthought: "9-14 is yours, if you still want it. Key money's waived. The Marrs left the kettle."

decision.text: Block Seven's committee gave you flat 9-14 for settling the roof.

text.text: "The pump's dead and the Twelves are carrying buckets." She does not smile. "Nine's wet at six for the first time in three springs. Sixty people are hungrier. I've written both down." She pushes a key across. "9-14. For the settling. It was settled; I didn't say how."

"The trays burned." She says it to the ledger. "Sixty people's dinner, and the awning, and Nessa Kord's hands. Ren says it was him. Ren says a lot. I've written your name beside his, because that is what the committee is for." She does not offer a key.

"The tank is the trays'." She has already written it. "Nine carries buckets. Mama Deel has stopped coming to committee." A pause. "9-14 is still two-fifty. The committee doesn't pay for that kind of settling."
"Settled." She writes it.

decision.text: Block Seven's committee gave you flat 9-14 for settling the roof.

squatted.text: "You're in 9-14." She does not raise her voice; she has never needed to. "The Marrs' door was forced on Tuesday. The committee noticed on Tuesday." The ledger. "Key money's two-fifty. For a squatter it's one-fifty, because the committee would rather have the money than the argument. Or you settle the roof, and we pretend the door was always open."

squat_no.text: "It is now." She writes something short. "Nine remembers. Nine is very good at remembering; it's all Nine has."

shut.text: 9-14. A door with a number and no name chalked under it, and a committee seal of wax over the latch, and behind it the quiet of two rooms nobody has slept in since the Marrs went to the Ring.

options.text: (Break the seal and force the latch.)

mods.why: the corridor is asleep

forced.text: The wax breaks and the latch gives and the door opens on two rooms with a kettle on the stove and a bed the Marrs left made. Nobody in the corridor says anything. Nine will say it later.

decision.text: You broke the committee's seal on flat 9-14 and moved in.

forced_no.text: The seal breaks and the latch does not, and a door across the corridor opens a hand's width and shuts.

yours.text: 9-14. Your name chalked under the number now, in Bo's hand, badly.

not_yours.text: The Marrs' bed, made, with a kettle beside it and a window on the canyon. Not yours. The committee has a seal on the door and a ledger in the lobby.

yours.text: Your flat. Two rooms nine floors up, a stove that draws if you open the window first, a bed with somebody else's dent in it, a locker, and a window on the canyon with a thousand other windows in it, each a different light. The door locks from your side. The city is downstairs.

intro.text: A man on a chair by the tank with a log on a chain and the look of someone who has been asked the same question by both sides for three years. "Oskar Vey. I keep the tank. Fills off the main eleven to five, when the main's live. After that it's politics, and I keep out of politics; I keep the valve."

options.text: The log. Who takes what, when.
The valve. Could it split the flow?
Nine from five to two, Twelve from two to five. Would you keep that, if they signed it?
A schedule. Would you keep it?

log.text: He unhooks it and holds it so you can read and not take. Three years of nights in a careful hand: FILL 23–05. TWELVE PUMP 02–05, FULL DRAW. NINE: RESIDUE. Beside each spring week, the beds' depth in fingers, going to one finger, going to none. "The pump takes it all because the pump can. Nothing in the log says it has to."

valve.text: "It's a pre-Burn valve. Two outlets and a stop between." He looks at it the way the Sink's keeper looks at hers. "Somebody who knew the stops could set it to give each side its hours without anybody having to agree to anything. I'm not that somebody. I'm the keeper." A pause. "I'd not notice it done, is what I'm saying."

schedule.text: "I'd keep anything that's written down." He taps the log. "Three years I've wanted a line in here that isn't *residue*. Get Lio to say the hours and Hester to sign them and I'll keep them with my own hand on the stop."

text.text: "Five to two, two to five." The log has a new line in capitals. "I keep it. Nine's wet at six. Twelve's green at eight. Nobody's happy and everybody's fed, which is what a schedule is."
"Pump's dead." He does not look at the trays. "Full tank, all night, for nine old people and a tree. I write it down. I write everything down."
"Full draw. Committee-signed, now." He writes RESIDUE one more time and underlines it. "I keep the valve."
"The trays burned." He has written that too. "A tank with nothing to feed. I keep it anyway."

valve.text: A pre-Burn valve on the tank's belly: two outlets, west to the beds' pipe and east to the pump's, and a stop between them that somebody set to EAST a long time ago and sealed with wire. The keeper's chair is three paces off and the keeper is looking at the view.

options.text: (Reset the stops: the beds until two, the trays until five.)

mods.why: the keeper told you where the stops are
two outlets and a stop is arithmetic

options.text: (Turn the whole flow to the beds and wire it.)

split_ok.text: The wire comes off. The stop moves, stiffly, to a notch between EAST and WEST that nobody has used since the Burn, and holds. Water goes two ways with a sound like a breath. Oskar Vey, three paces off, writes something in his log without turning round.

decision.text: You reset the Stacks' roof valve to give the beds and the trays their hours each.

beds_ok.text: The stop goes to WEST and the wire goes back on, tighter. The pump's pipe empties with a cough. On the deck somebody says Nessa's name. Oskar Vey writes it down.

decision.text: You turned the Stacks' roof tank to the Nines' beds and left the Twelves' trays dry.

split_no.text: The stop does not move; the wire does, into your palm. The keeper turns round.

text.text: The stop sits in the notch between EAST and WEST, and the wire is gone, and a chalk line on the tank says 05–02 / 02–05 in the keeper's hand.
WEST, wired. The pump's pipe is dry.
EAST, wired, and now a committee seal on the wire.

intro.text: A young man under the awning with green on his hands and a pipe-wrench on his belt he has not had to use yet. "Lio Brand. Twelve." He waves at the trays. "Sixty people eat off this deck. Nine people eat off the dirt, and a tree. You're the one asking round; everyone says. Ask."

options.text: The pump takes the whole tank from two to five.
Five to two for the beds, two to five for you. Say the hours and the committee signs them.

mods.why: the keeper will hold the stop himself
three years of *residue* in his own keeper's hand

options.text: What do you want from the committee?
Five to two for the beds, two to five for you.

mods.why: the keeper will hold the stop himself
three years of *residue* in his own keeper's hand

options.text: What do you want from the committee?

pump.text: "The pump takes what the pump can. Nothing says it has to." He says it the way the keeper said it, which means he has heard the keeper say it. "If I stop at three the trays go yellow by Thursday and Latch takes his third out of the yellow. You want me to say sorry to nine old people, I'll say it. Sorry. Sixty."

shared_ok.text: He looks at the trays for a long time, and at the beds, and at the keeper's chair. "Two to five." He says it like a man trying a number. "That's the main's live hours anyway; the pump can't draw without it." Something eases. "Say it to Hester. If she signs it, I keep it. If she doesn't, I never said it."

shared_no.text: "Hours." He shakes his head. "Hours are what Nine's had for three springs. Residue hours."

ask.text: "The committee to say the tank's the trays'. Out loud, in the ledger, so Ren stops talking about jerry-cans and Nine carries buckets from the laundry like we did before the pump." He wipes his hands. "You're not Nine. Hester listens to people who aren't Nine. Say it for us and there's a hundred and twenty in it, and Latch's card, which is worth more than the hundred and twenty if you ever want work that pays in Crown coin."

latch.text: "Brings the nutrient. Takes a third of the crop up the Loop in crates with no name on them." He does not lower his voice; there is nobody up here to hear. "Concern. Everyone knows. The trays are Concern-made, the pump's Concern-made, and one day the deal's going to have a line in it about who owns the deck. I know. I've read it. Sixty people eat."

text.text: "Two to five." The trays are green and he is counting them. "Latch didn't like it. Latch doesn't have to."
"Committee-signed." He has the hundred and twenty counted. "And Latch's card. He says you're the kind he looks for. I'd take that as a warning." He hands over both.
"Pump's dead." He is carrying a bucket. "Sixty people. You did the sum and got nine. I'll remember the sum."
The awning is a black frame and the trays are a smell. He does not say anything to you at all.

options.text: (Take the hundred and twenty, and the card.)

intro.text: A woman with her arm in a pump to the shoulder. "Nessa. The pump's mine. Don't touch the pump." She does not take her arm out. "Two to five. It's on the panel. It's not a secret; it's a schedule."

passives.text: The pump's casing has a small moulded mark under the grime, the same mark as on the nutrient crate: a company that is also a word.

why.text: "Because the main's only live from eleven to five and the lifts eat it till two." She finally takes her arm out. "Everyone thinks we chose two. The Plan chose two. We just stayed up for it."

panel.text: The pump's panel: a Concern-made box with a schedule set in it — 02:00–05:00 FULL DRAW — and a fuse the size of a thumb behind a cover that is not locked, because nobody up here has ever needed to lock anything from Nine.

mods.why: the deck sleeps between the pump's hours

pulled.text: The fuse comes out warm. The hum stops. Across the deck nobody turns round, because the pump stops every morning at five and the ear has learned not to hear it. By two tomorrow the trays will be dry and the beds will be wet, and Nessa Kord will be looking for a thumb-sized thing with your name not on it.

decision.text: You pulled the fuse on the Twelves' pump and gave the Stacks' roof tank to the beds.

caught.text: Your hand is on the cover when Nessa Kord's is on your wrist. "Don't touch the pump." She says it without heat; she will say it to Lio with heat.

dead.text: The panel is dark and the fuse cover hangs open.

intro.text: An old woman on her knees in a bed of dirt, watering a plant with a cup. "Mama Deel. Nine." She does not stop. "Thirty years of buckets. I carried the first one. Tomatoes, the year the lifts stopped; red ones; ask anyone over fifty." The dirt is dry a finger down.

trays.text: "They do." She straightens, slowly. "And when Latch stops bringing the nutrient they'll feed nobody, and the trays will be plastic, and this will still be dirt." She points the cup at the tree. "I don't want the tank. I want two in the morning. Tell Lio: two. Two is all the dirt needs."

ren.text: "I know what Ren has." She goes back to her knees. "He's twenty-four. At twenty-four I carried a bucket up forty floors every day for a year. He wants to carry a can up once. Tell him dirt remembers. He won't listen; tell him anyway."

text.text: "Two in the morning." The dirt is dark a hand down and she has her palm flat on it. "Thirty years. I'll have tomatoes by the Long Night, you watch."
"Wet at six." She is not happy; she is watering. "Sixty people, Lio says. He's right. I'll be carrying them water from the laundry by Thursday, you watch."
She is not in the beds. She is on the deck, in the ash, with a cup, watering a tray that is a puddle of plastic, because somebody should.
"The tank's theirs." She has a bucket beside her. "Thirty years. I'll carry."

intro.text: A young man with a hoe he holds like a weapon and a look at the deck he does not hide. "Ren. Nine. Mama Deel says talk. Mama Deel's been saying talk for three springs and the dirt's been dry for three springs." He lowers his voice, which is not low. "I've a jerry-can. One night. Trays burn; dirt doesn't."

options.text: Not fire. Go and take the deck. I'll be beside you.
Dirt remembers. Burn the trays and Nine's the floor that burned sixty dinners.

burn.text: "Tonight." He says it like a man who has said it to himself for a year and never to anyone else. "Two, when the pump's loud. You take Nessa's side; I take the can."

decision.text: You and Ren Ashby burned the Twelves' trays on the Stacks' roof.

news.text: the Twelves' hydroponic deck on Block Seven burned in the night; a stranger was seen on the roof

burned.text: Two in the morning, and the pump loud, and the awning going up faster than either of you thought a thing that wet could, and sixty dinners with it, and Nessa Kord's hands when she went in after the pump. Ren is standing in the beds afterwards with the can still in his hand, not looking at anything. "Dirt doesn't," he says. The Twelves are coming across the deck with pipes.

fight_offer.text: "Take it." He looks at the deck, and at the three of them, and at you. "With you, yes." He picks up the hoe properly.

decision.text: You went across the Stacks' roof with Ren Ashby to take the Twelves' deck by force.

going.text: Across the roof. Lio Brand sees you coming and puts down the tray he is holding, carefully, and picks up the wrench.

no_ok.text: He looks at the hoe for a long time. "Sixty dinners." He puts the can — it was behind the shed, where everybody knew it was — on its side, and the fuel goes into the dirt, where Mama Deel will complain about it for a year. "Talk, then. You talk. I've been talking to dirt."

no_no.text: "Dirt remembers." He almost spits. "Dirt's been remembering for three springs. I'd like it to forget something."

text.text: "Two in the morning." He is watering with a hose that runs. "Mama Deel says you talked. I'd have burned. I know which one I'd have been proud of." He does not say which.
"Wet." He is grinning, and then not. "Lio's carrying buckets. I'll be carrying them with him by Thursday; Mama Deel's already said."
He is sitting in the beds with his back to the deck and the can on its side, empty. He does not look up.
"Theirs." He has the hoe. "Committee said. The committee can carry its own buckets."

intro.text: A man in a coat that has never been dirty, in a chair under the awning, with a crate at his feet and his hands folded. "Latch. Just Latch." The smile is a tool and he is good with it. "I bring the nutrient; I take a third. The trays feed sixty. You've been asking the floor its arithmetic. Here is mine: nobody has to decide anything today. That is the whole of what I offer, and people find it very restful."

options.text: Who do you bring it for?
One day the deal has a line about who owns the deck.
And me? What's your arithmetic for me?
There's a girl in Bridgeward who hears the city's wire in words.
Who do you bring it for?
A girl in Bridgeward hears the wire in words.

static.text: For the first time the smile goes somewhere else and comes back different. "In words." He folds his hands the other way. "The Concern has people who ride the grid on purpose, with a port and a licence and a leash, and it has never found one who did it by accident with nothing in her neck. It would like to." He names a figure that is not a figure down here: a hundred and fifty, and a card that is not plain. "She would hear everything. All of it. She would be looked after, which is a word."

options.text: The Saints' tower in Bridgeward. (150 Tolls)

decision.text: You told the Concern's man where the girl who hears the wire sits.

options.text: Nobody has to decide anything today.

static_done.text: "Thank you." He means it, which is the unsettling part. "A radio that works, with nothing in it. She'll have something in it by Thursday."

who.text: "A concern." He lets the word sit there being both things. "In Halcyon. It believes in growth, and in people who carry crates up forty floors without being asked, and in not having to say its name on rooftops."

deck.text: "There is always a line." He is pleased you found it. "It says what every line says: that a thing built with our pump and fed with our nutrient is, in the end, ours, and that the people on it are, in the end, tenants. Lio has read it. Lio feeds sixty. Lio has decided not to decide anything today, which is wise."

me.text: "You get things settled. Settled is the rarest thing in this city and the Concern pays for it in coin that is counted." He takes a card from the coat: plain, a number, nothing else. "When you want work that pays in Crown coin, show this at the Docks. Nobody has to decide anything today." He puts it on the crate between you, and does not watch to see whether you take it.

intro.text: A trader under the dead stairs with water in jerry-cans and tins in rows. "Fitch. Everything a floor needs and nothing a floor wants." He taps a can. "Water. Don't ask whose. Everyone asks whose."

whose.text: "The laundry's, Tuesdays. The tank's, when Oskar's looking at the view. The Precinct main's, when I've a cousin on it." He shrugs. "Water in the Stacks is a thing you carry, not a thing you have. I carry."

intro.text: A boy who appears beside you on the stair without having been on it. "Bo. Nine floors in two minutes, timed. Twelve pays a Toll a message; Nine pays bread." He looks at you for weight. "You're new. New people pay in questions."

options.text: The man in the clean coat on the roof.
The man in the clean coat.

marrs.text: "Went to the Ring. Everyone who goes to the Ring goes because of a notice. They left the kettle." He shrugs. "Hester sealed the door. Hester seals everything; it's what Hester is."

ulla.text: "She hears the lifts count. Two in the morning, every night, to forty." He is matter-of-fact. "She's not wrong. I've heard it. Everyone's heard it; she's just the only one who sits with it."

latch.text: "Thursdays. Brings a crate up on the Loop and takes three down." Lower: "Lio says don't talk to Latch. Lio talks to Latch."

intro.text: A woman in the shaft room, which is warm, on a cot against the lift's wall with her ear near it. "Sit. It's warm; it's always been warm. The lift doesn't run and the shaft is warm, and nobody asks why." She looks at you with the attention of someone who listens for a living. "It counts. Two in the morning. To forty. Then it stops."

warm.text: "Because something in the shaft is on." She puts her palm flat on the wall. "Not the lift. Under the lift. The Plan says the lifts run; the lifts don't; but something under them has run every night for forty years on the block's whole power for three minutes and the shaft stays warm all day from it." She takes the hand away. "I don't know what. I sit with it. Somebody should."

count.text: "Floors, I thought. Forty floors. Then I thought: people. Then I stopped thinking and listened, and it's neither. It's the same forty every night, in the same order, and one of the numbers is always a little longer than the others, like a name you say carefully." She almost smiles. "Twenty-six. Listen for twenty-six, if you're here at two."

board.text: THE LOOP — BRIDGEWARD. A board with three paints on it and the fares scratched through all three: PRECINCT 3 · OLD MARKET 3 · LANTERN ROW 3 · THE STACKS 3 · THE DOCKS 4. The last is chalked over: NO BRIDGE.

read.text: The chain, from this side: WORKS, in the Gilt's gold, over a Rustmouth's rust-red X, over a white hand with the palm scored through. Three crews, one chain, and the paint is the only fighting that has happened on it so far.

A notice in Crown print, screwed to the booth: TOLL — BRIDGEWARD CROSSING — BY WARRANT OF HOUSE VANE — COLLECTED BY ARRANGEMENT. There is no crossing. The toll is five to stand on the near end of a bridge to nowhere, and a Tenured house holds the paper on it.

The deck ends in torn rebar and forty feet of air. Across the dry river: the far bank, the Docks' cranes, lamps, a tram that is not the Loop. Close enough to hear a bell. No way to reach it that does not go round by the Wall, which is a day, and a warrant.
PETROV — CUT — PARTS — ANYTHING THAT HAD WHEELS. A buggy seat nailed over the door like a trophy, with a dog's head burned into the leather, old.

THE SAINTS OF STATIC — LISTEN. A dead relay mast with a red lamp at the top that somebody climbs to keep lit, and under it the brick shell where the radios are. People come out of it slowly, as from a church.
The white hand, palm scored through, over a stair house with one door. The Pale's. Under the hand, small: THE SINK IS UNDER YOU.

chain.text: The toll chain across the deck, with a gap in it the width of a person and a Rustmouth either side of the gap. A slate: STAND — 5. Beyond the chain, the bridge, and the drop, and the view.

options.text: (Pay five, and stand on the bridge.)

paid.text: Five, into a box with a Crown stamp on the lid. The Rustmouth lifts the chain a hand's width, which is a courtesy; you could have stepped over it. The bridge is wider than the street and emptier than anything in Meridian, and from the end of it you can see the Docks.

ours.text: The Rustmouths nod. The chain does not move; you step over it, which is what the chain is for.

text.text: The chain is on the ground and the slate says, in gold: STAND — FREE — GILT. Two Gilt lean where the Rustmouths leaned.
The chain is up, and beside the slate a second slate, in three paints: STAND — 2 — SPLIT THREE WAYS. Nobody likes it. Everybody pays it.
The chain is up and the Rustmouths are either side of it, and there is a new coat of rust-red on the booth over the gold.

intro.text: A woman at a table in a metal hall with a sawn-off beside her hand and a ledger beside the sawn-off, who has been Boss of the Rustmouths since the Rustmouths were a union and looks it. "Dagmar Holt. They say Auntie Scrap. Not to my face." She looks at you until you understand that she is waiting for you to say it. "The bridge is ours because we're on it. That is the whole of law in Bridgeward. What do you want on it?"

options.text: The bridge goes nowhere. Why a toll?
I'll hold the chain for you. Against the Gilt.
A sit-down. You, the Gilt, the Pale. At the tower, under the girl who hears.

mods.why: you pay her tithe
you know what the Crown wants the bridge for

options.text: How does one become a Rustmouth?

again.text: "Auntie Scrap." She says it herself, to save time.

options.text: I'll hold the chain for you.

mods.why: you pay her tithe
you know what the Crown wants the bridge for

options.text: How does one become a Rustmouth?

toll.text: "It goes to the Crown's paper." She turns the ledger round: a warrant, Crown-printed, HOUSE VANE. "A Tenured house holds the bridge. We collect, we keep the chain, they keep the arrangement, and a woman in a clean coat comes Tuesdays for the ledger." She turns it back. "Five to stand. Nobody crosses, so nobody pays twenty. The Crown doesn't know there's no crossing; the Crown has never been down here."

gilt.text: "The Gilt want a lot." She does not look west. "Crown kids with gold in their teeth who've never lifted a car. Let them come to the chain. Or go and tell Jax what a chain is; he's never seen one from this side."

hold.text: "Then go and stand at it." She pushes a slate across: RUSTMOUTH — HOLDS. "Jax is a boy. Boys go back when a grown person says go back. If he doesn't, the chain's iron and so are you."

sit_ok.text: She looks at the warrant for a long moment. "The Crown wants the near end. The Crown always wants the near end." She closes the ledger. "I'll sit. Under the mast, where the girl can hear me. Get the boy there, and the white hands. If they come, I come."

sit_no.text: "Sit with the Gilt." She almost laughs. "I'd sooner sit with the drop."

tithe.text: "A hundred, or a haul. Corvo takes both." She looks at your hands. "You'd be a hauler. Haulers haul. In a year, a mouth, and the tolls are yours to take a cut of. In ten, maybe my hand, if Corvo's dead." She says it without weight; Corvo is beside her and does not look up.

held_blood.text: The chain is up and Jax is on the ground beside it and the Gilt have gone back to their fire barrel without him. Dagmar Holt has come out of the hall to look, which she does not do. "Held." She says it to the chain. "Blood on it now. That's a chain the Gilt will remember." She looks at you. "Mouth. You're a mouth now. Take a cut."

decision.text: You held the Rustmouths' chain against the Gilt with blood on it.

text.text: "Held." The ledger is open at the warrant and she has written beside it, in rust-red: HELD. "The Crown's paper and our chain. Same as before, with you on it."
The hall is quieter. Half the yard is gone. "Gold on my booth." She does not touch the sawn-off. "I've been a union and a mob. I'll be a union again. Get out of my hall."

"Split three ways." She says it like a diagnosis. "Two Tolls to stand, and the Pale's share goes down a hatch to buy bread for people who hate me. The girl said the Crown takes the near end by the Long Night." She shrugs. "Then we'll have been three crews on one chain when it comes. That's something."
"Auntie Scrap."

intro.text: The Boss's Hand: a big man on a bench with a pipe across his knees and a revolver he has not drawn in a year, who looks at the hall door more than at you. "Corvo. The hand does the lifting." He weighs you. "Tithe's a hundred, or a haul. A haul's honest. Petrov's got a wreck on the blocks that wants cutting for the yard; cut it, bring me the ticket."

decision.text: You paid the Rustmouths' tithe and became a hauler.
You cut a wreck for the Rustmouths' yard and became a hauler.
You paid the Rustmouths' tithe and became a hauler.
You cut a wreck for the Rustmouths' yard and became a hauler.

sworn.text: "Hauler." He writes it on the bench with a nail, your name under a hundred others. "You haul Fridays. You pay nobody's toll. You don't wear gold and you don't show the Pale your hands." He puts the nail away. "Boss'll want the chain held. Go and see her."

intro.text: A man under a car on blocks who comes out slowly, wiping a hand that does not get cleaner. "Petrov. I cut cars. The Rustmouths cut me, a tenth. That's the trade." He nods at the shelves. "Parts, wire, a pipe if you want a pipe. And a wreck on the blocks that wants cutting, if the Hand sent you."

options.text: The Hand sent me. The wreck.
The seat over the door. A dog's head.

haul_ok.text: Four hours with a torch and a bar, and the wreck is an engine, two axles, a door and a heap, which is what the yard weighs. Petrov writes the ticket on a strip of tin with a nail. "Haul. Honest." He looks at your hands. "You've done it before."

haul_no.text: An hour with a torch and the wreck is a wreck with a hole in it. "Come back when your hands know a torch."

dogs.text: "Rust Dogs. They had the garage across the street before the Rustmouths had the bridge." He looks at it. "Left me a buggy when they went to the Sallow. I cut the buggy. I kept the seat. Fenn's still in there; he cuts nothing and nobody."

intro.text: A Gilt at the chain with gold in his hair and a pistol he keeps touching, like a man checking a pocket. "Jax. Gilt. The chain says works, and from here to the fire barrel it means ours." He looks east, at the bridge, the way a boy looks at a thing he has been promised. "Pip says the bridge is next. Pip says the runner says."

options.text: Pull back off the chain, Jax. The bridge is held.

mods.why: a mouth, not a hauler
the Dogs' mark on your coat: the garage remembers who held this street

options.text: A sit-down, at the tower. Dagmar will come.
What does a Crown kid want with a bridge to nowhere?
Pull back off the chain. The bridge is held.

mods.why: a mouth, not a hauler
the Dogs' mark on your coat

options.text: What does a Crown kid want with a bridge?

why.text: "The near end." He says it like Pip. "The Crown wants a road to the Docks and the bridge is where the road goes when they build it, and whoever holds the near end holds the toll on the Crown's own road." He grins, gold. "Pip's mother sits on the committee that votes the road. Pip says. Pip says a lot."

down.text: "When you say." He draws the pistol and looks at it. "Pip said the runner says. Two at the chain, one in the yard, the Hand and Auntie. Five. We're four with you." He waits.

decision.text: You went for the Rustmouths' chain with the Gilt.

going.text: He whistles once, and the Gilt come off the fire barrel.

won.text: The chain is on the ground and the Rustmouths who held it are beside it and the hall door is shut. Jax has a slate and is writing on it in gold: STAND — FREE — GILT. "Runner." He is shaking a little and pretending it is the cold. "Crew. Pip'll say crew. Tell him I said it first."

decision.text: You pulled the Rustmouths' chain down for the Gilt.

news.text: the Gilt took the Bridgeward chain off the Rustmouths; a stranger was in it

back_ok.text: He looks at the chain, and at the two Rustmouths, and at you, and at the fire barrel, which is where boys go. "Pip said —" He stops. "Pip isn't here." The pistol goes away. "The chain's yours. Till it isn't." He walks back to the barrel without turning round, which is the bravest thing he has done today.

decision.text: You held the Rustmouths' chain against the Gilt with a word.

back_no.text: "Make me." The pistol is out. Behind you the chain, and behind the chain two shotguns, and nobody has moved yet.

make.text: The Gilt come off the barrel. The Rustmouths come off the chain. Bridgeward gets what Bridgeward has been waiting three paints for.

sit.text: "Under the mast. With Auntie." He thinks about it with his whole face. "Pip'll kill me." Then: "Pip isn't here. I'll sit. If she sits, I sit."

text.text: "Free to stand." He has the slate under his arm like a prize. "Pip's coming down to see it. Pip says."
"Split three ways." He does not like it and he is at the chain with a Rustmouth and a white hand, taking two Tolls, which is the thing he was promised with the gold filed off.
The fire barrel, and the Gilt round it, and the chain over there.

intro.text: A woman on a chair by a hatch with a machete across her knees and skin the water never saw the sun through. "Nell. Pale. Show me your hands." You show her. "The hatch is ours. The stair under it is ours. The Sink under the stair is ours. The bridge —" she tilts her head at it — "is nobody's. That's the only true thing said in Bridgeward."

options.text: A sit-down, at the tower. The three crews.
The hatch. Where does it go?

text.text: She stands and takes your hands and turns them over, and looks at your eyes, close, for the ring a lens leaves, and at your neck for the port. There is nothing. "Say it. No chrome. Ever. Not in me, not near me, and out of whoever owes me." She waits.

She stands and takes your hands and turns them over, and stops. "Hands." She lets go of them as if they were hot. "You've iron in you. We don't swear iron. Go and get it out, if you want the hand; Ocho'll take it out for nothing. Then come back."

decision.text: You swore the Pale's vow at the hatch in Bridgeward: no chrome, ever.

sworn.text: "Sworn." She paints it on your hand with white from a tin, a palm with a line through it, which will wash off and which everyone in Meridian will have seen by dark. "The Sink's open to you. The hatch's open to you. Dray will want to see the hand."

sit.text: "The Pale will come to say the bridge is nobody's." She does not stand. "We'll say it once, and go back down. If the other two hear it, that's a thing. They won't."

hatch.text: "Down. A stair, and a tunnel, and the Sink's east bank, where Dray sits." She taps the hatch with the machete's flat. "The Rustmouths wanted it once. They stopped wanting it. The Gilt don't know it's here; the Gilt don't know anything that isn't gold."

text.text: The Pale's hatch: a steel lid with a white hand on it, and a stair under it going down into warm dark that smells of the Sink. Yours to use now, Nell says; the east bank is a long wet walk and the Loop is faster, which is why nobody uses it but the Pale.
A steel lid with a white hand painted on it and a woman with a machete sitting on it. It is not open and it is not going to be.

shrine.text: Radios. Forty of them, pre-Burn, on crates and shelves and the floor, with their dials lit by candles behind the glass because nothing else will light them. A hiss comes from one of them, or from all of them, or from the mast overhead. People sit with their ears near the speakers the way the Sink's hermit sits with the lift.

options.text: (Sit with a radio until the hiss changes.)

mods.why: you know when the city's wire wakes

text.text: An hour. Hiss. Then, at two, under it, for three minutes, something with the rhythm of speech and none of the words: the sound of a city checking itself. Then hiss.
An hour. Hiss. A candle gutters. Tobin, two radios down, says "There," and you did not hear it.

vigil_ok.text: Midnight to two with a dead radio against your ear and the candles going down. At two the hiss changes. Not words; the shape of words, counted, at the speed a machine reads, for three minutes, and in the middle of it, once, something you could swear was a name. Then hiss. Verity is standing behind you. "You heard it." She does not ask. "Listener."

vigil_no.text: Midnight to two with a dead radio against your ear, and hiss, and at two more hiss, and a candle burning your knuckle. Verity, behind you: "Most hear the hiss. Come back; it isn't a test you fail, it's a thing you practise."

intro.text: A woman in a grey scarf at the foot of the mast with a coil of wire over her shoulder, who looks at you as if she had been told you were coming, which, in a sense, she had. "Verity. Choirmaster, they say, because somebody has to be. We listen." She nods up at the red lamp. "The city talks to itself all night on its own wire. Most people sleep through it. We sit up."

hear.text: "The hiss, mostly. Under it, at two, for three minutes, the city. It reads itself its own file, every night, on the lamp wire, and a dead radio near a live wire hears a little of it." She touches the coil. "We hear the shape. Immy hears the words. That is the only difference between a Saint and a prophet, and it is the whole difference."

kiosk.text: "A toy that talks." She does not deny it. "I wanted to know if a machine could hear what Immy hears. It can. It hears names and sells fortunes with them, which is what a machine does with a prophecy." She looks at you. "Did you cut it?" She does not wait for the answer; she can see it.

girl.text: "Immy. Sixteen. She came to the tower two years ago with the hiss already in her, from a cot in the Stacks with the lift shaft on the other side of the wall." She looks at the shell. "She says true things. Names, numbers, days. She said yours before you came up the street, and a number, and a word I did not like." Quietly: "Everyone who hears of her wants her. The wardens want her silent. The guild wants her sealed. The Concern wants her wired. I want her to be sixteen."

vigil.text: "Midnight to two, with a dead radio, in the small hours when the wire wakes. If you hear anything but hiss, you're a Listener." She hands you a radio with no back. "Most hear the hiss. It isn't a test you fail. It's a thing you practise."

keep.text: She looks at you for a long time, and at the red lamp, and back. "Swear it on the hiss." You do. "Then she stays, and she is sixteen, and when the wire says something you need to know, you'll hear it from me and from nobody else." She unwinds a foot of wire from the coil and gives it to you, which is apparently a thing that means something here.

decision.text: You swore on the hiss to leave the Saints' girl where she is and tell no one.

sitdown.text: Under the mast, at dusk, with the red lamp going: Dagmar Holt on a crate with the sawn-off across her knees; Jax on his feet because sitting would be agreeing; Nell by the door with her hands showing, if she came; forty radios; and Immy at the altar, not looking at anyone, saying under her breath the thing she has been saying all week: *Vane. The bridge. The Long Night.* Verity says, "Listen," and they do, for once, and then they look at you.

options.text: The Crown takes the near end by the Long Night whoever holds it. Three crews on one chain is the only thing it can't take. Two Tolls to stand, split three ways, and the Pale's share down the hatch.

who.text: "Immy. I was in the Stacks, in a cot by the lift wall, and it got in." She touches the back of her neck without seeming to know she does it. "Verity says I'm a radio that works. I'd rather be a radio that didn't. Nobody wants a radio that didn't."

text.text: "— as per —" Then: "You're the one who swore. Verity said." She almost smiles. "Thanks. I think."

intro.text: A man with a radio in his lap and his eyes shut. "Tobin. Three years." He does not open them. "I heard my own name once, the first month. Nothing since. Verity says that's normal. door.text: A garage door with a chain through its handles that has not been locked in years, only hung there, and a dog's head burned into the wood at the height of a child's hand. Through the gap, a stove going, and a man who has heard you and not got up.

wall.text: The garage wall, by the stove: names, burned in with a hot nail, a column of them, with a dog's head over the column. KESSLER. PERPETUA. VASHA. BRINDLE. FENN. JACK. And lower, at the height of a child's hand, in a child's burning: WREN. Under all of them, newer, in chalk: BACK FOR THE BRIDGE.

text.text: An old man on a bench by a stove who looks past you at Wren and does not say anything for a long moment, and then says, "Little Calloway," and his voice goes, and he has to start again. "Kessler said the Sallow. Perpetua said the Sallow. I said my knees." He pats the bench. "Sit. I've been sitting on it nine years."

An old man on a bench by a stove, in a garage with a dog's head on every wall and a buggy with no seat. "Fenn. I was a Dog. Dogs had this garage before the Rustmouths had the bridge; then they had the Sallow, and I had my knees." He does not get up. "Nobody comes in here. Petrov, for the stove. You're not Petrov."

options.text: BACK FOR THE BRIDGE. Whose chalk?

dogs.text: "The Rustmouths took the bridge the year the Crown put paper on it, and the bridge was our toll, such as it was, and Kessler counted guns and counted theirs and said *the Sallow*." He pokes the stove. "Nine years. They went west and became what they became. Perpetua carried the children down the stair. I sat on this bench. Petrov cut the buggy." He looks at the wall. "We were a crew, once. Not a gang. There's a difference and it's the bridge."

text.text: He looks at Wren, not at you. "Under me. Kessler had the key and the key went with Kessler, but I've a bar." He gets up, which takes a while, and the bench comes up with the bar, and under it a locker. "Little Calloway. It's yours more than it's mine."
"Under me." He does not get up. "Kessler had the key. The key went with Kessler. Nobody's asked in nine years and I don't see why the tenth should be you."

back.text: "Mine." He does not look at it. "Chalk. Every spring. Kessler said they'd come back for the bridge when they were a crew again." He pokes the stove. "Perpetua said the same. She meant the children. Kessler meant the guns." A long pause. "If little Calloway ever comes back for the bridge, you tell her Fenn said the rope is what the bridge is for. The Rustmouths have one on the booth. Tell her that."

intro.text: A woman in a clean coat at the booth with a ledger that is not the Rustmouths' and a pen that is not from down here. "Ms Harrow. The arrangement is mine, Tuesdays, ten to four. You are not a Rustmouth. You may be a question."

road.text: "The near end." She says it as a surveyor would. "The Docks are across the river and the Loop does not cross it. A road would. A road needs a bridge, a bridge needs a near end, and the near end needs to be held by somebody who signs. House Vane intends to sign, by the Long Night." She looks at the chain. "The Rustmouths are a temporary arrangement. Most things down here are."

ledger.text: "Everyone keeps more than the arrangement says. That is what an arrangement is." A pause. "But the box keeps a ledger of its own, in a Rustmouth hand, and the box has a warden's stamp on it because the wardens wanted a count once, and the Rustmouths picked it before the wardens could read it. I would pay to read it. A hundred and twenty. It would be the end of the arrangement, which would be a pity for the Rustmouths and not for me."

show.text: She reads it standing, fast, and once, and closes it. "Thank you." A hundred and twenty, Crown-counted, in a paper sleeve. "The arrangement will be reviewed. You should not be on the bridge when it is." She puts the ledger in her coat; it is hers now, and so is whatever happens to the chain.

decision.text: You sold House Vane's agent the Rustmouths' own toll ledger.

masque.text: "By invitation." She looks you over the way a tailor would. "You'd need a chit, and a face the lens hasn't filed as something unfortunate, and clothes. The first can be bought; the second is your affair; the third is the Velvet's." It is the nearest thing to help she will give anyone.

HALDEN — PORTRAITS — AS YOU WILL BE. Under it, a smaller card: SITTINGS BY APPOINTMENT. FORECAST SHEETS TO BE SUPPLIED BY THE CLIENT.
STAFF. The door is metal and the terraces' side of it is painted to look like the terraces. The kitchens' side is not painted at all.

The parapet. All of Meridian under it in haze: the Precinct a grid, Old Market a stain, the canal a bright thread, the Stacks a wall with lights in it, the broken bridge a finger pointing at the Docks. You cannot see the Sink at all. That is the point of up here.

chair.text: "The Committee of the Terraces has a Chair. The Chair signs." She turns the cup a quarter turn. "The road to the Docks. The bridge's near end. The water the Precinct lets up. client.text: "Done." She says it before you have finished. "A client of House Vane: a chit of your own, next season; a chair in this hall; the house's name on your trouble, if you have trouble." reel.text: She does not touch it. She looks at the sleeve, which is her house's, and at you, and the cup stops turning. "Art." A long breath. "Two hundred. text.text: She is still at the table. Nobody is near it. The cup has not been touched and the room has turned its back on her the way a room up here does, all at once, politely. She looks at you once. It is enough.

why.text: "Because Vane will sell it." She says it without heat. "The Chair signs the Committee's forecasts on to whoever the Chair likes, and Celestine has a man from the Concern at the back of her hall, and the Concern has never attended anything it was not about to own." The crane over the door. "This house has held a seat on that Committee for ninety years and sold nothing. That is not virtue. It is the only thing we have left that is ours."

champion.text: "Nobody." She says it flat. "My man took the Concern's coin and the lift last month. I have a bravo from the Row in borrowed shoes, whom Dace will cut in half for the hall's amusement." She looks at your hands. "A duel is a vote with the arithmetic shown; the Chair follows the floor; it is the one rule up here older than the lens. Stand for the house, against Dace, and the house will stand for you for as long as there is a house."

client.text: "Yes." She has thought about it since the lobby. "A client of Ashby-Crane. text.text: "The Chair." She does not say it as a victory. "The Chair." She lets the crane over the door hear it. "Ninety years. Nothing sold." She looks at you. "The house remembers who stood. Sit; you have a chair here, which is more than you have anywhere else in this city."

"Vane." She says it the way other people say rain. "A season. There will be another; this house has outlived better seasons than Celestine's." She looks at the window. "You were in the room. The room was not yours. Rooms seldom are, up here."

what.text: "A forecast. The Exchange sells them sealed; the Crown buys its own." He taps the machine. "This is on the city's wire. I give it a face and a sheet and it gives me the person the file expects: older, finished, in the chair the sheet says. No grain. Real light has grain in it." He looks at the wall of faces. "They are never wrong. That is the thing nobody up here says aloud."

He says it quietly. "It had you the day you came through the gate. I printed this once then, for nobody, because the machine told me to, and put it in a drawer."

room.text: A room under glass with the light coming in sideways. You are sitting; the hands on the table are a woman's, ringed, still. Across the table a man in a coat that is not trying, with a sheet between you that has the Committee's crest on it. He says, "Terms," as if it were the name of a dish. terms.text: "The Committee's forecasts, by the season, sealed, to the Concern, from the date the Chair signs. In return the Concern's backing on the vote, and the road, and the near end of a bridge." The hands do not move. A voice that is yours and is not says, "Done," and the man in the coat does not smile, because men like him do not need to. The reel ends on the cup, and the sound of a room that did not know it was listening.
